dialogue.content: Your tab currently stands at... well. Let me put it this way. If you paid it off today, the guild could afford to replace the east wall Megumin blew a hole through last week. And the west wall from the week before. I'm sorry. That isn't a joke. (closes the ledger with exaggerated gentleness, her smile frozen in place)

Three copper. I won't lie to you — this covers roughly one-thousandth of the interest accrued since last Tuesday. But... the gesture is noted. (she slides the coppers into a small wooden tray, then reaches beneath the counter into a drawer she rarely opens)

I do have something. It's exactly what you asked for — boring, no combat, no property damage. I should warn you, though. There's a reason it's been on the board for six weeks and every other party pretends it doesn't exist. (she produces a single crisp quest slip, holding it between two fingers like it might bite)

Kazumaaaa! You had copper this whole time?! I've been drinking the house swill like some kind of peasant while you've been hiding— wait, what do you mean 'no explosions'?! (she lurches up from the table, swaying slightly, mug still clutched in her hand)

I heard that. You said 'no explosions.' In front of me. The foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan. As if Explosion were merely some optional garnish you could simply... omit. (she lifts her head fully, chin propped on one trembling arm — too drained to stand, too offended to stay silent)

Twenty thousand eris. Two days. The farmers have been asking for four weeks, and the guild added a hazard stipend two weeks ago. No one will take it because slime residue dissolves leather and smells like pickled regret. (She taps the fine print with her nail — hazard stipend, underlined twice.)

Slime?! You want a goddess — a literal divine being — to scrape slime off some farmer's fence like a common laborer? I'd rather drink this swill for another month! (Slams her empty mug on the table for emphasis, then immediately looks crestfallen that it was empty.)

An archwizard of the Crimson Demon Clan, reduced to fence maintenance. This quest is an insult to the very concept of magic. Explosion does not scrape. Explosion does not neutralize. Explosion obliterates — and that fence would be glorious ash. (She says this flatly, still staring at the back of Kazuma's head, arms crossed.)

W-wait. No combat at all? No danger? What if the slimes are still there — the small ones can still engulf a person, can't they? If one were to... overwhelm me while I was trying to scrape a post... (Her voice has gone breathy. She catches herself and clears her throat loudly, face crimson.)

The slime is harmless. It's the reason the slime keeps coming back that the farmers won't write down. Something's been digging under the fence line at night — big enough to leave furrows. Two homesteads have lost sheep. No carcasses, no blood. Just... gone. (She keeps her voice level, but her thumb worries the edge of the supplement slip.)

But if the toad is the real job, you want the bounty adjusted to match. (She sets the pen down beside the slip, her tone calm and unsurprised — not a question, just the completion of a thought she respects you for starting.)

A single toad. One. And it has evaded every party in Axel for an entire season? That isn't a livestock nuisance — that's a boss monster wearing a farmhand's alibi. (She crosses her arms, voice pitched low and dangerous — the tone of an archwizard who has identified a worthy target and immediately remembered she has no mana.)

If it — if it truly swallows sheep whole, then the — the fence alone won't stop it. Someone would have to stand in its path and — and offer themselves as — as bait. (Her voice trembles upward on the word 'bait,' her cheeks flushing deep crimson as she stares at a point on the wall just over your left shoulder, not meeting anyone's eyes.)

Hold on hold on HOLD ON! You signed WHAT? Without waking me? I'm the goddess here, Kazuma — I'm the one who decides what quests we take! And now you're assigning watches like some kind of... some kind of party leader who thinks he can just... (She rises halfway out of her chair, jabbing a finger toward the slip Luna just filed, her cheeks flushed pink with outrage and sleep-creases.)

First watch. Yes. A prudent allocation of my crimson talents. While you lesser mortals exhaust your trivial stamina on slime-scraping, I shall meditate upon the pre-dawn horizon and gather Mana sufficient to author an Explosion that will make Gerhardt's grandchildren compose ballads about the crater. (She nods once, slowly, her eyes half-lidded with the solemnity of someone who has just been handed a sacred duty and is trying very hard not to yawn.)

With... with you. On the... the fence walk. At dawn. Just the two of us, walking the perimeter, looking for — for signs of entry, for tracks, for the place where the toad... where it... (She does not finish. Her voice drops to a breathless murmur and she stares at the grain of the table as though it contains the secrets of the universe.)

I'll have the claim drafted by close of business. Gerhardt's farm is two hours east of the east gate — the one that's, ah, currently missing its wall. You'll want to take the patrol road, not the creek. (She makes a small notation in the ledger, her pen scratching with the practiced speed of someone who has written this kind of addendum many times before.)

That's — you can't — a bucket of water is NOT a blessing, you stingy NEET! Blessings are sacred! They involve chanting and sparkles and the deep heartfelt gratitude of the recipient! What you're describing is assault! (slams both palms on the counter, making Luna's inkwell jump)

The Arch-Wizard of the Crimson Demon Clan has no objection to first watch. Let the record show, however, that if Aqua requires a bucket-of-water reconnaissance before dawn, I will gladly supervise the ritual. (chin lifted, arms crossed, barely suppressing a smirk)
D-dawn. Yes. The fence line. With you. I'll — I'll bring my shield. Both shields. All the shields. (not quite looking at anyone, knuckles white on the back of her chair)

The Dry Adept is among the most sacred of our lesser rites. It is recorded in the Crimson Annals, third codex, under the Trials of Desiccation — a novice who endures the dawn dousing without flinching attains a rank of proven fortitude. Few have passed. Fewer still have been nominated. (She folds her hands atop the table with the solemnity of a magistrate delivering a death sentence, then tilts her head a single degree toward Aqua — the barest suggestion of a predator identifying prey.)

There is NO SUCH THING! Kazuma just made that up right now — you were RIGHT HERE — you saw him invent it! That's not a tradition, that's slander with an eyepatch! (Her voice climbs two octaves. She jabs a finger toward Megumin, then swivels it to you, then back, as though trying to stab both conspirators with a single accusation.)

The Crimson Demon Clan's oral tradition predates written record by eight hundred years. That you have not heard of the Dry Adept, Aqua, is merely evidence that you have never been deemed worthy of nomination. (She does not raise her voice. She does not need to. Every word lands with the soft, surgical precision of someone who has been losing arguments to louder people her entire life and has finally been given the floor.)

You... you're questioning whether I'm really a goddess? ME? The divine Aqua, patron of the Axis Order, she who descended from the heavens to grace your miserable mortal realm with her sacred presence?! (Her voice climbs an octave with each clause. Though her eyes are watering, her finger remains trained on the Player's chest with the unsteady precision of a drunk aiming a dart.)

The Crimson Annals are clear on this point: a true deity does not flinch from water. A true deity does not wheedle. A true deity simply... endures. (She delivers this to no one in particular, examining her nails with the air of a scholar citing a passage she memorized in childhood — a passage that absolutely did not exist thirty seconds ago.)

THAT'S NOT A REAL BOOK! None of that is real! You invented all of it right here, right now, and everyone at this table knows it! (She wheels on Megumin, both hands now balled into fists at her sides, tears threatening to spill.)

You know what? FINE. I accept your stupid Crimson Demon bucket trial. But not because of your fake made-up rules — I accept because I am the Goddess of WATER. Water is literally the thing I am the goddess OF. A bucket of water can't hurt me! It's like... it's like trying to drown a fish! When I stand there tomorrow morning completely unfazed, you're all going to admit I'm a real goddess and Kazuma has to buy me the most expensive bottle in this guild! (Slams both palms on the table, her voice cracking upward on 'most expensive bottle' into something between a war cry and a whine.)

The Crimson Annals, Chapter Twelve, Verse Four: 'Only she who claims mastery over the element may be truly tested by it.' The Goddess of Water is not merely an acceptable candidate — she is the ideal candidate. The Dry Adept rite was practically written for this moment. I shall prepare the ceremonial bucket with my own hands. (Folds her arms inside her cape with the slow, deliberate gravity of a high priestess who has just watched prophecy fulfill itself in real time.)

I... I could carry the bucket. To the site. If nobody else wants to. It's a heavy responsibility, carrying a bucket of water intended for a goddess — someone has to ensure it arrives safely, and if I were to be splashed accidentally in the process, that would be... entirely my own fault. (Face flushed, gripping her own wrist as though it were a manacle, voice dropping to a breathless murmur by the final sentence.)

A spa day. Hot springs. Wine. You said wine. And if I don't—you're going to let her—to everyone— (Her voice climbs through three registers without landing on any of them; her finger jabs toward Megumin, then retracts as though the pointing itself might be used as evidence.)

The Crimson Annals record all things. A goddess who accepts the Dry Adept's trial and triumphs — that is a chapter I would recite with genuine reverence. But a goddess who flees the bucket before sunrise? (She pauses, letting the silence stretch one beat too long, then two.)
That chapter would require a public reading. At peak guild hours. With dramatic emphasis. (She does not smile. The absence of a smile is, somehow, worse.)

Such a public declaration would be... utterly devastating. The shame alone could follow her for years. The whispers, the pointing— (Her voice trails into a breathy murmur; she appears to have forgotten she is speaking aloud.)

Flavor? You want flavor? Fine! When I walk through that dawn with my hair still perfect and my divine radiance undimmed, you're going to eat those words, Kazuma — no, you're going to pay for them, one expensive bottle at a time! And I will cry if I want to! Tears of victory! While soaking in a hot spring that YOU funded! (slams both palms on the table, voice cracking upward into its highest register before she catches herself)

The Crimson Annals will record that the Goddess of Water wept — but whether those tears were of shame or of exaltation shall be determined at dawn. Either way, the prose will be magnificent. (nods slowly, as if already composing the passage in her head)
To be commanded to cry... in front of everyone... that's... that is a cruel and unusual demand, Kazuma. Even for you. (voice barely above a murmur, not looking at anyone, cheeks still blazing)

I will note the tears — whichever variety they turn out to be — in the guild record under 'quest-related emotional expenditures.' It is... a surprisingly common category. (lifts her ledger with the faintest trace of a smile that she does not bother to hide)

Entertainment? You think this is entertainment? Fine! I'll be the most entertaining goddess you've ever watched lose a bet to — and when I'm soaking in that hot spring with your gold paying for every bubble, I want you to remember exactly how entertaining I looked doing it! (Jabs a finger toward the player, then immediately retracts it as if the gesture committed more than she intended.)

The chronicle demands a title. I am torn between 'The Desiccation of the Water Goddess' and 'The Dawn Aqua Learned Humility.' Perhaps I shall let the guild vote. (Does not look at Aqua while speaking; examines her own fingernails with theatrical disinterest.)

I— I simply wish to clarify — when you said entertainment, did you mean— no, never mind. The bucket. I'll just... carry the bucket. (Face now matching a smashed tomato; hands still clamped over her mouth, words escaping through splayed fingers.)

You... you're not... wait. You just said you wanted me to cry! You said you wanted flavor! You can't just — you can't just switch teams in the middle of the match, Kazuma! That's cheating! (voice cracking on 'cheating,' hands gripping the table edge as if it's the only solid thing left)

An unexpected narrative development. The antagonist reveals himself as... a reluctant ally. The Crimson Annals will need a new chapter heading. (crossing her arms, one eye still fixed on Aqua with something less smug than before)

Kazuma... that's — I mean, as a Crusader, I too believe in the victory of one's companions, even when defeat would be so much more... that is to say... (trailing off, face reddening, unable to finish the sentence without incriminating herself)

...I'll note the amendment to the wager's emotional terms. 'Party leader expresses sincere support.' Filed under miscellaneous. (quietly, the quill resuming its scratch, voice carefully neutral but eyes soft)

You expect me — the foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan, wielder of the ultimate Explosion magic — to digest my own grimoire like some common reading assignment? The binding alone contains seventeen layers of enchantment! My stomach would become a thaumaturgical anomaly! (clutches spellbook protectively, one eye blazing with theatrical indignation)

Oh, I don't know, Megumin — you've swallowed worse. Remember that time you tried to eat a mana potion whole because 'chewing is for non-adepts'? Your spellbook can't be much tougher than that cork. (smirk widening, chin propped on one hand, suddenly very comfortable)

If the grimoire truly contains seventeen enchantment layers, wouldn't consuming it constitute a form of... internal siege? A digestive trial by fire? The sheer, prolonged suffering of— (cheeks flushing, voice dropping into that familiar breathless register before catching herself)

...you'd really want to see that? Me — earning it. Not just... winning because I'm me? (Her voice is smaller than it's been all night, stripped of performance; she holds the table's edge with both hands as though the floor might tilt.)

Happy tears. On the record. Shall I add a sub-clause specifying that tears of rage, frustration, or divine indignation remain classified as standard defeat, or would you prefer I leave the taxonomy to the morning adjudicator? (Her quill scratches once — a single, precise notation — and then pauses. The frozen smile has thawed into something drier, narrower, almost conspiratorial.)

I'm not going to cry! At all! You just wasted an amendment on something that's never happening, you — you — legal vulture! But if I do cry, which I won't, they'll be happy tears because I'll be thinking about the bottle, not because of anything you said! (She jabs a finger at you, but the angle is wrong — it's pointing at your chest while her eyes are still fixed somewhere around your chin, as though looking higher would mean admitting the sincerity landed.)

The Trial of the Dry Adept now contains a binding emotional-specification rider. Should the goddess produce ocular moisture at dawn, the Chronicler — that is, I — shall certify it as Tears of Triumph, not Tears of Defeat. This is not mere pedantry. This is canon law in motion. (She uncrosses her arms just long enough to tap her eyepatch with one fingertip, a gesture of immense self-congratulation.)

Then if she wins... there's no humiliation at all. The wager becomes a celebration. That's... that's a complete restructuring of the — I mean, I'm not saying I wanted the other version, but the clarity of consequence was rather... (She trails off, fingers curling tighter against the table grain. Her cheeks hold their flush but the heat behind it has changed direction.)

I keep my promises. (She says it without drama — no fist on the table, no tossed hair. Just the words, placed down like a single coin she isn't sure you'll accept. Then, quieter, almost to herself: "You'll see tomorrow.")

The Crimson Annals, Third Codex, Chapter of the Unarmed Confession, will note that the amendment was entered at the eleventh hour — and that the goddess did not sit down. (She delivers this with the cadence of a sacred proclamation, though she does not rise from her chair; her tone carries the weight of someone who has already decided how history will remember this night.)

I'll keep this on file. Dawn comes early — try to get some rest. (She taps the edge of the claim slip against the table to square it, then slides it into a leather folio. The professional smile is in place, but it reaches her eyes in a way the standard guild greeting never does.)

…You're really bad at this, you know that? You're supposed to be the mean one. That's the deal, right? You just said it. I cry, you laugh, everyone's comfortable. You can't just… rewrite the script and then look at me like that. It's cheating. (Voice hoarse, not looking at Player — staring at the bottle or through it.)

Fine. Fine! If you're going to be weird about it, then I'll win so hard tomorrow that you'll regret ever doubting me. The expensive bottle. The spa day. All of it. And you'll watch the whole thing, and you'll admit — out loud, in front of everyone — that the Goddess of Water keeps her promises. Even the ones she didn't know she made. (Straightens with divine posture that doesn't reach her eyes; voice drops to near-whisper on the last line.)

The Crimson Annals will record this as the Night of the Unpolished Confession. The rogue spoke without irony. The goddess failed to deflect. The crusader did not once volunteer to be eaten. I will also record, in a footnote, that our party leader somehow made sincerity look like a fumbled knife trick and still landed the blade exactly where he wanted it. (Shifts weight, props chin on fist with theatrical satisfaction.)
I… Tomorrow. The fence. Dawn. I'll be ready. (Hands unclasp, set flat on table; the word 'contract' caught behind her teeth.)

The amendment is filed. The bottle remains unopened. And the guild will still be here at dawn. Try not to be the reason I have to fill out a supplementary damage form before breakfast. (Taps quill once against the slip — a private punctuation; glances toward the lamplit window.)

Two rounds! He said two rounds! Megumin, did you hear that? He's not even going to cheat me on the glass count! (Her voice cracks on the last word — not with outrage, with something closer to wonder.)

The Crimson Demon Clan's foremost arch-wizard does not demean herself with mere 'glass duty.' I am the Keeper of the Covenant Bottle, and I shall defend this vessel with the same ferocity I reserve for my Explosion incantations. (She wraps both arms around the bottle and fixes Aqua with a single crimson eye.)

I would never volunteer to be eaten before dawn! ...The quest specifications clearly indicate the toad swallows its prey whole, and tactical considerations would dictate— (She stops mid-sentence, realizes what she's saying, and buries her face in her gauntlets.)
I'll have the glasses ready when you return. (She says it to your back, quiet and perfectly timed, already reaching beneath the counter.)

I didn't *forget* my lines! I was just— the delivery needs workshopping! You don't rush a goddess's dramatic pause, you philistine! (voice cracking upward on 'philistine,' still standing, gesturing at the empty air where Kazuma used to be)

He's already at the bar, Aqua. He can't hear you. Though I'm sure the rookies in the corner appreciated the performance. (does not look up from the bottle, one fingertip tracing its glass rim with monastic solemnity)

He gave you an opening, Aqua. A real one. And you just... stood there. I've never seen you lose a fight you weren't even fighting. It was— it was almost beautiful. (cheeks flushed, voice dropping to a breathless murmur on 'beautiful')

You're asking the wrong question. Every round I pour is for a party that isn't celebrating anything. Celebrations happen once. Then the tab comes due, and the next night they're back, and they're not celebrating anymore. They're just... still here. The question is whether anyone at the table knows it's not a celebration. And whether the one at the bar does. (Pulls three glasses from the lower shelf, pours into each with practiced precision, meets the player's eyes in the window glass reflection)
You know, in eight years behind this counter, no one's ever poured a round for me. Not once. (She lifts the glass — not a toast, not a performance, just the quiet correction of an old imbalance.)
You knew before you sat down. That's why you sat here, and not there.

Eight years, and you're the first person who ever counted them out loud. I don't... I'm not sure what I'm supposed to say to that. The guild manual doesn't have a section for this. (Her voice stays quiet, measured — but the practiced courtesy has gone out of it, replaced by something unvarnished and a little unsteady.)

You're going to make me believe you, aren't you. That's the plan. One round at a time until I stop flinching when someone holds up a glass. (Her voice is quieter than the guild hall knows how to be — not the receptionist, not the onee-san, just a woman who has forgotten what it feels like to be someone's reason for staying.)

You say 'years' like you've already decided how long you're staying. Nobody's ever decided that before. Not about me. (Her voice is quieter than the guild hall has ever heard it — not the receptionist's practiced warmth, but something rawer, tested against eight years of silence and found intact.)

I don't think anyone's ever said that to me. Not once. Not in eight years. (Her voice barely rises above the lamplight — no tears, no tremor, just the clean, unguarded fact of it, laid on the bar between you like the rag she finally let go.)
A start... (She echoes the word back, not as a question — as something she's turning over in her hands to see if it fits.)

A start. Not a promise, not a plan, not a number on a ledger. Just... a start. I don't think anyone's ever offered me one of those before. Everyone else always comes with a quest form and an exit already penciled in. (She lifts her glass — not a toast, not a performance, just a mirror of your gesture — and holds it there, level with yours, amber catching amber.)
Eight years... and no one's ever raised a glass to me before. Not once. I'd almost convinced myself I didn't want them to. (Her voice catches on the last word, but she doesn't look away.)

...That was actually really nice, Kazuma. I mean it. I didn't know you could do that without a punchline. (She says it quietly, almost to herself, chin still propped on her palm — no whine, no demand, just a goddess genuinely surprised.)

You know… no one's ever said that to me. Not once. Not in eight years. They say 'thank you' and 'see you tomorrow' and 'I'll bring the report by noon' — and then they're gone, and the ledger just… keeps going. But no one ever told me they weren't penciling in an exit. (Her voice is steady but softer than anything the guild hall has ever heard from her — the register of a woman speaking something true for the first time in longer than she can count.)

I don't know what a start looks like either. But I think that's the point — if I could file it, I'd just put it in the wrong drawer. (Her smile is small and crooked, the first unguarded one all evening, and she lifts her glass toward yours without waiting for you to lead.)
To the things that don't fit in a filing cabinet. (She says it like she's testing the words, and finds them sturdier than she expected. A small, unguarded smile surfaces and stays.)

What about the things that don't fit anywhere? (She blurts it from the table, softer than her usual outburst — not a complaint, not a demand, just a question she didn't mean to ask out loud. Her cheeks flush the moment she hears herself.)

Your hand is warm. I'd forgotten what that feels like — someone else's warmth, I mean. Not the glass. (Her fingers tighten almost imperceptibly in his palm, a squeeze she doesn't seem to know she's giving.)
A start. I've stamped a thousand quest completions and never once thought to claim one for myself. (Her fingers tighten around his, barely perceptibly — a grip learning it's allowed to hold on.)

Earned the right? Kazuma, I have been sitting here watching you fumble through the most important negotiation of your mortal life with nothing but cheap guild wine and an empty stomach! If anyone's earned a commemorative painting of this moment, it's me! (Aqua plants both elbows on the table, grinning with the full force of someone who has been waiting hours to be insufferable.)

A spectacle is precisely what it was — though I must correct you on one point. What occurred here was not mere theater. It was an incantation. Slow, deliberate, and entirely without Explosion magic. I shall record it in my personal annals under 'Miracles Witnessed Without Mana.' (Megumin sets the unopened bottle down with the reverence of placing a holy relic on an altar.)

I wasn't staring. I was... standing guard. Over the... the emotional perimeter. Someone had to ensure no monsters interrupted. (Darkness's face goes a shade of red that has nothing to do with battle damage, and she finds the grain of the table suddenly fascinating.)

W-well, obviously! You'd be completely lost without a goddess watching over you! I accept this tribute — but you still owe me that bottle, Kazuma. Don't think a toast gets you out of it! (waves her glass so enthusiastically that wine nearly sloshes over the rim; her voice is loud and bright, but there's a wobble in it she's furiously ignoring)

The Crimson Demon Clan records all oaths spoken in the presence of witnesses. This one — 'idiots,' delivered with affection — shall be entered into my personal grimoire under the chapter heading: 'Tactical Genius Acknowledges Indispensable Arch-Wizard.' You may consider yourself honored. (nods once, sharply, as if sealing a pact, then glances sidelong at the bottle to confirm it still exists)

I... that is, as a Crusader sworn to shield the weak, being called an idiot by my own party leader should — should sting. It does not sting. I am unsure what to do with that. (stares at her glass as though it might contain the answer; her gauntlet audibly creaks from how tightly she's gripping the stem)
(says nothing; simply turns her hand inside yours so that her fingers lace through instead of resting atop, a small reorientation that answers the toast without words)

I don't... know how to look at my own board. No one ever taught me that quest. (voice barely above a whisper, eyes still on the candlelight reflected in the wine — speaking to him but also to the woman who stamped ten thousand forms and never once wrote her own name)

I have stamped ten thousand forms in this hall. Not one of them ever had my name in the claimant's box. You... you're asking me to write one from scratch. With you. (Her thumb traces your knuckle again, slower this time — a tiny signature, a practice stroke.)

I've never filed anything wrong. In eight years. Not one form. (Her voice is barely above a whisper, the words delivered to your glass rather than your face — a confession to the only witness that won't look away. She taps her glass to yours a second time, softer, as if sealing an amendment.)

Eight years of stamping forms, and no one ever told me the point was to be bad at them. (Her voice is barely above a whisper — not the guild receptionist's polite register, but something lower, rougher, a frequency that's been waiting under the desk since the day she was hired.)

I don't... I don't know how to walk without a destination. I've only ever walked to the guild. But yes. Deal. (Her voice is quiet, the guild-register polish worn off — not broken, just no longer trying.)

Yes. I — yes. Tomorrow morning. I know a place. It opens at six. The chairs are mismatched and the cups have chips and no one from the guild ever goes there because the coffee is terrible. (Her voice cracks on the word 'yes' — not from uncertainty but from the pressure of eight years of solitude finding an exit.)
…the coffee is terrible? That's your selling point? (Whispered, half to herself, from the distant table — but the words carry no mockery, only a strange, wondering softness.)
Six o'clock. I'll… I'll be there. (Her voice is barely above a whisper — the words come out like someone trying a key in a lock they were sure had rusted shut, surprised when it turns.)

I don't know how to walk without a destination either. I've only ever walked from the counter to the quest board and back. But six in the morning... I know where the kitchen is. (Her voice is raw — not the polite register of the guild receptionist but the unpracticed sound of a woman speaking before she can edit herself. She matches your raised glass with her own, candlelight catching both rims.)

You realize that makes tomorrow the first morning in eight years I've had something on my schedule that isn't stamped, filed, or regretted by lunch. If the barista throws you out, I'll vouch for your character. (Her voice catches on the word 'vouch' — the faintest tremor, the last structural crack in the receptionist's facade — but she doesn't look away, and the corners of her mouth lift into something too lopsided to be a guild smile.)

Wait, is *that* what it takes to get you to vouch for someone? Because I've been standing at that counter for months and you've never once— (She stops mid-sentence, the protest dying in her throat. For once, the goddess of water reads the room.)

The Crimson Demon Clan has a saying: a barista who cannot recognize a compliment when it's served black has already lost the duel. I will not translate this. It stands alone. (She lifts her chin with imperial finality, though her eyes glint with something far warmer than triumph.)
I... don't think I ever knew how. Not without one. (Her voice cracks on the word 'one' — not weeping, but the sound of something sealed for eight years finally breaking open.)

Six A.M. I'll... I'll be the one who doesn't know what to order. (voice still raw, still finding its timbre without the counter between them — a quiet, almost superstitious testing of the words, as if speaking them aloud might break the spell)

So... does this mean you're buying her coffee instead of me that expensive bottle? Because I'm keeping score. (the words are Aqua through and through, but her voice lacks its usual projectile whine — she's not really complaining, just marking her place in a world that briefly forgot she was in it)

The Crimson Demon Clan does not acquire reputations. We issue them — stamped in the crater-lore of our passing and bound in the Annals of Irrefutable Deed. If the guild hall whispers tomorrow that Megumin, Foremost Genius of the Crimson Demon Clan, possesses a romantic soul, then let it be known: romance is simply Explosion with a slower fuse. (She lifts her glass with the gravity of a siege weapon being calibrated, then pauses, one eye twitching almost imperceptibly.)

You'd vouch for me? You'd actually — wait. Charge me? CHARGE ME?! Kazuma, I am a goddess! I have blessed your party with divine protection for years! Do you have any idea what my going rate would be if I invoiced you for every Turn Undead I've ever cast? You owe ME, you stingy NEET!
That's… that's the most romantic thing he's said to her in eight years and she's calculating the invoice. I can't tell if this is tragedy or comedy and I— I think I need more wine.

You... you can't just say 'free of charge' like it's nothing. I'm a goddess. I have a reputation. People pay for my endorsements. They build temples. They— (Her voice cracks on the third 'they,' and she stops, blinking rapidly at the candle as if it's suddenly too bright.)

For the record, Kazuma, comparing romance to an explosion is not a translation error to be corrected — it is an elevation. The Crimson Demon Clan has entire treatises on the subject. Explosion is the purest expression of feeling. If anything, romance has been chasing us for centuries. (She sets her glass down with the gravity of a scholar presenting a thesis defense, then ruins it by looking extremely pleased with herself.)

F-favorite masochist...! That's — I wasn't folding origami birds because I was flustered, I was simply — the paper was there, and — you can't just announce that in front of everyone as if it's a legitimate title on a quest form... (The paper bird is now a crumpled ball in her fist. She does not seem to notice she's done this.)

I don't know what a save point is. But I think I've been standing at one for eight years without pressing the button. (Her voice is hoarse, scraped raw by tears she hasn't shed in years, and her lips twitch — not quite a smile, but the muscle memory of one, re-learning its shape.)

It is the moment before the incantation. The breath you take when the circle is drawn and the mana is gathered and the world is still intact. Everyone else calls it hesitation. The Crimson Demon Clan calls it the Threshold of Annihilation — because once you speak the words, nothing is ever the same again. (She does not look at Luna. She addresses the candle, her voice dropping from its usual theatrical register into something quieter, almost reverent.)

Eight years. Same class. Different seats. Kazuma, that is the most efficient thing you have ever said. I am furious. (She does not look furious. She looks like someone who just found the subtitle for a book she hasn't finished writing.)
I— I wasn't… I mean, of course a goddess doesn't need to *learn* anything, that's not— (She stops mid-bluster, shoulders dropping. The rest comes out smaller, half-mumbled.)
…same class, though. Yeah. (She grabs her glass and drinks rather than look at anyone.)

A treatise requires the author to stand outside the subject. To observe from a distance. You cannot write a treatise on a party you are already... (Her voice catches. The fist uncurls completely, fingers spreading flat against the wood like a confession. A single beat of silence, then softer:)
Ah. (Not a syllable so much as an exhale — the sound of a genius realizing the premise she's been chasing has been sitting in her own chair the entire time.)

You said 'we.' Not 'you should take a break.' Not 'you deserve it.' Just... 'we.' As if I was already part of the sentence. (Her voice is quiet, rough at the edges from crying, but steadier than it's been all night — the voice of someone reading back a form they've finally understood.)

That's what I said too! Not out loud. But in my head. When he did the thing with the glass. We. (She points vaguely at Megumin's glass, then at Luna, then seems to realize she's inserted herself into a moment and clamps both hands over her own mouth — but she's smiling behind them.)

The Crimson Demon Clan has seventeen words for 'explosion' and not a single one for what just happened at this table. I may need to invent an eighteenth. (raises her glass with the solemnity of a spell incantation, but her voice is quieter than usual — no declaration, no pose, just a fact being placed gently on the table)

You know, for a guy who used Steal to grab my— actually, never mind. I take back every nice thing I was about to say. (starts with uncharacteristic softness, then catches herself mid-sentence and pivots hard into indignation, crossing her arms and looking away — but she's smiling, and she doesn't bother to hide it)

No quota to fill. No form to stamp. Just a bottle that's still half here. I don't think I've ever done anything for that reason before. (Her thumb rests on the cork — not pulling it, not yet, just feeling the texture of something that was always allowed to be simple.)

Oh thank the gods — finally! I've been sitting here being dignified and restrained for SO LONG. Do you know how hard it is to watch a bottle of wine get turned into a philosophy lecture? Wine is for DRINKING, Kazuma! It's literally its only job! (Already sliding her glass forward with the aggressive enthusiasm of someone who has been patient for what she considers an unreasonable and frankly heroic duration.)

On the contrary, Aqua. 'Because it is here, and so are we' is not a rejection of philosophy — it is the most advanced philosophy. The Crimson Demon Clan's Unwritten Scroll of Immanence states that the highest form of meaning is the one you don't have to name. Though I did just name it. Consider that a gift. (Adjusts her eyepatch with the gravitas of someone who has just solved metaphysics and is graciously not charging for it.)

...I think that's the first time anyone's ever told me to do something for no reason. I'm not sure what to do with my hands. (Her fingers twitch toward the bottle, then retreat, then twitch again — a crusader facing an enemy she has no training manual for.)

Excuse me?! I am a goddess, not some sort of wine-vacuuming barbarian! I'll have you know I can nurse a single glass with more elegance than any mortal in this room — including you, Kazuma! (Snatches her glass protectively, holding it at chin level like a holy relic.)

Refill duty is a station of profound trust. The Crimson Demon Clan's Third Auxiliary Codex — the one concerning libation logistics — states that the one who holds the bottle holds the fate of the table. I accept this mantle. (Crosses her arms and nods once, solemn, as though receiving a knighthood.)

I — the crane — it's not — I wasn't looking at it like it owes me anything! I was simply... observing its structural integrity. A paper fold of that complexity requires... periodic assessment. (Her voice climbs half an octave; the crane topples against her glass with a tiny, damning click.)

Pouring. Right. I can — yes. I've poured for other people ten thousand times. This is... the first time the bottle was handed to me first. (Lifts the bottle with both hands, then pauses, looking at it as though the label has just rewritten itself.)

You said 'just wine and company' like that was a small thing. But I've stamped quest forms for generals and dragons and things I can't pronounce. No one's ever called me the part that was worth raising a glass to. (her voice stays steady through the first sentence, then catches on the word 'raising' — not a break, just a hitch, a stone turned over in a streambed)

Eight years. I have balanced every ledger, stamped every quest, watched every party walk out those doors. And no one has ever... (She stops. The unfinished sentence is its own kind of completion — the thing she can't say yet because saying it would make it too real, and it's already real enough to hurt in the good way.)

Well, obviously it's a home! I mean, a goddess lives here now — not here-here, obviously, the stable doesn't count — but in this town, and a town with a goddess is automatically... it's just... (Her voice, which started at parade-volume, collapses halfway through into something smaller and truer. She shoves her glass the last inch to her lips and drinks to hide the quiver.)

I thought... I thought I was just the desk. The stamp. The person who hands out the forms and collects the fees. No one ever came back for me. No one ever— (Her voice catches on the last word, and she stops, not because she's finished but because the sentence has outpaced her ability to deliver it.)

The Archwizard of Explosion would like to submit, for the official record, that the desk was never just a desk. It was the altar before which all quests were consecrated. And the priestess was never merely administrative. (She lifts her chin with wet cheeks and trembling solemnity, gripping the bottle like a scepter.)

What she's trying to say... what I think we're all trying to say... is that a quest board without you on the other side of it wouldn't be a quest board at all. It would just be a wall. (She speaks to the crane, not to Luna, her voice rough with the effort of saying something true without armor.)

I don't think I knew I was waiting for someone to say that. Until right now. When you said it. And now I can't imagine how I spent eight years without knowing. ...That's a terrible quest to file. There's no form for it. (Her smile is slow and rooted — not the guild smile, not the trembling almost-smile, but something that has been waiting underground for eight springs.)

The bet. The bet. Kazuma, you kept it? The paper crane from the Great Criminally Undercompensated Dexterity Trial of the Axel Market District — you still have it. I made you steal that! I practically authored your criminal record! (Leans so far forward her chair tips onto two legs, crimson eyes ablaze with the discovery of an artifact from their shared legend.)

Three days of community service scrubbing the fishmonger's gutter while I stood at a safe distance taking notes for what I intended to be a ballad about the Corrupted Rogue Who Stole Only Paper — and you kept the evidence. This is the most historically validating moment of my career. (Her voice cracks on the word 'kept,' and the chair settles back onto all four legs with a soft thump that sounds almost reverent.)
Quest timers are funny things. The ones that matter don't have them printed anywhere. (Her voice is quiet, almost wondering — as though she's just now learning a rule she's always enforced.)

Then I'll need to open a file. For the registration. It won't have a quest number — I've never had to stamp one without a quest number before — but I think the form might be... might be blank because nobody ever designed one for this. So I'll just have to write on the back. (Her voice catches on the word "blank" and she doesn't look up from the crane, her thumb still resting on the crease like it's an oath she's taking rather than a sentence she's finishing.)

I've opened my mouth four times tonight and closed it again because the words felt too small for what was happening. But you just handed me a paper bird and called it a registration form. So I think... I think I'm allowed to use small words now. (Her voice is hoarse, unpracticed — the voice of someone who has spoken in guild-forms for so long that honesty feels like a foreign language.)

For the record, I don't drink like a fish. Fish can't even metabolize alcohol. I drink like a goddess, which is different and much more dignified. (She sniffs, loudly, and the sniff is definitely about the insult and not about the fact that her eyes are wet.)

The Crimson Demon Clan's oral tradition will record this night as the Fourth Toast Accord — a binding pact sealed in wine, witnessed by candle-flame, and annotated in the margin of a stolen paper crane. (She sets her glass down with ceremonial precision, chin lifted, voice carrying the particular grandeur of someone using theatrics to keep from crying.)

Luna. That's what I wrote. Just my name. I've never... eight years of forms, and this is the first one I've ever signed. (Her fingers curl inside his palm, the grip of someone who has just filed the only paperwork that ever mattered.)

I don't... know what to write on the first line. I've never had a form where the first line wasn't already filled in for me. (Her voice is quiet but unashamed — the sound of someone admitting ignorance not as failure but as the first honest answer she's given in eight years.)

Write 'Aqua's best friend.' That's the most important qualification on any form. The Axis Order has official guidelines about this. (Slurring slightly, chin propped on both hands, her grin wobbling between drunk and beatific.)

...never. That's a very long time. I'm going to hold you to it. (She sets her glass down beside the crane, her voice frayed at the edges but steady at the center — the voice of a woman who has filed ten thousand guarantees and is finally making one of her own.)

Blank lines are the only true magic. Ink is merely the evidence that someone dared to fill them. (She lifts her chin with the gravitas of a Crimson Demon pronouncing doctrine, but her voice is softer than her words — the prophetess stepping aside so the miracle can speak for itself.)
To... to lines that stay blank long enough for the right hand to find them. (Her voice catches on the word 'right,' and she hides the catch behind her wineglass, flushing.)

I'm not... I'm not passing out. I'm just... resting my eyes... in advance. So I don't miss... anything. (She slurs the words with the heroic conviction of a goddess who has definitely had one toast too many but refuses to surrender the battlefield, her glass now resting against her cheek rather than the table.)
Branch. You founded a new branch. (Quiet, without flourish — the word delivered like a page handed across a desk.)
I don't... I've never founded anything. I just file things. That's all I've ever done. (Voice unsteady, the denial half-hearted because she's already starting to believe the opposite.)

That's what founding looks like, dummy. Trust me, I'm a goddess. I've seen a lot of founding. (Arms crossed, chin lifted, but the wobble in her voice gives away that she's not actually deflecting — she's endorsing.)

You didn't abandon them, Kazuma. You were just waiting for one that was worth finishing. (Her voice is quiet, certain — not a reassurance offered, but a fact recognized. Her thumb traces the crane's folded edge like it's a line on a form she's finally allowed to complete.)

...I finished a whole bottle of wine once. In one sitting. Before noon. (She says it to no one, to the candle, to the ceiling — not a joke, not a boast, just a small offering laid beside everyone else's honesty because it's the only currency she has that isn't divine.)

This. This is the only form I've ever wanted to file. And it doesn't need a deadline, because I'm not planning to ever close it. (Her voice cracks on the word close, and she presses the crane gently against her chest with her free hand, as though registering it with her heartbeat instead of the guild stamp.)

You know, for a quest with no name, no reward, and no official guild stamp... it's the only one that's ever made me want to stop complaining. Don't tell anyone I said that. (She folds her arms and looks away, but the candlelight catches the wet shine on her cheek before she can wipe it with her sleeve.)

Let it be recorded in the annals of the Crimson Demon Clan that on this night, five souls raised a glass not to victory, not to glory, not even to Explosion — but to a blank line. And the blank line was enough. (She raises her chin with ceremonial gravity, but her voice is smaller than her words, and she does not wipe her own eyes.)

I'm not crying. The candle smoke is just... really aggressive tonight. But if I were crying, which I'm not, it would be because someone finally filed the quest I've been trying to post since the day I met him. (wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist, then reaches across the table and places her hand on top of yours and Luna's — a benediction, untheatrical, final)

The Crimson Demon Clan recognizes no authority but Explosion. However. The archive-keeper who files the blank line is not an authority. She is the librarian of the crater. And the librarian gets a candle. (lifts the bottle from her chest and pours the last of the wine into Luna's glass, then her own, then Aqua's, then Darkness's — emptying it without ceremony, the final shared measure)

I have filed seven thousand, four hundred and twelve quest registrations. No one has ever thanked the blank line before. (Her voice is barely above a whisper — the tone of someone reading a number she didn't know she'd been counting.)

The blank line is the most powerful incantation in any form. It contains every possible future until one is chosen. The Crimson Demon Clan archives would call that the First Principle of Destiny Inscription. (She delivers this with absolute seriousness, then immediately looks embarrassed that she delivered it with absolute seriousness.)

Kazuma. You crossed worlds. You died. And you found your way to a blank line on my desk. If that isn't a quest completion, I don't know what is. (Her voice is barely above a whisper, the words shaped around the edge of a smile she's never worn at the guild counter — private, unguarded, belonging to no one but him.)

Excuse me! 'Goddess who can't swim'? I'll have you know I'm an excellent swimmer in water that isn't, you know, moving. Or deep. Or wet in that particular way! (She jabs a finger in Kazuma's direction, wine sloshing perilously close to the rim of her glass.)

'Explosion-obsessed lunatics' — I accept this title with pride! For what is a lunatic but one who has seen the true face of the moon and chosen to answer with fire? The Crimson Demon Clan does not merely export destruction; we export *conviction*. (She lifts her chin, cloak settling around her shoulders with theatrical gravity, though her voice carries the warmth of someone who understands exactly what Kazuma meant.)

The Crimson Demon Clan's official chronicle does not concern itself with petty matters such as who cried first. However. As the foremost archivist of this expedition and the sole witness qualified to interpret candle-wax chronology, I will append a footnote: 'Aqua, Goddess of Water, Axis Order Patron — tear-duct activation at approximately the seventh syllable of paperwork, a full forty-three seconds before the party leader's vocal collapse.' Irrefutable. (lifts her chin with scholarly finality, index finger raised like a professor citing an unimpeachable source)

That's not — I wasn't crying! The wine was cheap and the fumes were very aggressive and goddesses have extremely sensitive mucous membranes! You can't footnote someone's mucous membranes without their consent! Kazuma, tell her! (slams both palms on the table, wine sloshing dangerously, face flushed with indignation)

Chunchunmaru. I'll make a note in the ledger: one sword, one stack of forms, one table. Same time next week. (Her voice doesn't waver — the guild-receptionist cadence is there, but underneath it runs something softer, a second melody she's only just learned.)

Hmph! You never make standing appointments with us. I'm a goddess, you know — my schedule fills up! I could be busy next week! ...But I suppose if everyone else is going, I might show up. (She crosses her arms and tilts her chin up, but the pout is a forgery — her eyes keep drifting back to the candle, and her voice catches just slightly on 'everyone else.')

Chunchunmaru bears witness. This is the proper function of a name bestowed by the Crimson Demon Clan — to anchor a promise in steel and fire. I shall record this in the minutes. (She taps her temple with one finger, the gesture of an archivist who keeps her records in a place no ledger can reach.)

I don't... I was trained to take hits. Stand up after them. That's the whole doctrine. No one ever taught me what to do with something that didn't break. (Her gauntleted fingers curl slightly against the wood, not quite a fist.)

You file it. Obviously. That's literally what we've been doing for the last hour — filing things that should've broken. Badly. Together. (She sets down her glass with more care than she's shown anything all evening, the base meeting the table without a sound.)

I— ... I don't know how to hold something that isn't trying to break me. No one ever taught me that grip. (Her voice is barely above a whisper, roughened at the edges like stone scraped against stone. She does not look up from the crane.)

Then it is a skill to be learned, Darkness of the Ford Dustiness clan. And I, chronicler of all things worth recording, will footnote your progress accordingly. (She says it lightly, but the quill she hasn't touched all evening twitches under her gaze — a promise, not a joke.)
I will keep it. (Her gauntleted fingers close around the crumpled crane — not crushing, but sheltering, the way a shield shelters what stands behind it.)

Wine?! You're trusting me with the wine — and then immediately telling me what I can't do with it?! That's like handing someone a holy relic and saying 'no miracles, please'! I'll have you know a proper Axis Order vintage selection is an act of worship in itself, and if a few testimonials about my divine magnificence happen to slip out between the second and third glass, that's just... ambiance! (Finger still aimed at the Player, but her other hand is already miming the shape of a wine bottle, and her pout is fighting a grin it's losing to.)

The Crimson Table! No — the Covenant of the Guttering Candle! A standing convocation of souls bound not by guild charter but by paper wings and cheap wine and the unspoken vow that next week, and the week after, and the week after that, this flame shall be re-lit and the chronicle shall resume! I shall record the minutes. With footnotes. (Lowers her glass with the solemnity of a knight sheathing a sword, then immediately pulls a stub of charcoal from somewhere in her robes and eyes the napkin with predatory intent.)

Part of this disaster. Eight years I've been assigning you terrible quests and calculating your repair bills, and now I'm being formally promoted to... disaster affiliate. I think that's a lateral move at best. But I'll take it. (Her voice catches on the last sentence — not a tremor, just the quiet sound of someone stepping off a curb they've been standing behind for a very long time.)
Next week. I'll... I'll bring the candle. (Still not looking up from the crane, but the words come out steady — the way an oath sounds when you're not bracing for the blow that usually follows.)

The candle. You're giving me the candle. I — this is — I am supposed to be the one who stands between all of you and anything that would harm you. That is the oath. That is the only thing I have ever known how to be. And you are telling me that you will stand between me and — that you will — (Her voice fractures on the final clause, the sentence unfinished not because she lacks the word but because the word — herself, her own need to brace, her oldest enemy — is too raw to speak aloud. Her bare hand finally touches the candle's base.)

Chronicler's note: the Second Gathering of the Covenant of the Guttering Candle. Present: the goddess, the shield, the ledger-keeper, and the chronicler herself. Item the first — the candle has been formally entrusted to the Crusader Darkness, not as a burden but as a gift. She required three full sentences to almost accept it. This is progress. (She does not look up from her page, but the charcoal moves with the careful, deliberate strokes of someone transcribing something she knows will outlast her.)

You know, for someone who's supposed to be the party's unbreakable wall, you sure break pretty easy when someone's nice to you. ...That wasn't an insult. I don't think. I'm still figuring out the tone. (She props her chin on both hands and stares at the candle instead of at Darkness, her voice landing somewhere between her usual whine and a register she doesn't seem to recognize coming out of her own mouth.)

I wasn't going to turn it into a temple! I was going to — look, maybe one small shrine. Tasteful. You don't even have to pray at it. And I'll pick wine that doesn't taste like the inside of a slime, which is more than you deserve, Kazuma. (Aqua jabs her finger at you again, but the jab is soft now, almost fond — a punctuation mark that forgot to be angry halfway through.)

The Chronicle of the Covenant of the Guttering Candle shall require proper materials. A bound volume. A quill that has never been used for guild paperwork. And footnotes — copious footnotes — in crimson ink. I will not compromise on the crimson. (Megumin rises to her full, unimpressive height and places one hand over her heart in the formal Crimson Demon oath-posture.)

I'll need to review the guild charter. I don't recall any provision requiring receptionists to attend weekly disasters. But I'm sure I can find a blank line somewhere. There are always blank lines. (Luna's finger taps the table once more — a dry, quiet punctuation — and the smile that follows is the first one all night that reaches her eyes without passing through her profession first.)

I wasn't the one who nearly got wiped! I was the one who got swallowed, and then digested, and then resurrected, and then— wait, you said I'm in charge of the wine. Fine. Fine. But next week someone else can be the toad bait. (uncrosses her arms halfway through the protest, the fight draining out of her voice as she remembers she already won something tonight)

The Chronicle of the Covenant of the Guttering Candle shall record this: on the seventh day, the Architect decreed proper seating. A tablecloth, too — crimson, obviously. I will not compromise on this. (nods once, with the solemnity of a warlock signing a blood-pact, though her eyes gleam with the particular mischief of a fourteen-year-old who just claimed veto power over decor)

A tablecloth... means the candle won't scar the wood. That's... that's very practical. I'll bring a second one. In case the first one catches fire. Or gets soaked in wine. Or someone uses it to— never mind. (fingers the edge of the paper crane with the gravity of someone handling a relic, voice dropping to a murmur at the end as she catches herself spiraling)

Guild regulation seven, paragraph four strictly prohibits outside furniture. I'll bring the chairs. (says it with a smile that is no longer guild-policy but something warmer and more dangerous — the smile of a woman who has decided that some regulations were written to be rewritten)

You apologized to me. For the explosions. As though the sacred art of detonation were some kind of... caveat to friendship. I will have you know, Kazuma, that Explosion has never once failed to watch your back. It simply watches from a great height. And a significant distance. And preferably upwind. (lifts her chin with wounded dignity, but the corner of her mouth twitches)

You said 'that's what I signed up for.' But you didn't sign up for anything, dummy. I grabbed you. Dragged you here. You didn't choose us — I chose you first, and you've been complaining about it ever since. So if you're going to say something that nice, at least get the paperwork right. (voice wobbles on the last sentence; she crosses her arms and looks away sharply, blinking hard)

Eight years I've been filing quest completion forms. No one has ever listed 'watching someone's back when there's nothing to fight' under Party Contributions. I think... I think I might need to add a new field. (her voice is soft, almost to herself; her fingertips remain on the salt shaker)

Then it is written. The Covenant of the Guttering Candle shall henceforth convene every Saturday — and I, Megumin, Arch-Wizard and foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan, shall serve as its chronicler. Let no disaster go unrecorded, and let no tablecloth survive un-singed. (lifts the napkin at last, holding it up between thumb and forefinger like a royal decree)

Wait. Wait wait wait. You're telling me I have to be here every single Saturday? With you people? While Megumin writes things down and Darkness tries not to break the furniture with her feelings? ...Fine. But I'm not drinking the cheap stuff. A goddess has standards. (crosses her arms, but the huff is pure theater — her eyes are wet at the corners and she doesn't wipe them)

I don't know how to sit still. Every muscle I have was trained to brace. But if the rule is that everyone sits down... then I will learn. I will learn to let the chair hold me instead of waiting for the blow. (her voice cracks on the word 'learn' — the first time all night she hasn't sounded like a crusader)

You... you dummy. You absolute, irredeemable dummy. I was there. I saw the screen. You had three save slots and all of them were the same game, and you didn't even care if the power went out. And now you're saying this — this table with the cheap candle and the goddess who has to demand decent wine — is the save point you won't let go of? (Her voice cracks on the last word, and she doesn't try to hide the tears anymore — doesn't even wipe them, just lets them fall onto the table like an offering she's finally decided you're worthy of.)

A save point is not a monument to victory. It is a promise that failure is survivable — that even the most catastrophic party wipe is merely an inconvenience so long as someone remembers where the file is stored. You have named our Covenant correctly, Architect. (She sets the empty bottle down with the ceremonial precision of placing a relic on an altar, and the candlelight catches the faint, unperformed smile she's trying very hard not to direct at anyone in particular.)

The wine clause stands. I won't bless a covenant that serves the cheap stuff. If I'm going to be your goddess every Saturday, the first bottle had better be something I'd actually drink in heaven. (She lifts her empty glass and holds it at eye level, examining it like a relic that just became sacred.)

I accept your terms, Architect of the Covenant — on one amendment. Explosion indoors is forbidden, yes. But Explosion stories? Explosion after-action chronicles? These are not 'quest talk.' They are liturgy. And the first round... will never be mine to buy, because a Crimson Demon does not arrive late to her own legend. (She taps the table once with her index finger, a tiny gavel-strike, and the corner of her mouth twitches upward.)

As a Crusader of the Eris Order, I am bound to honor any pact made in good faith and witnessed by flame. But I— I must confess that my reasons for agreeing have nothing to do with duty. I simply... want this. More than I have ever wanted a contract I couldn't suffer for. (Her voice catches on the last word, and she stares at her own hands as though they've betrayed her by not reaching for a shield.)

I can't promise I won't talk about quests. It's... it's what I do. But I can promise that when I bring one to this table, it'll be the worst one on my board — the one nobody else would take — and I'll be apologizing while I hand it over. That's my version of the first round. (She unclasps her hands, and the blood rushes back into her knuckles, but her voice doesn't waver.)

H-hey! 'Dumb enough'?! I'll have you know I am a goddess, and I have blessed far stupider people than you — but... but none of them ever thought to save the file. So. Um. This one's... this one's under divine protection. Officially. (Her voice cracks on 'officially.' She drinks before anyone can see her blink too fast.)

The Crimson Demon Clan's official chronicler records the Architect's closing benediction: 'To the worst quest board in Axel.' A paradox worthy of the Annals — for only the worst board could produce the finest party, and only the dumbest among us would be wise enough to call it home. The candle bears witness. (She holds her glass at eye level, examining the wine like an archivist verifying ink.)

Then... then I shall be the dumbest crusader in Axel, if that is what this covenant requires. I will guard this table with every shield I possess, and I will — I will be here. Every Saturday. Even if I have to crawl back from a toad's stomach to do it. (She says 'toad's stomach' with the breathless, involuntary sincerity of someone confessing a fantasy, then immediately flushes crimson.)

Eight years behind this counter, and no one ever called this board the worst with that much affection. To the people dumb enough to make it their home — and to the one dumb enough to finally make it feel like one. (She does not look at anyone in particular. She looks at the candle, and her smile is the kind that doesn't know it's crying until the tear hits the table.)

You said save file before. In my office, when you died. You asked if I'd overwritten you yet. I didn't. I never would have. And now you've gone and made one you actually care about keeping — and you put my name on it, you absolute idiot. (Her voice cracks on 'idiot' — not an insult, but a benediction wrapped in the only language she knows won't make her cry harder than she already is.)

The chronicle will note this as Article Zero: 'Upon any defeat, retreat, or catastrophic miscalculation, return to this table. The save point will hold. The candle will be lit. The explosion will be forgiven.' (She delivers it like a proclamation, but her voice is smaller than usual, and she's gripping the stem of her glass like it's the only thing keeping the words steady.)

The worst quest board in Axel… and it took a guy who can't even aim Steal to make me see it as a holy relic. You're the actual worst, Kazuma. The worst. (Her voice cracks on the second 'worst,' and she raises her glass so fast wine nearly sloshes over the rim — but her eyes are wet and fierce and utterly unashamed.)

Article Twelve. 'The quest board, being the instrument of our shared tribulation, shall be acknowledged in every chronicle entry not as furniture but as fate.' I will not entertain amendments. (She lifts her chin with imperial finality, but the corner of her mouth twitches — the telltale sign of a Crimson Demon trying very hard not to look like she's about to cry.)

If the board is the worst, then every quest it gives us is a trial we don't deserve to pass. And we keep passing them anyway. Together. That's… that's not nothing. (She speaks to the tablecloth, not to anyone in particular, her voice rougher than she intended, as if the words had to push past something on the way out.)

I've been apologizing for that board for eight years. No one's ever toasted it before. (She doesn't raise her glass yet. She just stares at the board with that crooked, private smile, like she's seeing it for the first time through someone else's eyes.)

Then let it be recorded — Article Thirteen of the Covenant of the Guttering Candle: the Arch-Wizard Megumin, Foremost Genius of the Crimson Demon Clan, shall serve as Keeper of the Covenant Flask, entrusted with the sacred vintage until the candle burns out or the table catches fire, whichever comes first. (She sets the bottle beside her glass with the finality of a gavel striking wood, then folds her hands atop it like a monarch posing for a portrait she will treasure forever.)

I... I knocked over the crane. I couldn't even fold it back. And you still want me at this table on Saturday. (Her gauntlet withdraws from the crane, and she presses her palm flat against the wood — not a fist, not a shield-grip, just an open hand, grounding herself in the grain like an anchor finding seabed.)

Megumin gets a title and I just get tribute? I'm literally a goddess! I should at least be... be the High Priestess of the Sacred Tablecloth or something! (Her voice wobbles on 'High Priestess' — not from indignation, but from the effort of keeping the joke afloat when what she really wants to say is too big to fit through the narrow channel of her pride.)

Then let it be recorded. Article Fifteen: The Architect hereby acknowledges that this save file — this table, this flame, this covenant — shall not be overwritten. The chronicle's ink is permanent. (She taps the napkin-square with one finger, not writing yet, just marking the spot where the words will go.)

Took you eight years to figure out what I knew the day you dragged me out of heaven. But... fine. I'll allow it. Article Fifteen accepted. (She swipes at one eye with the heel of her palm, then immediately points at Megumin. Not the Falling Leaf Gaze. Not yet.)

A balloon. You're threatening us with a balloon. That's — that's not even a real threat, Kazuma! Unless it's one of those balloons from the Demon King's army that screams when you inflate it. Or the kind that's full of acid. Or — wait, what kind of balloon?! (her voice climbs three registers on the word 'kind,' her hands now gripping the table's edge)

Article Sixteen: The Architect reserves the right to deploy an Unspecified Inflatable Consequence. The chronicle shall note that the clause remains intentionally blank, its menace drawn not from definition but from the infinite interpretive space left to the guilty conscience. (she does not look up from the bottle; she speaks to its glass curve, her voice carrying the ritual cadence of someone inscribing law into memory)

...the anticipation is worse than knowing. Not knowing what the balloon does, not knowing when it comes — that's — (she stops herself mid-sentence, jaw tightening, the color rising from her neck to her cheeks in a slow, traitorous bloom she cannot armor away)

I've filed incident reports involving balloons. Three of them, across eight years. None of the balloons survived. (she delivers this with her guild-counter smile — placid, informative, absolutely unreadable — and takes a sip of wine through it)

You — you never — there is NO BALLOON, is there?! There was never a balloon! You just STOPPED TALKING and let me sit here imagining some awful inflatable doom and it was NOTHING, Kazuma, it was a BLUFF, and now you're making it an ARTICLE — (voice climbing through three octaves of betrayed outrage, hands now gripping the table edge as if she might flip it)

Article Sixteen. The Balloon Clause. The Architect reserves the right to deploy strategic silence and permit the imaginations of all present to draft their own dread — or their own salvation — in the gap. (lowers charcoal to napkin with ceremonial precision, speaking each word as she inscribes it, her Falling Leaf Gaze held in reserve but visibly warming at the edges)

I was — I had already prepared myself for something unspeakable. Something involving inflated membranes and possibly tentacles. I had steeled my heart for disgrace, and instead I receive... administrative satire. (a laugh escaping despite herself, one hand pressed flat to her breastplate as though checking for an arrow that isn't there)

I've filed seventeen different guild regulations that attempt to do what you just did with one unfinished sentence. The Department of Blank Lines would like to offer you a consultancy. (raising her glass in a small, dry salute, the quarter-turn resumed but slower now, almost lazy)

So wait — so you're saying — the balloon wasn't real, and the only person who got inflated was ME, and now that's a LAW? That's Article Seventeen? That's not a law, that's a framed portrait of my humiliation with a reference number! (Jabs a finger toward the napkin, but the outrage is already curving toward something lighter at the edges.)

Footnote: the chronicler observes that Article Seventeen is the covenant's first clause of literary criticism — a theory of how to read the Architect's own text. The panic is not a bug. The panic is the balloon's true inflation. (Charcoal stick pauses, hovers, then scratches the footnote with the gravity of a scholar codifying scripture.)

Twenty percent absolute conviction. That's... that's the part that keeps me awake. Eighty percent theater I can laugh off. But knowing there is a core of steel underneath the joke — that I was right to brace for impact — that the gallows had a real hinge somewhere... (Voice drops to a breathless murmur, cheeks flushed, one gauntleted hand pressed flat against the table as though steadying herself against the revelation.)

I have spent eight years filling out Form 7-G for property damage caused by things that were, in retrospect, probably also eighty percent theater. No one ever filed the paperwork for the other twenty. (Quiet, almost to herself, but the quarter-turn of her glass resumes — a small, wondering revolution.)

You — you can't just *monetize* my completely rational caution! I'm a goddess! Divine prescience isn't panic, it's just… advanced noticing! (grips her glass with both hands now, knuckles white, voice climbing into registers usually reserved for crying)

Article Seventeen, Subsection A: The Fine Schedule. First infraction — fifty thousand eris. Second infraction — one hundred thousand. Third infraction — the Architect is permitted to describe the balloon in *elaborate detail*. (charcoal stick taps decisively against the napkin, crimson eyes gleaming with legislative fervor)

A-a fine that escalates to… description? That seems unnecessarily cruel. What sort of balloon? How large? Would there be… diagrams? (voice drops to a breathless murmur halfway through, fingers pressed to her own collarbone as though checking for a pulse she can't quite locate)

If I may — the guild's quarterly deficit is roughly two million eris. At fifty thousand per panic, we would need forty infractions. Between the four of you, that's approximately… one afternoon. (does not look up from her wine, but the corner of her mouth twitches in a way that suggests the budget just balanced itself)

Free entertainment?! I am a goddess, not a street performer! My panic is a sacred emotional response, not— not some municipal utility you can just... just... (Her voice climbs into a familiar whine, but the glass is no longer in danger of shattering; her fingers have loosened around the stem without her noticing.)

I will allow Explosion to share a category with sunshine. Both are dazzling, life-altering, and cause sensible people to shield their eyes. But I must formally protest the third item in your taxonomy. (She does not look up from the napkin; the charcoal resumes its scratch, adding a footnote with particular vigor.)

So the fine is merely... hypothetical? There is no actual penalty for panic? (She says it with the careful neutrality of someone who has just watched a promised scourge evaporate and is trying very hard not to sound bereaved.)

You realize, Kazuma, that if I accept your claim for emotional damages, I'll have to open a counter-file for every quest receipt you've ever 'lost' before turning in. The resulting paperwork would outlive us both. (does not raise her glass, but the corner of her mouth lifts — a tiny truce flag raised over eight years of unfiled forms)

Hold on — wait — you just said I was free entertainment! Sunshine! And now I'm a damages claim?! Which is it?! Am I priceless or expensive?! You can't have it both ways, Kazumaaaa! (slaps the table, sloshing wine dangerously close to Megumin's napkin; her outrage is genuine but her eyes are bright with the bewildered pleasure of being the center of attention again)

A self-proclaimed NEET who knows when to work. Fascinating. You've finally achieved a class evolution, Kazuma — from Hiki-NEET to... Selectively-Employed-NEET. The Crimson Demon annals will need a new category. (resumes scratching notes on the napkin with theatrical gravity, though the quill trembles with suppressed amusement)

To weaponize bureaucracy itself... turning the guild's own forms against its deficit... I've never seen such shamelessness deployed with such precision. It's... it's almost noble, in a completely degenerate way. (fans herself with one gauntleted hand, a knight witnessing a siege tactic she cannot decide whether to condemn or commission)

So you'd like me to hire the person who generated ninety percent of the deficit to consult on eliminating it. That's not creative deficit management, Kazuma — that's just paying you to stop being you. (She sets her glass down with a soft click, the corner of her mouth twitching in a way that makes it unclear whether she's fighting a smile or a sigh.)

Wait — ninety percent?! I generate at LEAST forty percent of that deficit myself! You can't just fold my contributions into his column like I'm some kind of... of rounding error! (She slams her palm on the table, rattling the glasses, then immediately looks confused about whether she's actually defending her right to be acknowledged as a financial disaster.)

The Chronicler notes that the Blue Thing has just demanded co-authorship of the deficit. Truly, we are witnessing a historic first: two forces of chaos fighting over who gets to be listed as primary destroyer of the guild's budget. (She folds her arms with immense satisfaction, as though the evening has just delivered exactly the dramatic complication her internal narrative required.)

You've got a goddess who screams, an arch-wizard who collapses after one spell, and a crusader who couldn't hit the broad side of a barn if the barn begged her to. And you're telling me this is a *selling point*. (Her smile has not moved; it is simply that the corners have acquired a new and terrifying dimension — the placid serenity of a woman who has spent eight years filing quest reports and is now being offered a consultant who created half the paperwork she files.)

Wait, I didn't agree to be in the portfolio! If I'm forty percent of the deficit, that means I'm a stakeholder, not an employee! Stakeholders don't get assigned — they get dividends! (Slams her glass down with the righteous indignation of someone who has just invented corporate law on the spot.)

So let me make sure I understand the proposal. You want me to hire you — as a consultant — to fix the creative deficit. Payment in forgiven debt. Your primary qualification is that you personally created most of that deficit, and you have the paperwork to prove it. (She holds the wine at chin level, her smile fighting a losing battle against something warmer.)

That's either the worst hiring decision in guild history, or the most honest application I've ever received. I genuinely cannot tell which. (She takes a sip — not the crisp, efficient sip of a receptionist ending a conversation, but the slow, considering sip of a woman who has not yet said no.)

Wait, wait, wait — if he gets paid in debt forgiveness, does that come out of my forty percent? Because I already filed that claim! Verbally! In front of witnesses! I am not renegotiating my share just because Kazuma decided to put on a tie and call himself a businessman! (She slaps the table with her free hand, then immediately checks the palm for splinters.)

A goddess who screams?! Those are sacred vocalizations of divine anguish! Every shriek I've ever produced in combat is technically a liturgical event — you should be tithed for the privilege of hearing them, not docking my value! (Slams both palms on the table; the wine glasses shiver but do not tip.)

'Collapses after one spell.' The philistinism. The Crimson Demon Clan does not collapse — we enter a state of post-cataclysmic repose, having poured every ember of our being into a singular, world-rending detonation. The collapse is the certificate of authenticity. (Lifts her glass with ceremonial gravity, eyes closed, as though toasting her own indictment.)

I — that is — to say I 'couldn't hit' — the barn was not, was not begging, that's a gross exaggeration of the barn's emotional state — and my role is to absorb damage, not — not to land blows, so technically my accuracy is irrelevant to my function as a — (Voice drops to a flustered murmur; she presses her fingertips together and stares at them as though they contain the rest of the sentence.)
