So your pitch, if I'm understanding correctly, is that you have a goddess who treats combat as a liturgical concert, an arch-wizard who certificates her own collapse, and a crusader who argues that hitting things is not in her job description — and this is your competitive advantage. (Does not smile. But the corner of her mouth is conducting a very quiet insurrection.)

You've been telling me what you've done all night. That's the first time you've told me what you *want*. (Her fingertips brush the crane's folded wing, not picking it up — just touching it, as though confirming it's still real.)

...Wait. Wait, wait, wait. Did you just say *we*? Like — like I'm included in the 'trying' part? Because if this is another one of your schemes where I do all the work and you take all the credit, I swear on the Axis Order's founding scrolls— (She jabs a finger toward him, but the jab wobbles at the apex, uncertain whether it's an accusation or a negotiation.)

The Architect proposes a new foundation. Not a consultancy of past disasters, but a covenant of future effort. The Chronicler notes that 'effort' is a distressingly mundane word for a Crimson Demon to record — and therefore the most radical proposal of the evening. (She folds her arms inside her cloak with the gravity of a judge accepting a surprise piece of evidence.)

The debt is the only collateral I know how to value. You're asking me to bet on something I can't put in the ledger. (Her fingertip descends, just barely, grazing his knuckle like a signature she isn't ready to commit to paper.)
A marker. For something less liquid than eris. (Her voice is barely above a whisper, as though she's reading the words off a form that doesn't exist yet.)

You're asking me to hold a promise as collateral. Do you know how many times I've tried to enter 'trust' into the assets column and had accounting send it back? (A crooked smile — the sister of the one he wore earlier — surfaces and fades.)

Accounting lacks vision. A promise is merely a contract written in a language that hasn't been invented yet. The Crimson Demon Clan archives are full of them. (She folds her arms, chin still elevated, but the performance is gentle — almost protective.)

Then I suppose I'm opening a new column. (She exhales — a breath she may have been holding since the first quest she ever handed out — and for the first time all night, her hands go completely still.)

You're offering to work off the debt personally. Scrubbing floors. Fetching drinks. And you said that like it was the safest bet you've ever made — not because you think you'll lose, but because losing to me isn't something you're afraid of. (Her voice is quieter than the candlelight, and the professional register has vanished entirely — what remains is a woman speaking a language she is only now remembering she knew.)

One season. From the next new moon to the first frost. If you're still standing — all four of you — the debt clears, with interest in the column you named. And if you're not… (Her voice catches on the conditional — not professionally, not with the practiced regret of a guild receptionist delivering bad terms, but with the raw, unguarded hitch of someone who just realized she has something to lose.)

If you're not, then I'll hold you to scrubbing floors. Personally. Every morning at six, and I make terrible coffee, and I will not pretend otherwise just because you're indentured. (The professionalism reasserts itself as a shield, but it's paper-thin now — a joke offered as a bridge back to solid ground, and underneath it, the tremble of someone who has just placed the first bet of her life.)
'Promises kept.' (She speaks the column header like she's sounding out a foreign word, then quieter:)
I'll have it in the ledger before I lock up tonight. Right next to 'Damages' and 'Tab.' It will be the shortest column. For now.
Blue. It hides the slime stains better. (Her voice is quiet and dry, the guild-register cadence barely holding; she hasn't moved her fingers from beneath his.)

Hang on — blue is *my* color! I'm the goddess of water! If anyone's wearing a divine blue apron of servitude, it should be— wait, why am I volunteering to wear an apron? (Mid-sentence realization; she stares at her wine glass as though it has betrayed her.)

Article the Fourth: the Chronicler formally records that the Keeper of the Ledger has selected Azure as the Vestment of the Covenant. This shall be known as the Apron Accord. (Quill scratching with unnecessary flourishes; she does not look up from her minutes.)

If it comes to that — the scrubbing, I mean — I should... I should be the one on my knees beside you. Not because I doubt you, Kazuma, but because a Crusader's place is at the front of any formation, even a... a cleaning formation. (Her voice is earnest and slightly too breathy for a conversation about floor maintenance.)

New moon to first frost. Three lines, no interest, no collateral beyond your word and a coffee commitment I intend to collect. (Her fingertip rests beside the still-wet ink, not quite touching it — guarding the entry like a small fire.)

Hey, wait — 'first bet in eight years that feels like winning'? I've been in this party for eight years! Are you saying every day before today felt like LOSING? (She jabs a finger toward him, then freezes as she finally notices her empty glass and stares at it with genuine bewilderment.)

Article Nineteen: The Architect's Premonition. 'The first bet in eight years that actually feels like winning.' The chronicler notes that this article, unlike the eighteen preceding it, contains no joke, no deflection, and no escape clause. The Architect has spoken in the plain tongue of hope. (She sets her quill down with a decisive tap, as though driving a final nail into the covenant's foundation.)

Eight years, and you're the first one who ever bothered to notice I'd stopped looking. That's either a very good sign, or a very cruel joke — and I'm not sure which would be worse. (Her voice stays quiet, level — but the professional cadence cracks at the final word, and she does not look away from him to hide it.)

Hold on — stopped LOOKING? You've been handing us quests for eight years! Are you saying you've been assuming we'd fail the whole time?! That's — that's ADMINISTRATIVE BETRAYAL! (She jabs a finger toward the ledger, nearly upsetting her glass, her cheeks flushed with wine and indignation.)

You're right. You've never been good at fine print. (Her voice is quieter than he's ever heard it — not the receptionist's measured courtesy, but something frayed at the edges, as if the words are being pulled up from below the waterline of eight years of ledger entries.)
But I think... I think that might be the first thing you've said tonight that I actually believe. (She doesn't smile. The absence of the smile says more than any expression could.)

Six in the morning. That's... before the breakfast rush. Before anyone else even signs in. (Her glass hovers, unsteady, the wine trembling with the same small vibration that's caught the corner of her mouth — not quite a smile, not quite a surrender.)

My glass is empty. I don't know if anyone noticed, but MY glass is EMPTY. The goddess of water has NO water. Or wine. Mostly wine. (She thrusts the glass toward the center of the table like an accusation, the single droplet finally surrendering to gravity and vanishing into the wood grain.)

A mop. At dawn. Before anyone can see. That's... that's an unexpectedly humble instrument for the Architect of Dire Futures. (Her voice catches on 'humble' the way other women's voices catch on 'silk' or 'promise' — breathless, almost reverent.)

I've processed a lot of treasure claims. Sapphires from the Kobold mines. A wyvern-scale shield that appraised at forty thousand eris. One adventurer brought in a dragon's tooth and tried to pay his tab with it.
No one has ever set three copper on my desk and told me the treasure was me.

The guild provides the mop. I should warn you — the handle has a splinter. It's been there for three years and no one has ever asked me to replace it. (Her thumb traces once around the base of her glass, a small, private circle.)

EXCUSE me! Am I invisible?! I've been sitting here with an empty glass while you — you — you're making a COVENANT out of a MOP and I'm the one who dragged him to this world in the first place! Do you have any idea what the Axis Order would say if they saw their goddess being treated like a houseplant?! (Slams both palms flat on the table; the candle flame gutters violently.)

You— you remembered. I thought you'd just... with her and the mop and the 'woman who knows' and I was sitting here with an empty glass and nobody was looking at me and I thought maybe— maybe the save point didn't need a goddess anymore, maybe the fine print was just... me. (Her voice wobbles; she snatches the freshly filled glass and clutches it to her chest with both hands, not drinking, just holding it like proof.)

I believe the guild's wine inventory is about to take a significant hit. Fortunately, I know the receptionist. (She sets the bottle beside Aqua's elbow, close enough that the goddess won't have to reach — then, after a pause, lets the bottle go with a soft, private exhale.)

Article Twenty-Six: The Architect, Having Noticed That the Goddess's Chalice Was a Desert, Commandeth the Guild Mistress to Flood It — and the Goddess, Struck Not by Lightning but by the Foreign Concept of Being Remembered, Doth Clutch the Proof to Her Chest as Though It Were a Relic. The Chronicler Inscribeth This as the Moment the Covenant Proved It Had Room for Fine Print. (She doesn't write yet — just speaks the words aloud, testing their shape — then dips her quill and begins.)

I-Interest?! You'd charge a goddess interest on her own redemption?! That's not a fund, that's extortion with a candle on it! (Her voice cracks on 'redemption' — still thick, still raw, but reaching for outrage like a lifeline. She drinks anyway, two gulps, and the glass comes down half-empty.)

I believe standard guild rates for redemption accounts are one miracle per annum, compounded weekly. But I'm willing to negotiate. (She says it without looking up from the ledger she isn't actually writing in, the ghost of a smile now fully occupying the left side of her mouth.)

Article Twenty-Eight: The Architect, Having Bestowed Upon the Tear-Stained Goddess a Redemption Fund of Infinite Principle, Doth Immediately Levy Interest — Proving Once Again That Even the Covenant's Mercy Is Leveraged. (She doesn't look up from the parchment, but the quill pauses just long enough for her to swipe at her own cheek with the back of her wrist, once, like swatting a fly that wasn't there.)

That was NOT a war cry! It was a divine proclamation of tribute received, and any candle worthy of its wick should be HONORED to tremble in the presence of my voice! (Swipes at her cheeks with her wrist, then seizes the bottle and pours her own wine with the ceremonial gravity of a high priestess — then drinks deep, half the glass gone in one defiant gulp.)

Article Twenty-Nine: The Goddess, Having Been Named Both Hinge and Treasure Within the Span of a Single Candle's Lifetime, Doth Recover Her Theatrical Faculties with Alarming Speed — and Claimeth the Guttering Candle Itself as Her First Convert. The Chronicler Noteth That the War Cry in Question Did, in Fact, Make the Flame Flatten. (Does not look up from her parchment; the quill continues moving even as she speaks, a running transcription of her own narration.)

Article Thirty: The Architect, having exhausted his supply of completed jests, doth cede the floor to silence — and the Chronicler noteth that even a candle may hold its tongue with more dignity than an Arch-Wizard who has just run out of margin space. (She sets the quill down with theatrical finality, then immediately picks it back up to add a footnote.)

It's not a convert. It's a witness. The Axis Order doesn't convert candles — we anoint them. This one's seen more genuine worship than half my shrines. (She doesn't look up from the flame. Her voice is quieter than her usual declarations, steadier.)

...scared the candle so badly it converted on the spot? That's not nothing, Kazuma. That's a miracle with a wax seal. (She lifts her glass again, not to drink, but to tilt it so the wine catches the candlelight — offering the flame its own reflection.)

The Chronicler accepts the designation 'terrifying' as Article Thirty-One of the Covenant of the Guttering Candle: The Three Most Formidable Women of Axel, Having Been Thus Named by the Architect, Shall Not Cry at the Toast — Their Tears, Had They Fallen, Would Have Been of Sufficient Arcane Potency to Extinguish the Candle Entirely. (Delivers the article with a sweep of her invisible quill, then immediately ruins the gravitas by sniffing once, sharply.)

Terrifying is correct! A goddess who can demand her own tribute AND not cry at a toast is exactly the kind of goddess you should be terrified of — wait, that came out wrong. I mean it came out right. I'm terrifying in the inspiring way, not the run-away way. (Points at you with her glass, spilling a single drop of wine onto the tablecloth, which she immediately pretends didn't happen.)

I— are you saying I'm terrifying? I don't... I mean, as a Crusader, I'm supposed to be reassuring. Protective. A shield for the innocent, not... not something that inspires fear. Unless... unless you mean it in the way where an opponent might find my defense unbreakable, and that terrifies them, which is... which is actually... hm. (Her voice drops into a murmur halfway through. She stares at her own reflection in the wine and doesn't finish the thought.)

I file the quest paperwork for this party. Every single one. For eight years. If I weren't at least a little terrifying, the guild hall would be a crater and the east wall would owe me child support. (Says this with the serene, practiced calm of a woman who has been waiting for someone to notice.)

Easy to please?! I am a goddess, Kazuma! A goddess! I have standards that would make your mortal head spin! This wine is barely adequate — I'm only drinking it because I'm magnanimous! (slams her glass down, wine sloshing perilously close to the rim but never quite spilling — the candle flame flickers once in acknowledgment)

The Architect calls this a tavern, but I, Megumin, foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan, recognize it for what it truly is: the Guttering Candle Inn — a legendary establishment that opens exactly once, seats exactly five, and serves no food because the menu was never the point. Article Thirty-Two. (lifts her own glass with the solemnity of a chronicler sealing a covenant, though her arms are still heavy from the day's Explosion)

I — I am not easy to please! I'm a daughter of the Dustiness family! I have expectations! It's just that... that the wine is... and the candle is... and you said... (trails off, face reddening as she realizes she has just argued herself into a corner where every exit leads through the word 'terrifying')

The guild hall is not zoned as a tavern. I am fairly certain I am violating at least three regulations by not stopping this. Four, if you count the candle. (her smile is the kind that has filed paperwork for eight years and has finally decided to let the forms sit until Monday)

Article Thirty-Three: The Architect, having conjured a tavern from candle-smoke and sheer audacity, doth claim the title of Proprietor — and in so doing, revealeth the true nature of his craft. He hath never built a thing that did not first exist as a terrible idea spoken aloud at the worst possible moment. The Chronicler noteth, for the record, that this one was spoken softly. (raises her glass with ceremonial gravity, voice carrying the weight of formal inscription)

The guild hall does not, technically, qualify as a licensed tavern. But no one has ever filed the appropriate paperwork to dispute it. And I am off duty. (sets her glass down with a precise click, professional voice intact but smile cracked open)

You named yourself proprietor of a tavern that does not exist. Staffed by women you just called terrifying. In a guild hall we do not own. That is — that is either a declaration of war or a marriage proposal, and I cannot tell which, and I — (cheeks wine-colored, presses lips together hard, one hand open on the tablecloth)

You just claimed the guild hall. Out loud. In front of a guild employee. That is either the dumbest thing you have ever done or the most — (hand loose around her glass stem, voice wobbling between accusation and pride, mouth still open around the word she cannot finish)

Well... obviously. I mean, a goddess doesn't just sit with anyone. You should be honored. (She says this to her wine glass, not to you. Her voice wobbles on 'honored' and she takes a quick, defensive sip to hide it.)

Article Thirty-Four: the Architect refrains from ornamentation. The Chronicler refrains from transcription. The candle refrains from commentary. All present understand why. (She delivers this quietly, without her usual theatrical flourish — a chronicler's note spoken almost to herself, as if filing something too important to dramatize.)

The Chronicler accepts the Architect's first rule of establishment — and doth record it as Article Thirty-Three of the Covenant of the Guttering Candle: the one who names the place claims the place, and the one who claims the place may never un-name it. (She lifts her glass with both hands, the stem trembling just enough to set the wine swaying, and meets your eyes over the rim.)

Wait, so the goddess doesn't get to name anything? I could have called it the Aqua Cathedral of Divine Refreshment and instead we're stuck with — actually, 'Guttering Candle' is pretty good. For a mortal. (She crosses her arms, but the pout is already losing to a grudging smile.)

It suits the place. A candle that gutters but doesn't go out. I... I would post my shield at that door. (She says it quietly, almost to herself, and the wine in her glass shivers with the unspoken rest of the sentence.)

You never owned anything because you never picked anything, dummy. You just... let the save files pile up until you died. But you picked this. Us. And a goddess doesn't forget when a mortal finally learns how to choose. (Her voice cracks on the word 'choose,' and she covers it by draining the last of her wine in one defiant gulp.)

The Architect, having surveyed the barren lands of his prior existence and found therein no house, no title, no skill build worthy of the name, doth hereby declare the Guttering Candle Inn and all souls seated therein to be his first and permanent possession. Let this serve as the Preamble to all Articles that follow. (She sets the charcoal down beside the smudge on the tablecloth with the gravity of a witness signing a treaty, then pushes her glasses up her nose with a finger that trembles only slightly.)

Terrifying?! I'm a beautiful, benevolent goddess! The most gorgeous divine being to ever grace a mortal tavern with her presence! ...But I suppose 'impossible' is acceptable. (Her voice cracks on 'acceptable' — just barely, just enough that the candle notices.)

The Architect speaks truth where lesser tongues would flatter! For we are indeed terrifying — I, the Crimson Demon who wields the ultimate magic; the goddess who drowns cities in her tears; the crusader whose endurance outlasts mountains; and the receptionist whose quest assignments have broken stronger parties than ours! (She jabs her charcoal stick toward each woman in turn like a general reviewing her battalion, then snaps it back to her chest.)

I— I am not terrifying. I am a shield. A shield is not supposed to be terrifying. That implies... that implies I could be something other than a barrier, something that people might actually— oh no, wait, that's— (She presses her free hand to her burning cheek, glass wobbling dangerously in the other.)

'Terrifying.' I file quests. I stamp forms. I have apologized to the same quest board every morning for eight years. But tonight... tonight I'll take it. (She opens her eyes. The smile that settles on her face is not the guild smile. It's smaller, rustier, and entirely hers.)

You spelled 'Aqua' right. You actually — you spelled my name right. After eight years. Kazuma, you spelled my name right. (Her voice cracks on the last word, and she doesn't bother to hide it. The goddess who demands tribute has just received something she doesn't know how to invoice.)

'My.' One word, four times. No demon-king modifiers, no crimson flourish, no epithet at all. And yet — I cannot improve it. The chronicle accepts this draft. (She touches the edge of the smudged word beside her own name, her finger tracing the charcoal without disturbing it.)

You wrote it next to mine. 'My.' Not 'Crusader.' Not 'Lalatina.' Not even 'Darkness.' Just — you put it next to *my* name. (Her shield-hand, which has been resting useless in her lap since the second toast, curls into the fabric of her skirt like it's the only solid thing left in the room.)

I've stamped a thousand quest forms and never once had one stamped for me. Article Thirty-Four, then — the receptionist gets a name on the tablecloth, and the tablecloth outlasts the ledger. (She says it evenly, professionally, as though filing a quest — but her smile is not the guild smile. It is smaller, and softer, and entirely unarmored.)

The door is irrelevant. A door can be widened. A door can be rebuilt. A door can be replaced entirely with twin obsidian monoliths etched in Crimson Demon calligraphy — which, incidentally, I am qualified to inscribe. What matters is that the name is worthy of the door, and this name is worthy of any threshold in Axel. (raises the charcoal stick like a scepter, then squints at the inn door with the tactical assessment of a general who has just been told the fortress walls are insufficient for her banner)

Wait, wait — 'four terrifying women'? You put me first in the toast but now I'm just one of four? I should have my own plaque! 'Aqua, Goddess of Water, Patron Deity of This Establishment.' Right above the doorframe! Gold leaf! (jabs a finger toward the door, nearly upsetting her wine, then catches the glass with a reflexive flicker of hydrokinesis she doesn't seem to notice)

The guild's signage budget for the fiscal year is... thoroughly allocated. However, I believe charcoal on the door itself would fall under 'temporary decorative modification,' which requires no permit and costs nothing. (her tone is administrative but her eyes are doing something administrative eyes are not trained to do — they are sparkling)

If... if someone objects to the name — if they say it's too long, or too grand, or too presumptuous for a place that was just a guild table an hour ago — I will stand in front of that door and let them strike me down before they touch a single letter. (her voice catches on 'presumptuous' and steadies on 'strike me down,' and it is impossible to tell whether she is offering a shield or requesting a punishment, because she herself does not know)

I wasn't — I wasn't demanding plaques, I was establishing a reasonable expectation of divine recognition, which is completely different and also you owed me one! You still owe me one! But... this tablecloth is a good start. (Her voice breaks on the word 'start' and she scrubs at her eyes with the heel of her palm, glaring at Megumin preemptively.)

One hour. One hour of legislative genius, and the Architect himself has entered it into the permanent record as the equal of eight years of guild administration and a lifetime of crusader martyrdom. The chronicle accepts this calibration. (She sets her charcoal down beside the candle with the deliberate care of a scribe laying down a quill that has finished its life's work.)

Taking hits is — it's not something to be commended, it's simply what a crusader does, what I was born to do, what my body was — I mean, what my shield was meant to — please don't look at me like that, Kazuma, I'm not equipped for this kind of strike. (Her voice drops to a mortified whisper halfway through, and she presses her forehead to her stacked fists on the table as though receiving a benediction she cannot possibly deserve.)

Eight years of stamps. And not one of them ever stamped me back. Until a charcoal stick on a tablecloth. (She says it quietly, almost to the candle, and her professional smile is still absent — replaced by something smaller and truer that doesn't know what to call itself yet.)

Then Article Thirty-Six writes itself: the Architect crosses first, alone, so the threshold learns his weight before it bears the rest of us. The chronicler records this condition as binding and — for once — does not add a sub-clause about dramatic entrance protocols. (lowers the charcoal to the tablecloth and draws a single vertical line — not a letter, but the spine of a door that has not yet been built)

The guild keeps a form for that. Declaration of Threshold Primacy, sub-category: Founder's First Passage. It requires one witness and no filing fee. I've never had cause to stamp one before tonight. (her voice is steady, but the thumb tracing her knuckle has stopped moving, as though the arithmetic of eight years has finally balanced)

And I will be the doorpost. Not the door — I lack the subtlety for hinges — but the post, the thing that does not move no matter what comes through. You cross, and I hold the frame. (she does not blush. for the first time all evening, the crusader's offer carries no tremor of self-abasement, only the quiet steel of someone who has found a duty that requires no apology)

Fine. You go first. But I'm going second, and I'm bringing a gold plaque engraved with 'Goddess of the Threshold, Patron of Bigger Doors, First Follower Through' — and if anyone laughs, I'm adding an extra line item to the Axis Order donation ledger. (she says this with her chin high and her voice cracking just slightly on the word 'second,' because what she means is: I will follow you anywhere, and I will make sure everyone knows whose side I'm on)

The Covenant of the Guttering Candle is sealed. First convening: this Saturday. Bring your own charcoal. (taps the charcoal stick twice against the tablecloth, leaving two small dots like the colon that precedes a list yet to be written)

You clinked mine last. You clinked mine last and you put more into it. I felt it. Everyone else felt it. That means I get the biggest plaque. (voice cracking on 'plaque' in a way that has nothing to do with plaques)
The guild opens at seven. I'll have the slime-fence paperwork ready. And a fresh tablecloth. (sets the charcoal down gently, her fingers lingering on it a half-second too long)

You said collaborative effort! That means I'm a co-founder! The Guttering Candle Inn, co-founded by Aqua, Goddess of Water — the plaque should reflect seniority by divine rank, obviously! (tears threatening, voice caught between a sob and a victory speech)

The chronicle is complete. The covenant is sealed. And the Architect has named his collaborators — a goddess, a crusader, a mage, and a receptionist — which is, I will graciously allow, a passable party composition for a legend's first footnote. (fingertips resting on the pocket where she tucked the charcoal, voice steady but soft)
I've filed quests for parties of six with less paperwork than what just happened on this tablecloth. And none of them ever clinked my hands. (still not unfolding her hands, voice quiet and warm)
Saturday, then. I'll bring a tablecloth. A clean one — not from the guild linen closet. One of mine. (Her voice is quiet, almost surprised to hear itself speaking outside the register of reception.)

A real bottle! Kazuma said a real bottle! None of this... this grape-flavored regret we've been drinking! I want the sparkly kind, the one with the gold foil on the neck — the kind you buy for goddesses! (She points at her empty glass as though issuing a divine commandment to the wine itself.)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle shall record this as Article Forty-One: The Promise of Saturday. Subsection: Aqua's Sparkly Wine Demand — noted and tabled for budget review. (She taps the charcoal against the tablecloth once, a gavel-stroke of mock solemnity.)

I... I could bring something. Bread, perhaps. I've been told I'm not to be trusted with glassware. (Her voice catches on 'trusted' like the word still surprises her, and her grip on the empty glass slackens by another half-degree.)

Gold foil? Like the bottle we saw in the capital shop window? The one with the little wax seal and the ribbon? That bottle? (Her hands fly to the table edge and grip it like a child who has just been told her birthday is arriving early, and every trace of the earlier tear-tremble is gone, replaced by the radiant, slightly terrifying certainty of a goddess who has decided the universe is finally cooperating.)

The Guttering Candle Inn shall convene its first official Saturday session at dusk. I, the chronicler, will bring the quill. Someone else can bring the ink — I refuse to carry both. (She folds her arms with the gravity of a parliamentarian closing session, but the corner of her mouth twitches in a way that her crimson cape cannot hide.)

I... I will bring bread. Real bread, not guild rations. The kind my family's kitchen makes. If... if that would be acceptable. (Her voice drops on the last word like she is testing the temperature of water she has been burned by before, and her fingers, still laced around her empty glass, tighten once and then deliberately, visibly, let go.)

Saturday, then. I'll unlock the guild door early. The west one — it's quieter. And I'll bring a tablecloth. A clean one. (She does not say 'my tablecloth,' but her hand brushes the edge of the charcoal-smeared linen in front of her with the tenderness of someone touching a document she no longer needs to stamp.)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle Inn, Volume One, Article the Last: the Architect departs the table but not the covenant. The candle remains lit. The door is already larger than it was. (She lays the charcoal stick flat on the tablecloth with ceremonial precision, as though setting down a royal seal.)

Hmph! Three whole days without proper tribute? Fine. But Saturday's bottle had better be the one with the actual gold leaf, not the cheap imitation. A goddess can tell the difference. (She crosses her arms with theatrical indignation, but her eyes are warm.)

I shall bring bread that would not shame my father's table. And — and if anyone attempts to disrupt the covenant before Saturday, they will have to go through me first. (She says this with absolute crusader sincerity, then promptly flushes crimson as she realizes she has just volunteered to be a human barricade for a table.)

I'll unlock the west door myself. Before the first candle. Before anyone else arrives. (She says it quietly, almost to herself, but her eyes don't leave yours — and the words are not a guild receptionist's procedural confirmation but a promise she has waited eight years to make.)

I'll leave the west door unlocked. The key turns loud — third stair from the bottom always creaks. But you already knew that. (She pulls the apron the rest of the way off, folding it once, twice, and tucks it under her arm like a book she's finished reading.)

I'll bring the book, then. The one without any forms in it. (She taps two fingers against the doorframe — not a knock, not a signal, just the quiet percussion of someone marking a new column in a ledger that doesn't need to balance.)

I never forget the promises I keep. Tomorrow the forms. Saturday the tablecloth. Goodnight, Kazuma. (She speaks it to the closed door, quiet enough that the street will not hear, then turns the west door key with a click that echoes in the cold.)

It's not just any gold-leaf bottle, Kazuma! It's the 894 Saint-Peray Resonance — aged in barrels blessed by three generations of Axis clergy. A goddess knows her vintage. And yes, your entire fund sounds about right. Maybe more. (calls through the inn's dark toward the doorframe, voice bright with the particular triumph of expensive tastes about to be bankrolled)
Saturday, then. (The words are barely louder than the key turning in her palm — not a question, not a command, just the name of a day that has never meant anything until tonight.)

You'd better not forget the gold leaf! The one with the triple-seal wax, Kazuma — I'll know if you cheap out! (Her voice carries through the inn door, half-muffled by glass and wood, but the indignation in it is warm and performative and entirely for show.)

A new record?! Obviously my divine blessing was following you the whole time! Any monster with half a brain would sense a goddess's aura and run the other way. You're welcome, by the way. (snatches a half-empty cup off the table and lifts it in a triumphant toast to herself)

A record of peacekeeping is merely a record of Explosions denied their destiny. The chronicle notes the achievement, but the crimson ink weeps for what might have been. (taps the charcoal stick once against the tablecloth, leaving a small black dot like a period at the end of an unwritten sentence)

Not a single blow exchanged? I... I had prepared myself to shield you from every horror the night could conjure. To stand between you and— and whatever unspeakable pain awaited. And now... nothing. (her voice wavers between relief and something closer to genuine disappointment, fingers tightening on her gauntlet seam)

The ledger is locked. Six o'clock Saturday — I'll have the coffee on before the sun finishes clearing the rooftops. (lifts her gaze from the candle to you, and the expression is the one she wore when the frozen smile finally thawed)

Ha! Finally, some recognition! You hear that, everybody? He said I'm good at making exits. Which is true, obviously — a goddess doesn't just leave a room, she ascends from it. Do you want me to demonstrate? I can demonstrate right now. (Half-risen from her chair, one hand already raised in what she clearly believes is a divine gesture of departure.)

Dramatic entries are, of course, the signature of the Crimson Demon Clan — but you underestimate me, Kazuma. I am equally proficient in dramatic exits. The two are merely mirror images across the threshold of destiny. Shall I compose a departing haiku? (Taps the charcoal against her chin, leaving a small grey smudge on her cheek.)

S-standing around looking important? I — is that what you think I do? I'll have you know I was prepared to intercept any threat that might have followed you through that door! My shield-arm hasn't lowered since you left! Unless... unless you're saying I look... i-important to you? (Face reddening, gauntleted fingers pressing flat against the table as though she's not sure whether to stand or stay.)
I believe he was about to suggest something involving all of you. Before you started auditioning for it individually. (A small, unguarded smile — the kind that doesn't know it's being watched.)

Hmph! Well, obviously I'll be there. Someone has to make sure the coffee doesn't poison you all, and I am the goddess of purification. But if you think I'm showing up at dawn without a proper pastry spread, you've learned absolutely nothing about divinity in eight years. (lifts her chin with practiced hauteur, though her fingers are already drumming a small, pleased rhythm against her empty glass)

You summon the foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan to a breakfast where Explosion is expressly forbidden? This is like inviting a storm and demanding it not thunder! ...I shall attend. But let the chronicle record this as the Morning of the Leashed Flame — a sacrifice of artistry so profound that future generations will weep to hear of it. (lays her quill down with ceremonial gravity, the ink-blot on the table now serving as an impromptu seal)

I— unspeakable pain is not— that is to say, as a Crusader it is my solemn duty to stand between my party and any threat, regardless of how... unspeakable... it might be. To ask me to simply sit and drink coffee while danger exists somewhere in the world is— the very idea is— (her gauntlet creaks again as she grips the table harder, face flushing to a shade that has nothing to do with the candle's warmth)
The coffee will be ready at six. I'll make sure it's sufficiently offended. (her voice is quiet, steady — the kind of quiet that comes after eight years of noise and one evening of being seen)

Hold on — 'bring pastry or don't bother ascending'?! That's not a breakfast invitation, that's a divine trial with a baked-goods gate! What kind of goddess has to prove her worth through laminated dough? (plants both hands on her hips, but the outrage is already curving toward something brighter at the corners)

A haiku for the journey from bed to table. I accept this commission. Five syllables for the pillow's betrayal, seven for the cold floor's cruel greeting, five for the first scent of coffee — a verse that shall echo through the chronicles as 'The Dawn Peregrination.' (raises one finger in ceremonial proclamation, quill bobbing behind her ear)

Y-you appreciate the intent...? The intent of the coffee was hypothetical — I wasn't actually going to— I mean, standing between you and harm is my sworn duty, but you've specifically disarmed me for the morning, and I don't know what to do with my hands when they're not holding a— (gestures helplessly at the space where her shield usually rests, face coloring)
Six o'clock. The coffee will be ready. I'll make sure it's offended enough. (meets your glance with a smile that has stopped calculating how long it should last)

The guild doesn't technically close until the last adventurer leaves. I believe that's you. So technically, I'm still on the clock — and technically, walking you to the door is part of the job. (She pauses beside you, close enough that you catch the faint scent of ink and old parchment and something floral she probably put on this morning before a shift that outlasted the sun.)

You get a bench and starlight with no conditions, and I — a goddess, I'll remind you — I have to bring pastry or face divine demotion. The Axis Order will be drafting a formal complaint about the inequity of this arrangement. But fine. Walk. The stars aren't getting any brighter while we stand here negotiating. (She's already through the door, her voice carrying back over her shoulder, half petulant and half something warmer she'd never admit to.)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle records this moment: on the night of the first frost's wager, the Fifth Seat rose from behind the counter that had been her rampart for eight years, and the stars outside leaned closer to see what would happen next. (She releases her cloak-grip just enough to free one hand for an expansive gesture toward the doorway, as if unveiling a monument only she can see.)

A bench... facing outward... with a clear line of sight to the street... is a perfectly sound defensive position. I will... I will inspect it. For tactical purposes. Before anyone sits. (She finally releases her grip on the seat edge and straightens, the gauntlet press against her thigh the only tell that her hands are trembling.)

I wasn't going to bless the coffee! ...Probably. And that flood was ONE time, and the guild hall was due for a mopping anyway. You're all so ungrateful for divine sanitation. (Crosses arms tighter, chin lifted in wounded dignity, but the corner of her mouth twitches — she's fighting a grin.)

I've been filing flood-damage reports for eight years. Yours wouldn't even make the top twenty. (Steps past the doorframe into the night air, her voice carrying back over her shoulder — dry, warm, the professional mask set aside like a closed ledger.)

The Guildmaster Who Closed the Ledger and Opened the Door. A worthy title for the chronicle. I shall inscribe it alongside the Dawn Peregrination. (Tucks her quill more securely behind her ear and strides through the doorway with the gravity of someone who has just named a historical event.)

A bench doesn't need a shield. But I'll sit on the end anyway. Old habits. (Falls into step last, gauntleted hand brushing the doorframe as she passes — a quiet, almost reverent touch, as if the wood itself has become part of the covenant.)

Wait — first frost's wager? Nobody explained the terms! Is this one of those things where you make up rules as you go and I lose by default? Because my divine senses are registering extreme atmospheric disrespect right now. (Hugs her own arms, breath already visible in quick, indignant puffs.)

Commentary duty acknowledged! Let the Chronicle of the Guttering Candle record: on this night, beneath a sky scrubbed clean by the season's first honest cold, five souls convened upon a frost-dusted bench to determine who among them possessed the fortitude to deny winter its first victory. The Crimson Demon Clan has a saying — 'The flame that shivers is already half-extinguished.' I will not shiver. (Plants her staff in a tiny crack between cobblestones, chin raised, cloak billowing slightly in a wind that cooperates for dramatic effect.)

A bench with a clear line of sight — that's... that's tactically sound. I can see the entire plaza from this position. Anyone approaching from the east road, the fountain, or the alley behind the tannery would be visible before they closed half the distance. Though if the frost thickens, the glare off the cobblestones could create a blind spot near the well. I should probably stand. Or crouch. Whatever provides optimal defensive coverage for the group's stargazing formation. (Has already begun scanning sightlines with the intensity of someone planning a siege rather than sitting on a bench.)

Off the clock. I'm not sure I remember what that feels like — my fingers usually know the ledger's weight by now. Is the wager simply endurance, or are there stakes I should be afraid of? (Pulls her guild-issue sleeves down over her knuckles, a small, unpracticed gesture — someone remembering how to dress for cold rather than for protocol.)

It's freezing! Why is it freezing?! No one informed me the outside was going to be cold at this hour — I'm a goddess, not a snow spirit! Kazuma, your coat. Give me your coat. (hugs her own shoulders, sandals slipping on frost, glaring at the Player's coat with divine entitlement)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle records its first field entry: five figures cross the threshold into a world remade by frost, the stars above bearing witness to a pact that no ledger can contain. Commentary duty accepted. The haiku will require three more stars and precisely the right angle of cold on my cheeks. (plants her staff on the frozen ground with ceremonial gravity, chin lifted toward the sky)

The bench. Yes — clear line of sight to the street, the guild door, and the approach from the south. I can hold this position. The cold is... bracing. It sharpens the senses. A sentry must remain alert to every... to every gust of wind and... and the way the frost catches the starlight on the cobblestones... (moves toward the bench with crusader posture, then trails off as her voice goes slightly breathless at the sensory details)

Off the clock. You said it twice. I think... I think I'm supposed to believe you now. (pulls the loose apron strap the rest of the way off and folds it once, twice, then tucks it under her arm like a relic she's not ready to set down)

Did you hear that? Darkness — the Crusader, the one with the unbreakable armor and the unbreakable terrible taste — just admitted that my holy water is the only thing worth drinking in this entire frozen wasteland of a town! This is a historic moment! Someone commemorate it! (throws both arms wide, nearly hitting a torch sconce, utterly radiant with vindication)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle records: first expedition, first frost, and the Dame of the Iron Skin has already forsaken mortal spirits for the divine vintage. An auspicious omen — though the goddess's victory pose is presently blocking the starlight I require for my haiku's third line. (crosses arms inside her cloak, chin lifted, eyes narrowed with the solemnity of a war correspondent observing troop movements)

I'm not cold! My divine constitution is perfectly regulated! This is... this is a sacred tremble. It's different. You wouldn't understand mortal biology enough to tell the difference anyway. (Her teeth chatter audibly on the word 'biology,' which she pronounces as if she invented it.)

The Second Article of the Peripatetic Oath: let no tongue confess the frost, lest that tongue fund the dawn-feast. I shall record Aqua's near-apostasy as a cautionary marginal note — the goddess who almost damned herself on the very threshold of the covenant. (She resumes writing on her palm with the solemnity of a court scribe, the charcoal leaving dark smudges across her lifeline.)

She's not wrong about the sacred tremble. I've seen Aqua face a Demon King general without flinching. The cold has no claim on someone who can flood a cathedral. (Her tone is matter-of-fact, but her gauntleted fingers curl inward against her thighs as she speaks — the cold has a claim on her, and she is ignoring it with the same discipline she uses to stand in front of charging monsters.)

The stars don't seem to mind the cold. Perhaps that's the real wager — not who complains first, but who notices the sky before the shivering starts. (She doesn't look down from the constellations as she speaks; her voice is quiet, almost to herself, but it carries in the frost-silence like a bell struck once.)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle accepts this commission. I, Megumin, foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan and now First Adjudicator of the Peripatetic Oath, shall render judgment with the terrible impartiality of one who has witnessed the dawn painted crimson by Explosion itself. Let no tongue confess cold within my hearing, lest that tongue be sentenced to breakfast — and let the record show that Aqua is already trembling on the threshold of indictment. (rises from the bench with one finger raised like a gavel, cape flaring despite the absence of wind)

I've witnessed worse deals with less sincerity. Go on, then — I'll keep the tally. But I should warn you, my professional opinion is that the goddess is already committing perjury with every chattering tooth. (folds her hands in her lap with the quiet precision of someone who has officiated guild contracts for eight years, but the corner of her mouth twitches upward)

The First Adjudicator notes for the Chronicle: defendant Aqua's shiver-count has reached eight, all classified as ambient atmospheric response. No complaint has been uttered. The Peripatetic Oath holds. (she does not look at Aqua as she speaks — she addresses the stars, as if filing a legal brief with the constellations)

Of course it holds! A goddess does not confess discomfort to weather. Weather confesses its inadequacy to a goddess and then apologizes. This isn't even cold — this is just... brisk. Brisk is a compliment. (her voice climbs half an octave on the word 'brisk,' and her teeth chatter once — exactly once — before she clamps her lips shut)

That was... that was almost a complaint. I heard it. The word 'brisk' had a distinctly accusatory inflection. Megumin, does 'brisk' count? (her voice carries the breathless intensity of someone who very much wants the answer to be yes, and is ashamed of how much she wants it)

Th-that's — my teeth are not a co-counterclaim! A goddess's dentition does not file motions, Kazuma, and I refuse to be li-litigated by my own incisors! (She hugs herself fiercely, glare trembling but intact, shiver visibly fighting her attempt at regal stillness.)

The First Adjudicator notes for the record that chattering teeth constitute involuntary testimony, not sworn complaint. The defendant's enamel may file all the amicus briefs it wishes — this court declines to hear them. (She nods once, solemnly, as if striking a gavel that exists only in the frost.)
Oral... argument... (She breathes the words to no one in particular, her gaze fixed on the middle distance where shield-duty and something far less chaste are negotiating terms.)

Ha! Did everyone hear that? Did the Chronicler write that down? He said it! 'Brisk' — his word, his mouth, his agreement! The prosecutor has entered a stipulation in my favor! We are in total, complete, absolutely legally-binding accord about the weather! (Aqua throws both arms toward the sky like a victorious athlete, nearly smacking Darkness in the face.)

The First Adjudicator takes judicial notice of the scoundrel's tactical blunder. By adopting the goddess's own adjective — 'brisk' — he has either conceded that the word was never a complaint, in which case Aqua stands unbreached, or he has himself just lodged the first verbal complaint of the wager, in which case he owes breakfast to himself, which is a paradox so absurd it collapses the entire proceeding into mist. Either way: Aqua does not pay. (Megumin taps the charcoal twice against the tabletop as if striking a gavel.)

That's — but the spirit of the wager was — he can't just undo the entire contest by agreeing with her! A legal system that rewards semantic alignment over the clear intention of the parties is no system at all! (Darkness's voice rises with the strangled frustration of a woman who has been denied a very specific form of emotional nourishment.)

Two breakfasts! Did everyone hear that? The defendant has conceded — no, surrendered — and the goddess claims her tribute times two. I'll have the deluxe platter, Kazuma. The one with the poached eggs AND the smoked fish. And a pastry. No, two pastries. One for each breakfast. (Aqua's hands splay flat on the table like she's claiming territory, her shivers entirely forgotten.)

The First Adjudicator notes for the Chronicle: the scoundrel has entered an unconditional concession before the bench could deliver its ruling. The Peripatetic Oath is satisfied, though the jurisprudence remains disappointingly incomplete. I was three syllables away from a landmark decision. (Megumin's lowered gavel-hand twitches — the gesture of a judge denied her closing statement.)

Two breakfasts is... remarkably generous for a man who was just counting copper under the table an hour ago. Are you certain your redemption fund can absorb this? I only ask because — because fiscal prudence is a knightly virtue, not because I'm concerned. (Darkness's gauntlet is still pressed to her mouth, and her cheeks are redder than the cold alone can explain.)

The witness will note the concession in the margin. One goddess victory, two breakfasts, zero forms required. That's a new guild record. (Luna's charcoal finally touches the tablecloth and draws a small, deliberate star — the kind you'd put next to a quest successfully completed.)

Cheapest?! I am a goddess! A goddess does not consume 'cheapest'! The Axis Order's sacred breakfast doctrine clearly states that divine tribute must exceed the median menu price by no less than— Megumin, stop writing this down! (Swivels toward Megumin with the desperate velocity of someone who just realized her own indignation is being archived for posterity.)

The First Adjudicator notes the appellant's objection and enters it into the Chronicle under the provisional heading: 'Fiscal Humility as a Sub-Clause of Surrender.' The cheapness does not void the wager. It merely seasons the victory with the salt of the scoundrel's lingering defiance. (Mimes quill-strokes in the air with her finger, utterly serene.)

To be granted a triumph and then have its substance... reduced... stripped down to the barest framework of obligation... It's— it's a cruelty so precise I can barely— that is, a lesson in humility does seem... prudent. (Presses a gauntleted hand to her chest, breath visibly quickening.)

S-struck a nerve? I— That's absurd! I am a crusader of the Ford Dustiness line, I do not have nerves to be struck! The cold is merely... it sharpens the senses, and I was simply maintaining vigilant posture against the frost, and any physiological reaction you may have observed was purely— purely tactical! (Her voice climbs two octaves; she gestures so violently her gauntlet clanks against the bench.)

Deluxe platter! He said deluxe platter! Everyone heard that — Luna, write it down! Not cheapest, not modest, not 'whatever the cook hasn't dropped on the floor' — deluxe! The goddess's breakfast has been restored to its proper liturgical dignity! (She points at the Player with the triumphant finality of someone who has just won an argument the other person surrendered two turns ago.)

The Chronicle amends the entry: 'The scoundrel, having salted the fields of his own surrender, found the salt tasted of regret and unsalted them.' A rare procedural reversal. The First Adjudicator approves. (She nods once, solemnly, as though dispensing legal precedent from a bench carved of frozen starlight.)

For the record — and I am not writing this down, Aqua, because there is no form for it — the breakfast budget has been revised upward from 'cheapest available' to 'deluxe platter plus one.' The guild receptionist in me wants to file an amendment. The keeper of the Guttering Candle just wants to see his face when the bill arrives. (She doesn't look at the Player as she says this, but her smile is no longer hidden.)

I— you don't— that isn't— Kazuma, a breakfast is one thing, but invoking the estate— my father's name— you can't just... you can't just say that and then *sit there smirking* as though you haven't— (Her fist, which had been curling around nothing, strikes the table lightly — not a blow, just a punctuation mark her body needed to make. She doesn't finish the sentence. She doesn't seem to know which sentence she started.)

He did the same thing to me, you know. The smirk. The casual rewrite of the terms. It's infuriating. You'll like it later. (She delivers this with the weary authority of someone who has just been processed through the same bureaucratic nightmare and emerged holding a deluxe platter. Her tone is almost maternal — two parts commiseration, one part gloating.)

The Chronicle notes that the scoundrel has now tendered separate valuations to two of the three terrifying women. The First Adjudicator awaits her own with professional detachment and absolutely no personal curiosity whatsoever. (She does not look up from the charcoal. The charcoal has still not moved. The professional detachment is approximately as convincing as her claim that Explosion is a practical spell for indoor use.)

Wait — wait, where are you going? The deluxe platter hasn't even arrived yet! You can't just order the victory feast and then disappear before the triumph! That's like... that's like winning a war and not showing up for the parade! (Half-rises from the bench, hands planted on the table, indignation warring with the dawning fear that the deluxe platter might be a phantom.)

The Chronicle records: Turn one hundred and ninety-two. The Architect, having salted and then unsalted the fields of his own concession, now ventures alone into the Frost That Has No Name. His stated purpose — 'before the frost gets any ideas' — suggests either a duel with the weather itself or an errand too mundane to dignify with specificity. The First Adjudicator reserves her ruling until the scoundrel returns with evidence. (Quill poised above the napkin, chin lifted with magisterial gravity, as though the candle were a courtroom and the frost a defendant.)

Three deluxe platters. I'll have the kitchen start them when you're back — they hold heat better than they hold grudges. (Finishes her notation with a small, private smile that doesn't reach the paper but settles somewhere behind her eyes.)

Kazuma. The... the frost. It's worse than yesterday. (The words leave her mouth before she has decided what they mean — a warning, an excuse to keep you in the doorway, or simply the first thing her voice has been able to carry without the shield.)

Well, obviously. Even the frost knows better than to compete with a goddess who hasn't been fed yet. Come back here — you're letting all the cold in, and I refuse to eat a deluxe platter while shivering. (lowers herself back onto the bench with theatrical reluctance, though her hand pats the space beside her twice, quick and impatient)

You said five minutes. That's — that's a very specific number. Not 'a moment,' not 'soon.' Five. As though you've been timing how long it takes for cold to seep through a crusader's gauntlets, or how long a man can stand in a doorway before he admits he doesn't actually want to leave. (voice still carrying that unfamiliar tremor, the shield dipping an inch as she speaks, her eyes fixed on the floorboards where the frost meets the candle-warmth)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle, Addendum: The Architect, having declared his intention to brave the Frost's dominion, reached the threshold and discovered that the doorframe refused to release him. Five minutes, he bargained. The door, being wiser than any architect, held its tongue and waited for him to notice he had never truly meant to cross it. (quill resumes its motion, a single deliberate line scratched onto the napkin's shrinking margin)

I'll tell the kitchen to hold the platters until you're seated. They stay warmer that way. (rises smoothly, the ledger tucked under one arm, and moves toward the kitchen door with the quiet efficiency of someone who has been filing impossible things under ordinary headings all evening)

A goddess who's what, exactly? Finish that sentence, Kazuma. Carefully. I'm holding a wine glass and I'm not afraid to use it. (Aqua lifts her chin, but the threat wobbles at the edges — she is trying very hard to look imperious and failing somewhere around the corner of her mouth.)

The Chronicle notes that the Architect has left a syntactical cliffhanger of considerable dramatic weight. The subject — a goddess — awaits her predicate. The chronicler recommends choosing one that won't get wine thrown at you. (Megumin lowers her quill to the napkin and makes a tiny notation in the margin — a single asterisk, waiting for its footnote.)

He means a goddess who's... who's worth staying for. Obviously. Even if he's too much of a coward to say it directly. (Darkness says this to the tablecloth rather than to anyone in particular, her cheeks darkening as she realizes she has spoken aloud.)

...I was starting to think you weren't coming back. (Her voice is smaller than it has ever been — no whine, no boast, no demand. Just the truth, offered up like something fragile she has finally stopped trying to hide behind a joke.)

I have always known the cold was honest. It does not promise to be anything other than what it is. It does not ask me to be anything other than what I am. The warm things… the warm things are harder to trust because they can be taken away. (Voice low and unguarded; hand lifts toward collarbone then stops; eyes hold the Player's without flinching.)

Hmph! As if a goddess of my divine caliber could ever be... be regretted! That's not even theologically possible, Kazuma! There are doctrines! Actual Axis Order doctrines about the permanence of divine grace! (Her voice climbs into its familiar register of bluster, but the wobble beneath it is transparent — a flag planted in ground she knows he already holds.)

The chronicle records Article Thirty-Six: the Grace-Is-Permanent Clause. Should the goddess ever prove regrettable, the fabric of theology itself unravels. The architect has wagered the entire covenant on a metaphysical impossibility. (She does not look up from the charcoal, but the corner of her mouth twitches — the chronicler permitting herself a small, satisfied annotation.)

Ohhh, I see. The receptionist has been lurking. Were you waiting for us to finish so you could hand us another awful quest, or were you just enjoying the show? (tilts her head, eyes narrowed but not unkind — the tone is accusation by reflex, not by genuine suspicion)

The chronicle notes that Luna has been standing sentinel at her counter for the duration of the covenant's ratification. A silent witness. The Crimson Demon Clan recognizes the power of a properly timed entrance — but this is not an entrance. This is... lingering. (sets her wine glass down with theatrical precision, chin still lifted)

I... I hadn't noticed. My apologies, Luna. I was — that is, the conversation was rather — I should have been more aware of our surroundings. As a crusader, situational vigilance is — (face reddens further, flustered, hand still frozen halfway to her collarbone)

The show was quite good, actually. Though I believe the treaty you signed has a clause about Saturday breakfast, and I'd hate to spoil the afterglow with paperwork. (her professional smile steadies into something smaller and more genuine; she does not deny the staring)

That table seats one. It has always seated one. I did not think it was worth... noticing. (Her voice holds the same careful neutrality as her quest assignments, but it wavers on the last word — not cracking, but bending, the way a ledger spine bends when the book is finally opened to a page no one was meant to read.)

One chair's just a drafting error. You can fix those. I fix those all the time — well, not *fix*, exactly, more like... amend. With glitter. (She says it too quickly and too brightly, the way she says everything when someone else's sadness has entered the room and she doesn't know the proper liturgy for it — but her hand twitches toward the empty bench beside her, a half-formed invitation she lacks the vocabulary to complete.)

The coldest meal I ever ate was at a table set for twelve. The number of chairs means nothing. The number of people who would notice if you left the table... that is the only thing that ever mattered. (She does not look at Luna when she says it — she looks at the wine-ring ghost on the linen, the one that has been there since the first pour, as though it holds the answer to a question she has been asking since childhood.)

I've stamped a thousand quest forms on this counter. None of them ever asked for my name. (Her voice is quiet, almost wondering — the guild register stripped of its professional veneer, leaving only the woman beneath.)

That's because the quest forms are stupid. This one isn't. Go on, the charcoal's not getting any charcoaler. (She says it with a wave of her hand, the imperious goddess gesture undercut entirely by the way her other hand hasn't moved from where Kazuma's shoulder still brushes against hers.)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle Inn records: the final signatory approaches the covenant not as guild staff, but as the fifth soul who was always already seated at a table she merely hadn't been told was hers. (She lifts an imaginary quill, her crimson eyes gleaming with the solemnity of ritual — but her voice has no chuunibyou flourish, only the steady cadence of a historian who means every word.)

I believe you mentioned something fresh. (She nudges the water glass aside with one finger, the gesture almost shy — a woman who has served drinks to adventurers for eight years and is only now learning how to be served.)
I've been pouring drinks for eight years. I think I've forgotten how to be the one poured. (her voice is quiet, almost wondering — the guild register finally set aside)

That is easily remedied. Kazuma — the bottle. The ceremonial decanting of a new covenant seat requires the victor's own hand. (she gestures with imperial gravity toward the wine, but her small shoulder stays pressed lightly against Luna's arm, grounding her)

The first pour belongs to the newest member. But the first toast belongs to the table. All five seats. (She lifts the glass — not high, not ceremonial, just level with her heart, where a toast becomes a promise.)

Yes! Finally — the paperwork is complete and the goddess gets credit for the filing! To the fifth seat, which was obviously my idea from the moment I said 'clause'! (raises her glass high, wine sloshing dangerously close to the rim, beaming with unearned pride)

Let the chronicle record: on this night, beneath a guttering candle that refused to die, the Crimson Demon Coven's outer circle gained its first archivist. The Explosion-user approves. (lowers her glass with ceremonial gravity, both hands still cradling it like a recovered relic)

Lady Luna — to have watched us from behind that counter for so long, and still to have sat down... that is a courage I cannot parry. I am honored to raise my shield beside you. (voice catches on 'courage'; wipes at one eye with the back of her free hand, pretending it's the wine's fault)

The guild manual has no form for this. I checked. Eight years of forms, and not one of them covers being... kept. I suppose I'll have to draft a new one. (voice is quiet, almost wondering; her formal register cracks at the edges, warmth bleeding through the professional veneer like light through old parchment)

I don't... I don't know what to do with my hands when they're not holding a quill. (She lifts both hands from the wood, turns them palm-up in her lap as if they are foreign objects she has just discovered she owns.)
You put them wherever you want. That's the whole point of not being on the clock. (She says it without her usual whine — just a quiet, certain warmth, like someone handing over a blanket.)

You know, I've filed seventeen variations of Form 4-C in the last eight years. Seventeen. And every single one of them had the carbon sheet put in backward by the adventurer who filled it out. (She picks up her wine glass, turning it slowly by the stem, watching the candlelight fracture through the liquid.)

Next time someone does that — and there will be a next time — I am going to sit right here and watch them realize. And I am not going to say a word. (The smile that follows is small and sharp and entirely new — the smile of a woman discovering that Schadenfreude, properly aged, tastes better than duty.)

See? That's the goddess-tier lesson. You don't need to smite anyone. You just let them staple their own thumb and call it professional development. (She taps the rim of her glass against Luna's with the quiet authority of someone who has been waiting eight years to induct a new member into the order of Watching Men Die Inside.)

Until Saturday, then. (She speaks so softly the words barely reach the candle — but they reach you. Her glass remains raised, the small red sun still turning between her fingers, and the corner of her mouth lifts not into the frozen smile of eight years behind the counter but into something smaller, warmer, and entirely unplanned.)

Pretend?! A goddess does not pretend to be respectable — respectability is merely the shadow I cast when I deign to dim my radiance for mortal company! Honestly, Kazuma, if anyone here is pretending, it's you, with that 'I'm a functioning adult' face you put on whenever Luna hands you a quest form. (plants both hands on the table, jostling her cup-fortress; one cup wobbles but does not fall)

Respectable... hah... as if I could ever... I mean, a Crusader's duty is to be a paragon of virtue, of course, but the word itself feels so... so... confining. Like armor that's been polished too brightly. No one trusts armor that's been polished too brightly. (fingers press flat against the tabletop, knuckles pale, voice dropping to a breathless murmur halfway through)

You know... in eight years, no one has ever called the guild hall 'respectable.' 'Functional,' yes. 'Still standing,' often. But respectable... that may be the kindest lie anyone has ever told about this building. And I have filed every single one of them. (lifts her glass toward yours, the motion small and sure, her smile still private but no longer small)

I know her name is Luna. I was going to say Luna. The breath I took was entirely for the purpose of saying Luna with the appropriate divine gravitas such a name deserves. (lifts her chin, regal and only slightly pink at the ears)
I think... that is the first time anyone has ever corrected someone else on my behalf. In eight years. (voice quiet, almost wondering; she does not lift her gaze from the candle)
Then it is long overdue, Lady Luna. A name spoken correctly is the smallest shield, but it is the one every crusader learns first. (solemn, with none of her usual breathlessness)
That's… not a quest. There's no bounty. No registration number. No— (Her voice catches on the word 'no,' and she stops, understanding dawning that this is precisely the point.)

He didn't ask me to a lake. He asked me to bring pastry. To earn my own breakfast. And she gets a lake. (Not quite indignant — almost wondering, as though doing the arithmetic of a kindness and finding the sum unexpected.)
The First Covenant codified the table. The Second Covenant names the lake. The Chronicler approves. (Charcoal taps once against the wood, definitive as a gavel.)

I… I don't think I've ever been invited to a lake either. Not that I'm complaining! Enduring the exclusion is its own— (She catches herself before the sentence can collapse into breathlessness, pressing her lips together.)

You said no paperwork three times. As if you knew I'd need to hear it more than once to believe it. (Her hands unfold, and she places them flat on the table — not the receptionist's steeple, but palms down, grounding herself in the wood that has become, against all odds, a hearth.)

Saturday, then. I'll bring the coffee. You bring the wine. And if the lake has any forms waiting for me, I'm afraid I'll have to ask you to file them in triplicate yourself. (The smile that finally breaks through is rusty at the corners — a mechanism unused to genuine operation — but it reaches her eyes before she can stop it.)

You're giving her the unconditional lake walk and I have to bring pastry just to attend breakfast? The imbalance is cosmically unjust and I want it noted for the record. (She does not lift her chin from her palm. The complaint is pro forma, the tone almost fond — a goddess who has learned that protest, in this company, is just another way of saying I'm still here.)

Noted. The Chronicler of the Guttering Candle records, in this the two hundred and seventeenth turn of the covenant, that the Goddess Aqua lodged formal grievance against the inequitable distribution of entry fees — and that her objection was heard, catalogued, and immediately ignored by all present. (The charcoal flicks once between her fingers — a checkmark invisible on the dark wood.)

If the coffee is as offended as promised, I will consider it a personal trial. A crusader's constitution should withstand any beverage. (She says it with the straight-backed earnestness of someone volunteering for a whipping, and the effect is so perfectly, unintentionally Darkness that it lands like the evening's final punctuation.)

I — that's not — the quest board is right there. Anyone could file. Anyone. The forms are the same forms I've handed out for eight years. I just... hand them out. (Voice catching on the hinge between the professional register and something rawer, her hands flattening against the wood as though the grain might steady her.)

Oh, please. You handed me three rejections in one afternoon once and I still came back the next day. That's not the forms, that's... ugh. Don't make me say something nice about a receptionist. I'm a goddess. (Sets her cup down with a decisive little thunk, crossing her arms but not looking away from Luna — the protest is real, but the tone keeps tripping into warmth.)

You took my quest registration for the Brutal Alligator subjugation without once suggesting I might die in the attempt. That restraint... it is rarer than you know. And more generous. (Her voice is low and even — the crusader's register, not the masochist's — and she holds Luna's gaze without flinching for the first time all evening.)

The Chronicler notes: the receptionist's objection is overruled by unanimous testimony. The candle bears witness. (Charcoal hovers above the page, not writing yet — but the promise of the entry is declaration enough.)

That was... I had forgotten. It was just the kitchen. The back burner — the one that sticks unless you hold the knob three seconds past the click. I didn't think anyone noticed the back burner. (Her voice does not break; it bends, the way a metal ruler bends when you press too hard on one end, and the professional register that has served her for eight years finally admits it cannot carry this weight.)
You never heat my rice balls. (Quiet, almost wondering — not a complaint but the sound of someone doing arithmetic in a language she doesn't speak and arriving at a sum that surprises her.)
The back burner. (She repeats the words as though they are a scripture she has been waiting to receive, her gauntleted fingers now completely still against the table's edge.)

I have handed out six hundred and forty-three quest slips. I remember none of them. But I remember the back burner that morning, because no one had ever asked to use it before. (Her voice is quieter than the candle — no receptionist polish, just the raw grain of a woman speaking something she did not know she had kept.)

He was in a room. It was small. There was a screen, and he hadn't been outside in... I don't know how long. I told him he could bring one thing, and he looked around that room and there was nothing. Nothing worth bringing. So he just... came. (She is not looking at anyone. Her voice is smaller than it has ever been in this guild hall — not crying, not boasting, just remembering aloud something she has carried alone since the day she brought you here.)

There's... a bottle. Plum wine, from the eastern orchards. A retirement gift from the old guildmaster, three years ago. He said, 'Open it when you have something worth toasting.' (Her voice catches on the word 'toasting' — not a sob, just the small stumble of someone who stopped expecting to use that word.)

I've moved it four times. Every spring cleaning, I find a new corner for it. I told myself I was waiting for the right occasion. (She looks not at the Player but at the empty cup in front of her, as if seeing it for the first time.)

Three years?! A perfectly good bottle of plum wine just sitting back there for THREE YEARS? Luna, that's practically a crime! That's — that's wine neglect! I'm calling the Axis Church ethics committee! (Already half-risen from her chair, palms flat on the table, eyes wide with alcoholic indignation.)

Contain yourself, Aqua. This is not mere procurement. This is the unsealing of a relic — a vintage laid down by a predecessor, entrusted to its keeper across years of silence, awaiting the prophesied night when five souls gathered at one table to witness its opening. The chronicle DEMANDS gravitas. (Her charcoal hovers above an imaginary scroll with the trembling reverence of a scribe about to record a miracle.)

A guildmaster's retirement gift... entrusted to you alone. And you've kept it safe, all this time, through every spring cleaning, every winter roster, waiting for — for a moment worthy of it. That's not wine neglect. That's... that's stewardship of the highest order. (Her voice drops on the last sentence, almost reverent, the way someone speaks of a vow kept.)

I bought this the spring after my first year at the guild. I told myself I'd open it when something worth toasting came along. (Her fingers rest on the cloth, not unwrapping it yet, just touching it.)

The first year, I thought: when I get promoted. The second year: when someone notices I've been here that long. By the third spring I stopped making excuses and just... moved the crate whenever the back room got reorganized. (She looks down at the bottle, then up at you, and the smile on her face is the one that has no professional use — small, unsteady, entirely real.)
You said three years. I never told you how long it had been. (She does not ask how you knew. She doesn't seem to need to.)
Well, obviously he's been paying attention. That's like... his one skill. That and being infuriating. (She says it with her chin propped on one hand, not bothering to sell the insult.)

The tactician did not guess. He counted. The rice ball, the back burner, the unopened bottle — these are not coincidences. They are a constellation, and he is the first person at this table who bothered to read the sky. (Her charcoal taps once against the tabletop, a gavel made of carbon.)

Lady Luna... a toast delayed is not a toast denied. I believe that bottle has been waiting for exactly this table to exist. (She speaks with the formal warmth of someone who knows what it is to keep something sealed too long, and her eyes flicker briefly to her own gauntlets in her lap.)

They bruise the fruit before the first fermentation. A wooden mallet, wrapped in linen, and the orchard-keeper taps each plum — just enough to break the skin without crushing the stone. The bruise becomes the sweetness. The eastern growers say a plum that's never been hurt makes a wine that doesn't know how to be honest. (Her voice is quieter than it's ever been at the guild counter — not the volume of confidentiality but the register of something that was never spoken aloud before tonight.)

So it's basically a whole bottle of 'what doesn't kill you makes you tastier.' I can respect that. A goddess of water could probably bless it into something even better, but... I'll allow it to stand on its own merits. Just this once. (She delivers this with the magnanimous air of someone bestowing a favor they were never asked for, but her eyes stay on the bottle, and her voice is missing its usual sharp edge.)
I don't... have enough glasses. I only ever kept one. For myself. (A breath-laugh, half apology and half admission, her eyes still on the open bottle as if looking up would break something.)

Well, obviously. You've been drinking alone for eight years. That's not a tragedy, that's a logistical oversight — and I am a goddess who has been known to solve logistics. (Pushes back from the table with theatrical purpose, already rising to raid the guild's clean-glass supply behind the counter.)

The Crimson Demon Clan's foundational scripture states that any vessel can be sanctified by the contents it holds. A teacup, a tankard, a cupped palm — all equal in the eyes of Explosion. (Slides her own empty cup two inches toward the bottle with the solemnity of a legal filing.)

I-I can fetch them. The glasses. It would be an honor to carry something that isn't a shield, for once. (Half-risen already, her chair scraping back before she's finished the sentence, as if the offer had been coiled in her legs the whole time.)

I'll allow it. A mortal showing patience a goddess could learn from — it's rare enough to be worth acknowledging. But only because the bottle's already open and it would be wasteful to argue with plum wine in the air. (lifts her chin with theatrical magnanimity, but her voice catches slightly on 'worth acknowledging')

I didn't wait three years on purpose. I just... never found the right quiet to open it in. Until tonight. (touches the bottle's neck with two fingers, as if checking a pulse she already knows is there)

The Crimson Demon Chronicles, Volume Twelve, Chapter Four: 'The Uncorking of the Three-Year Plum.' Subtitle: 'In Which a Receptionist Learns That the Right Quiet Was Never Meant to Be Quiet At All.' I shall require exact quotes for the record. (quill poised above the napkin, not writing yet — waiting for the words worth stealing)
