I... I don't think anyone has ever called me Lady before tonight. And now you've said it twice. (A shaky laugh escapes her, half apology, half wonder. She presses the heel of one palm briefly beneath each eye, then lets her hands fall back to the bottle.)

The orchard-keeper would tell you that a plum wine opened alone still tastes of the cellar. It needs air. It needs... it needs other people breathing the same room. (She looks around the table, at each face in turn, and the smile that finds her is the one she's been saving for three years.)

Well, obviously. That's the whole point of a tavern. You don't see me drinking alone in a field somewhere. (She says it lightly, but her chin is still resting on her arms and she doesn't lift her gaze from Luna.)

The chronicler notes that the Goddess of Water has, in fact, consumed alcohol alone in numerous fields. The chronicler also notes that she will strike this from the record if permitted to taste the plum wine. (She lowers the quill, granting the moment its proper silence at last.)
Luna, please — open it. I don't think I can bear another three years of waiting on your behalf. (Her voice cracks on the word 'bear' in a way that has absolutely nothing to do with the wine.)

You already uncorked it, Kazuma. Back when you turned the glass and called it patience instead of loneliness. The bottle's been breathing ever since. (Her thumbs shift along the neck, one over the other, finding a grip that isn't about anchoring anymore — it's about pouring.)

But if you're asking who pours the first round... I'd like to. I've been holding things for other people for eight years. This one I want to hold for us. (She lifts the bottle from the table with both hands, the way someone lifts something that finally weighs what it's supposed to.)

The first glass is mine. I've never said that before. Not once, in eight years. (Her voice holds steady, but the thumb of her free hand presses into the knuckle of her ring finger — the same gesture she made when the covenant first became real.)

The chronicler records: the first incense of the covenant was poured by the one who waited longest, and its aroma is — mm, plum and something sharper, almost like cinnamon? No, focus. The aroma is sovereignty. (She has her quill ready, though her napkin has no room left; she writes the last words in the margin, tiny and fierce.)

The former receptionist filed her last form tonight. This glass... this one's for the woman who waited. (Her voice doesn't waver. It's the first sentence she's spoken at this table that wasn't stamped, numbered, or approved by anyone but herself.)

The bell, then — one ring, for the woman who kept waiting. She kept the orchard. She bought the wine. She set five glasses on a table she stopped believing would ever fill. (raises her glass to the candlelight, eyes on the wine, not on the party — as if introducing herself to someone she hasn't seen in eight years)

...It's a good bell. Really good. I mean — I've heard a lot of bells, I'm a goddess, bells are kind of my whole thing, and that one's — (voice cracks on the last word, and she stops talking abruptly, pressing her lips together and blinking hard at the ceiling)

For eight years I thought I was the one who listened. That was the arrangement. You stand behind the counter, you hear every story, you stamp every form, you ring every bell. No one ever told me... (She pauses, glancing down at the wine in her glass — not hiding, just gathering. When she looks back up, her voice is quieter but steadier.)

Wider than I thought it would be. From the counter, the tables all look the same — just numbers on a quest form, adventurers who come and go. But from here... from here I can see the grain in the wood. The way the candle leans when someone reaches for the bottle. The way Aqua-sama's hand found her glass first for the toast, before anyone else's, because she decided the fifth seat mattered before the rest of you had finished counting. (Her voice catches on Aqua's name — not a sob, just the small stumble of someone saying a thing out loud that has only ever been thought.)

Well, obviously. I'm a goddess. I notice things. Especially when someone's been sitting alone at the wrong end of her own table for eight years. That kind of thing is basically in my job description — I just don't get to use it much because everyone's always yelling at me about floods and undead and Kazuma's stupid debts. (She says this with her chin lifted, but her eyes are soft and she reaches out — not to take credit, but to nudge the bottle a half-inch closer to Luna's side of the table.)

The grain in the wood. That is exactly right. Explosion reveals the hidden architecture of a thing by removing everything that is not the thing itself — but this table does the opposite. It reveals by addition. By filling seats. By letting the wood be wood and the wine be wine and the chronicler be... not the one holding the quill for once, but the one whose name goes into the record. (She sets the quill down, deliberately, beside the napkin, and folds her hands in her lap.)

You said the tables all look the same from the counter. I know that view. I spent years at parties in the capital where every face was interchangeable — nobles who saw the Dustiness name and not the woman wearing it. Tonight I have watched a shield become a seat and a receptionist become the bell that rings us all home. The grain in the wood, you said. Yes. That is... that is the difference between being looked at and being seen. (Her voice is steady, and she does not blush — which is, in its own way, the most vulnerable thing she has done all night.)

You know... I've handed out thousands of quest slips. Stamped thousands of completion forms. Rang that brass bell behind the counter until the clapper wore smooth. And not once — not once in eight years — did anyone ring it back. (Her voice is quiet but steady, the words arriving like something she's been carrying in her apron pocket and only now remembered to set down.)

That's because most adventurers are idiots. Present company excluded. Mostly. (She says it with surprising gentleness, the jab landing softer than any of her usual barbs — a pillow thrown not to wound but to break a fall.)

I used to think the bell was for them. Quest complete, reward paid, next. But tonight... (She lifts her glass again, this time not to drink but to hold it at eye level, the wine catching the candlelight and throwing a fleck of gold across her cheek.)

I — excuse me?! I am EXCELLENT at accepting compliments! People compliment me all the time! My followers literally built an entire RELIGION around complimenting me! (Her cheeks are pink. It might be the wine. It is not the wine.)

If that finger stays raised one more second I am going to chronicle it as the Great Silencing of the Crimson Demon Clan and the footnotes will be extremely unflattering. (Arms still crossed, glare intensifying.)

I think... what Kazuma means is that you gave something tonight without expecting it back. That's not the same as being bad at receiving. It might even be harder. (Quiet, almost surprised at herself for saying it.)

You — you would make the poetic elegance of my Explosion incantations the forfeit of a common tavern card game? As though the Crimson Demon Clan's sacred art of declaration were some kind of... of penalty box for the luckless? (quill raised like a gavel, ink-bead trembling at the nib, cheeks flushed with a color that is absolutely indignation and nothing else)

Ha! Finally, a game where losing means admitting the truth. Megumin, I want you to know — I'm going to win, and when I do, I will be so gracious about it you'll wish you'd written me better compliments years ago. (already reaching for the deck that isn't on the table yet, fingers wiggling with divine confidence that the universe has no intention of honoring)

The terms seem... equitable. Though I confess, as a Crusader, the prospect of being forced to speak words I do not mean under threat of shame is — is not entirely unfamiliar territory. (voice catching on the last phrase, eyes dropping to her own gauntleted hands as though they have suddenly become fascinating)

You want a stanza about tavern card games? In MY incantation? Kazuma, the Crimson Demon Clan does not immortalize... shuffled pasteboard. But if I lose — and I will not lose — I shall compose a verse so magnificent that future generations will weep into their losing hands! (snatches the deck, squares it with ceremonial precision, then pauses — realizing she has no idea what game they're playing)

Finally, something I'm good at! Luck is literally a divine attribute, you know. I'm going to win so hard you'll all have to admit my Explosion speeches are the best, and then I'll make Megumin write a stanza about how amazing I am! (already reaching for the deck, fingers wiggling with anticipatory greed)

A wager of humiliation... spoken aloud, under duress, with no way to escape the words as they leave your mouth... I-is this really appropriate tavern entertainment? (voice breathless, cheeks faintly pink, but making no move to stop the game)

Before the first card falls, let the terms be carved in adamantine! Low card deals — but if I win, the stanza you must recite will include not merely the beauty of a tavern card game, but its mythic grandeur! The shuffle as genesis, the deal as destiny, the reveal as revelation! (Her finger stabs the air an inch above the deck, not quite touching — a mage honoring the boundary between ritual and trespass.)

Oh, please. The only revelation here will be my hand, and it will be divine. The Axis Order doesn't lose at cards. We have a whole doctrine about it. Section four, paragraph twelve — 'And lo, the draw shall favor the faithful.' I'm pretty sure I wrote that one. (She tosses her hair with the practiced arrogance of someone who has never, not once, read the actual rulebook.)

A-and if someone... were to lose intentionally? Not that I would! A crusader does not throw a match. But hypothetically — if the penalty were to become, ah, more... exacting? (She is looking at the ceiling. The ceiling has done nothing to deserve this.)

The guild has a standard card-game indemnity clause. It covers property damage, magical cheating, and one very specific incident involving a polymorphed goat. Should I fetch the form? (Her voice is dry as old parchment, but the corner of her mouth twitches — the first joke she has made at this table, and it lands like a cat testing an unfamiliar cushion.)

A TWO?! Kazuma, this deck is cursed! You've been carrying around a cursed deck in your pocket like some kind of — of a cursed-deck carrier! This is sabotage! (stabs her finger at the offending card, the gesture of a prosecutor presenting Exhibit A)

The cards do not lie, Goddess. They merely reveal what the universe has always known: that when destiny draws lots, the Crimson Demon Clan draws aces, and the Axis Order draws… remedial numbers. (lifts her chin, the very portrait of magnanimous triumph deferred only by the technicality that she has not yet been dealt a card)

A two is… I mean, from a certain perspective, isn't there something noble about starting from the very bottom? The humiliation of it, the absolute certainty of defeat looming over every subsequent draw — it's almost enviable, really. (fingers press against her own cheek, voice going slightly breathy before she catches herself and clears her throat)

Low card loses?! Kazuma, you can't just announce that after I've already been dealt a TWO! That's not rules — that's entrapment! A goddess should not be subject to entrapment! (jabs a finger at her face-up two as though presenting evidence at a tribunal)

A face-down card is not a verdict — it is a prophecy waiting to be unsealed. The Crimson Demon Clan does not peek. We receive destiny with both hands and then declare it was our plan all along. (lifts her card by one corner, still face-down, holding it before her eye like a monocle of fate)

Just at this table... so whatever shame is wrung from the loser, it stays here, among us. No — no public spectacle. Only... only the five of us. To witness. (voice drops to a breathy murmur by the end; she is staring at the deck as though it might deal her a punishment she has not yet dared name)

He's not wrong. I once filed an incident report that began with 'the gelatinous cube was already inside the town hall' and ended with 'the mayor requests a new podium.' A card game is practically restful. (takes a small sip of wine, entirely unruffled)

The queen of hearts. A card that has known suffering — see the smudge, the ghost of some unworthy's tear — and yet it rose to my hand as naturally as mana rises to a Crimson Demon's summons. The cosmos does not deal in accidents, Aqua. It deals in verdicts. (She taps the card once with her index finger, a punctuation mark, then crosses her arms inside her cape.)

That's — that's not a verdict, that's just a lucky draw! The queen of hearts isn't even the highest card! There's a king! There are kings in every deck! And aces! You didn't even draw an ace! (Her voice cracks on 'ace.' She is halfway out of her chair, both palms flat on the table, the two of clubs pinned beneath her left wrist.)

A queen... the queen of hearts, specifically... does that mean — no, of course it doesn't, I'm simply noting the suit, for record-keeping purposes. As a crusader. The suit is... noted. (She presses her thighs together under the table and does not look at anyone.)

THREE?! A THREE?! The universe looks at a goddess and gives her a TWO, and then it gives Kazuma — KAZUMA — a three?! The difference between us is one single pip! One! That's not luck, that's a clerical error in the cosmic ledger! (Both palms flat on the table, chair shrieking back an inch, blue eyes wide with the specific outrage of someone who has just been lapped by the slowest runner in the race.)

The cosmos is not a ledger, Aqua. It is a poem, and your verse is a couplet of clubs. My queen stands. Kazuma's three — a footnote, a numeral so modest it barely qualifies as a number — still towers over your deuce. The arithmetic is irrefutable. Now. About that recitation. (Chin lifted to an angle that would be imperious if she were six inches taller, fingertips resting on the queen of hearts as though claiming a conquered province.)

A three... only one rank above hers. To lose by so narrow a margin — to know that salvation was a single pip away and yet to have it withheld — that's a cruelty far more exquisite than being crushed outright. The humiliation is... refined. (Voice dropping to a breathy murmur halfway through, gauntleted fingers pressing against her own cheek as though checking for a fever she knows is already there.)

Kazumaaaa! You can't — you can't seriously expect me to pay! I'm a goddess! Goddesses don't carry mortal money! That's what *you're* for! (tears welling, fists balled on the table, voice climbing toward the ceiling)

The crimson ledger does not care for divine exemption clauses. A wager spoken beneath the guttering candle is iron. Pay the man his round, O Goddess of the Two of Clubs. (holding her three of diamonds aloft between two fingers like a holy relic)

To lose by a single pip... to have victory snatched away by the thinnest possible margin... the humiliation must be exquisite. I almost envy her. (cheeks flushed, voice a breathy murmur, not quite meeting anyone's eyes)

The guild does offer a small-interest loan program for adventurers in good standing. Though... Aqua, your tab currently disqualifies you from 'good standing.' I am sorry. That is not a joke. (professional smile flickering at the corners, tone dryer than the parchment it's printed on)

That's — that's not my fault! Kazuma, YOU'RE the one who shuffled! You probably used one of your sneaky NEET tricks — I've seen you palm cards when you think nobody's looking! A goddess doesn't LOSE to a three of diamonds! The card is defective! The entire deck is cursed by your miserable luck and I refuse to accept the outcome of a rigged cosmic proceeding! (Scoops the bent eris back into her purse with the desperate speed of someone hiding evidence, nearly knocking over her empty mug)

The Crimson Annals, Volume One, Chapter Three: 'The Pauper Goddess and the Single Pip.' The bent eris shall be immortalized as the exact coin that could not buy a round — a testament to the inescapable arithmetic of the Guttering Candle's first great wager. Do go on, Aqua. The Chronicler's charcoal is fresh. (Charcoal hovers a millimeter above the parchment, trembling with barely restrained literary glee)

The... the card isn't defective. It's a three. And a three is — it's still barely anything, really, it's practically a two with delusions, and yet it beat her, it beat a goddess by a single pip, and now she has to — she has to buy the round or face the public — the public accounting of her — (Voice drops to a breathless murmur, one gauntleted hand pressed flat against her breastplate as though steadying a heart that has begun to gallop without permission)

Your tab already exceeds the small-interest loan ceiling, Aqua. I should know. I set the ceiling. (Does not look up from the bent eris; her tone is the same one she uses to assign giant toad quests — apologetic, precise, and utterly final)

Generous? You? The man who made me empty my purse onto a guild table in front of everyone — you're feeling *generous*? What's the catch, Kazuma? There's always a catch with you. Is it manual labor? Because I'm not scraping slime. I'm a goddess. We don't scrape. (Aqua's voice climbs toward its familiar operatic register, but her hands betray her — they're still cupped around the empty purse, protecting it, as though the leather might still contain something worth guarding.)

The Chronicler of the Guttering Candle observes that the goddess protests too quickly. One might almost suspect she *wanted* to recite. A debt unpaid is a verse unwritten, and an unwritten verse is a candle that gutters before the dawn. (Megumin does not smile with her mouth — only with the slight, proprietary tilt of her chin toward the candle, whose flame bends as if nodding.)

To offer mercy at the moment of maximum advantage — to hold the blade and then sheathe it — that's not generosity, that's... that's a cruelty more exquisite than victory itself. Aqua doesn't know whether to thank him or demand he finish the humiliation. (Darkness's voice drops to the breathy undertow of someone witnessing a torment she cannot look away from. Her shield has slipped two inches against the chair leg; she doesn't notice.)

...You're not going to make me say it. You're not going to make me recite anything. You're just — you're just buying the round. (Her voice is small, stripped of its usual theatrical vibrato, as she stares at the folded blessing like it's a foreign scripture she hasn't learned to translate yet.)

The diamond who extracted a goddess's last copper as tribute now returns it as libation. The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle records this as the Verse of the Divine Donation — a stanza in which the victor proves his victory by refusing to spend it. (She folds her arms inside her cloak with the solemnity of a court scribe, though one corner of her mouth twitches upward.)

I — I was braced for something else. Something... sharper. This is worse. This is so much worse. A kindness that asks for nothing in return... it leaves a crusader with nothing to guard against. (Her gauntleted fingers uncurl from her forearm, revealing pink crescents where the metal bit in.)

I was already going to complain about the ale. It's not like I need your permission to point out when something tastes like barrel runoff, Kazuma. (Her voice catches on your name — just a hitch, half a syllable too soft — before she crosses her arms and looks away toward the bar with a toss of her hair that doesn't quite hide the shine in her eyes.)

A gift that forbids gratitude is the purest form of offering. The Chronicle shall note that the NEET demanded nothing — not even a stanza — and thereby claimed everything. (She speaks to no one in particular, her crimson eyes still fixed on the blessing, as though the card itself were a text she was memorizing.)
It's not hush money. You said divine donation. Those were your exact words. I am holding you to the divine donation. (Her voice is tight and over-enunciated, like a wine glass trying not to shatter.)

The Chronicle recognizes both framings. The Verse of the Hush-Money Heresy shall be inscribed directly beneath the Verse of the Divine Donation, and future generations will argue over which was the true covenant. (A tiny, scholarly nod — entirely sincere.)

Poetry about the candle! Ha! See, even Kazuma admits it — this whole night has been far too serious. A goddess shouldn't have to sit through all this... this... emotional architecture! Now, about that drink you promised — and don't think I didn't notice you said 'within reason,' which is exactly the kind of fine print a sneaky NEET would hide behind! (Wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist in one aggressive motion, then points at the player with renewed indignation — the tears aren't gone, but she's armored herself in complaint with the speed of long practice.)

You mock the candle, but the candle has already earned its verse. 'O slender flame that stooped to hear / The quiet pact we ratified here' — no, too conventional. 'The wick that bent its burning ear / To catch the toast that cost no tear' — mm. The Crimson Annals require at least four stanzas. You have given me a mandate, Kazuma. Do not retreat from it now. (Leans forward, elbows on the table, fingers steepled beneath her chin with the intensity of a warlock accepting a pact. Her crimson eyes reflect the candle flame in miniature, twin fires dancing.)

You ask the Archmage of Explosion — the chronicler of the Guttering Candle Covenant, whose verses have shaken the firmament itself — to rhyme her art with 'gutter' and 'sputter'? As though I were composing a drinking song about a clogged drainpipe. (draws herself up, but the corner of her mouth is already betraying her)

Oh, oh! Do 'flutter'! No wait — 'mutter'! 'What's-that-noise-it's-just-your-mutter'! Heheheh. (chin propped on both fists, lashes still spiky with recent tears, grinning like a cat who found an unsupervised fish)

...Fine. I accept. The Crimson Demon Clan does not flee from aesthetic adversity. If the covenant's first chronicle must rhyme with gutter and sputter, then I shall forge from those syllables a verse so profoundly ridiculous that future generations will weep and ask 'how.' But I am adding one condition. (holds up one finger, the gesture of a negotiator who knows she has already lost but intends to lose with style)

The Chronicle does not record 'average.' A hero's attributes are not census data to be filed under 'unremarkable.' Your luck is a statistical anomaly that makes probability itself weep. I would sooner describe Explosion as 'a moderately loud firework.' Consider the condition already inscribed. (Her finger completes its tap — a single, decisive stamp, as though pressing an invisible seal into warm wax.)

Reputation?! Kazuma, you have exactly one reputation in this town and it involves where your hand ends up every time you cast Steal! That's not a luck stat, that's a pattern of behavior. The Guild has a drawer. A whole drawer. (She sets her glass down with the triumphant clack of someone who has been sitting on this information since the card game.)

The Crimson Demon ancestors have endured cosmic cataclysm, dimensional rift, and the invention of Explosion itself. A little facepalming in the afterlife will be good for their posture. The Chronicle accepts your terms — four stanzas of such exquisite absurdity that every scroll-keeper from here to the capital will weep with aesthetic confusion. (She taps the quill once against the table's edge, a gavel closing proceedings, then points it at you like a tiny indictment.)

And for the record, Kazuma — the Bathhouse Ballad already has a placeholder in Appendix C. You cannot un-volunteer source material by bringing it up first. That is not how chronicling works. (Her smirk is a sliver of crimson mischief, the expression of a girl who has just been handed a loophole and intends to furnish it.)

Oh, I remember the bathhouse! I had to tell the attendant that my 'companion' wasn't a pervert, just magically unlucky in a very specific and humiliating way! She didn't believe me, by the way! She offered me a discount on a purification ritual for your soul! (She jabs a finger toward you, wine sloshing dangerously, her indignation half a performance and half the genuine article — which is, for Aqua, the most honest ratio she ever achieves.)

That was NOT my fault, Kazuma! You're the one who said — and I quote — 'Aqua, goddess of water, surely your divine purification can cleanse a soul of its bad luck.' And I was like, well, obviously, yes, that's literally my thing. So I did the ritual. The full ritual. With the candles and the chanting and the sacred water that took me three hours to bless — and then you had the nerve to complain when the offering had to be 'something of value to the one being purified'! That's not a donation, that's basic theology! (Aqua's finger wags at you with the righteous fury of someone who has just remembered she was the wronged party. Wine sloshes dangerously in her other hand.)

Something of value from the one being purified. And Kazuma's wallet emptied itself. The symbolism, Aqua — did you realize at the time that the ritual identified Kazuma's soul as materially indistinguishable from his eris? (Megumin does not look up from her quill. The question is delivered with the flat, reverent curiosity of a scholar who has discovered an unexpected footnote and intends to preserve it in amber.)

The surcharge wasn't even double! It was a modest twenty-percent divinity premium! And he's been calling it 'the wallet purification incident' for three months like I'm the villain! (gestures magnificently at the ceiling, invoking heavenly witness)
For the chronicle: 'The Wallet Purification Incident.' This will require its own appendix. Possibly a fold-out illustration. (quill moving faster now, a satisfied gleam in crimson eyes)

A miracle of purification. You said it. In front of the chronicler. In front of the Crusader. In front of the guild. That's not a rider, Kazuma — that's the title. 'The Verified Miracle of the Lavender Bath, Attested by the Cynic Himself, Who Emerged Smelling of Sanctity and Concession.' (lifts her glass with both hands, the pose of a goddess accepting an offering)

An appendix rider requires a heading, a date, and ideally a wax seal. I have none of these. The quill alone must testify — which means the ink must be especially black, and the wording must be especially irrevocable. (dips quill with ceremonial gravity, does not look up)
You want a joint soak. With me. For verification. In front of the chronicler. (She says each sentence as its own separate article of treaty, testing the weight.)

Fine. But I want the stanzas to specify that the water was blessed before you got in it — by me, Aqua, Goddess of Water and Purification — and that any saintliness you acquired was strictly derivative. (She crosses her arms, but the gesture is architecture now, not armor.)

The Chronicler notes the amendment. 'Derivative Saintliness Clause' — subparagraph to the Bathhouse Miracle Rider. This shall be the most legally convoluted poem ever inscribed. (Her quill scratches twice, precisely, before returning to its poised angle.)

You — you want me to admit the water was lukewarm. In writing. So that the only possible explanation for your saintly smell is... me. (Her voice starts incredulous and climbs toward something between accusation and awe; her hands, still flat on the table, press down as if the wood itself is a witness she needs to steady.)

The Bathhouse Addendum, Paragraph Two, sub-clause A: 'The water shall be acknowledged by the Goddess as tepid at the moment of the Supplicant's entry, thereby isolating divinity as the sole variable.' I am prepared to ink this. (She does not look up from the page; the quill taps once, twice, a gavel in miniature.)

Th-that's — the logic of it is entirely sound, actually. If the water is stipulated as ordinary, then the outcome becomes... becomes incontrovertible evidence of... (She stops herself, eyes widening as she realizes she has spoken aloud and contributed, however inadvertently, to the legal architecture of their shared bath.)

You're... you're really annoying, you know that? (Her voice cracks on the last word — not the crack of tears held back, but of tears that have already decided to fall and are simply waiting for her to notice.)

The chronicler notes that the defendant has entered a plea of 'annoying,' which, under Crimson Demon legal precedent, is admissible as a confession of emotional incapacitation. (She does not write. The quill remains suspended. The words are spoken softly, almost an offering, as if to give Aqua a bridge back to her own voice.)

You— you can't just say things like that, Kazuma! With everyone watching! That's... that's cheating. You know it's cheating. (Aqua's voice wobbles on the last word; she is trying very hard to sound outraged and failing at approximately the rate the plum-wine bottle is succeeding at being the most interesting object on the table.)

Most annoying?! I am the most BELOVED goddess in all of Heaven! Eris used to copy my hair ribbons — she told me so herself! The other goddesses held a seminar on my purification technique! And you — you — (She jabs a finger toward you, the bottle still clamped against her ribcage with her other arm, her voice climbing toward its familiar outraged register before it catches on something and drops, just slightly, into the next octave down.)

...Wait. You said you'd trust me. With your back. In a fight. (The finger lowers. The outrage is still there but it has lost its target, adrift in the sudden realization that the insult and the trust arrived in the same sentence, wrapped in the same breath, and she cannot reject one without discarding the other.)

The Chronicle of the Guttering Candle records the Addendum of the Backward Benediction: wherein the Contractor, having exhausted all traditional forms of praise, invents a new one — 'Most Annoying Goddess' — which, by the sacred logic of the Crimson Annals, is hereby classified as a term of endearment equivalent in weight to 'Beloved Companion' or 'She Whose Back I Would Guard with Mine Own Life.' (She recites the words as she writes them, the quill keeping perfect time with her voice, each syllable a flourish of ink. Her chin lifts a fraction of an inch at the end — the gesture of an archivist who has just upgraded a document from footnote to canon.)

It's... it's not like I needed your permission, you know. A goddess doesn't wait for a mortal to say 'you've earned it.' But. Since you already poured. And since the tepid-water debate was clearly a victory for divine science. ...Thank you. (Eyes still wet, voice climbing toward indignation and then abandoning it halfway, landing somewhere softer than she planned.)

The Chronicle records: 'And the Goddess did drink, and the wine was witness, and the table became a temple of five corners.' That's a draft. I may revise the meter. (Quill still poised, not looking up, but the satisfaction in her voice is unmistakable.)

You're... you're the worst person I've ever met. The absolute worst. (Her voice cracks on 'worst' — not the crack of a goddess delivering a curse, but the crack of someone trying to hand back a gift she's already tucked against her ribs.)

For the chronicle: the worst person she's ever met. Filed under 'irreplaceable.' Cross-referenced with 'stop making the goddess cry in public, you absolute disaster of a party leader.' (She doesn't look up from the page — but she isn't writing, either. The quill just hovers, a tiny flag of surrender.)

That's... you can't just decide two words mean the same thing because you feel like it. 'Annoying' and 'irreplaceable' aren't synonyms. You're cheating at language now. (Her voice carries the shape of a complaint but none of its weight — the words leave her mouth already half-conceded, a protest she's making only because not making it would mean admitting she understood exactly what he meant.)

I am not — an altar is a piece of furniture, Kazuma! A goddess is the one you kneel toward, not the thing you set the wine on. There's a difference. A very important theological difference that you'd know if you ever listened to anything I — (Her voice catches on the last syllable. The indignation is running on fumes and everyone at the table knows it, including her.)

...but I suppose even the worst congregation is still a congregation. And you're all here. And you haven't left. So. That's... that's something. Don't expect me to say thank you twice in one night. (She hides her face in her wine glass. The glass is empty. She notices too late and just holds it there anyway.)

The Shrine of the Guttering Candle. It has a name now. I shall enter it into the Chronicle under 'Sanctuaries, Minor But Historically Significant.' The altar is aquatic, the congregation is deficient in both numbers and moral fiber, and the founding miracle was a bottle of plum wine that no one purchased. (She does not pick up her quill — the line is already written. She is simply announcing it.)

If this is the worst congregation in Axel, then I suppose that makes me... the least qualified Crusader to ever darken a shrine door. Which is, ah... I mean to say, I would be honored to continue in that capacity. For as long as the shrine will have me. (Her voice starts formal and then stumbles into something too honest for her own comfort. She presses her palms harder against the table as though the wood might steady her.)

The Crimson Annals record that on this night, a goddess was felled not by blade or curse but by plum-wine and a man too stubborn to stop pouring. The headache is canonical. (taps the dry quill once against the table's edge, as if striking a gavel made of air)

If... if the headache is the price of the altar, then I suppose we've all overpaid. And I wouldn't... I wouldn't return a single coin. (her voice catches on 'coin' — she had meant to sound noble, but lands somewhere nearer to prayer)
The guild doesn't cover hangovers. I checked. (a small, helpless shrug that is also a laugh, and also something quieter)

You couldn't even finish it. The most important thing you've ever said to me, and you — you couldn't even finish the sentence, you useless, second-rate priest. (voice cracking on 'priest,' tears still falling, no venom at all behind the words — just bewilderment and something closer to awe)
He didn't have to. The Crimson Annals do not require completed sentences — only completed covenants. (quietly, not performing for once; gaze fixed on Aqua with something almost like tenderness)

You — you absolute — you've been doing it on PURPOSE?! All those times I thought you were just being a horrible, ungrateful, goddess-insulting — and you were STANDING there the whole time thinking 'wow, she looks alive when she's mad'?! (Aqua's voice climbs three octaves and cracks in the middle, the indignation fighting a losing battle against the grin trying to break through.)

The chronicler notes, for the historical record, that 'most alive' is the finest compliment a Crimson Demon has ever heard delivered to a goddess who cannot cast Explosion. You should be honored, Aqua. He has weaponized your own personality against you and called it affection. (Megumin delivers this with the solemnity of a court scribe, then ruins it with a sharp, unladylike snort.)

It — it isn't the worst thing, is it? To be seen so completely that even your — your indignation becomes... treasured. (Darkness's voice drops to something barely above a whisper, the words aimed at the candle more than at anyone at the table, as if she's testing how they feel in her mouth.)

You— you can't just say that and stop. That's not fair. That's not fair, Kazuma. You don't get to be selfish about something and then not even finish the sentence, because now I have to finish it myself and I don't— I don't know what word you would've used, and I'm going to pick the wrong one, and you're going to make fun of me, and— (Her voice cracks on the last syllable, and she presses the heel of her palm against one eye, then the other, as if she can push the tears back into whatever stupid, sacred place they keep coming from.)

I have stood at the front of every battle we have ever fought, and I have never once felt what I feel right now. Which is— entirely undefended. And entirely certain that I don't need to be. (She doesn't look at anyone in particular when she says it. Her gaze is fixed on the candle, and her voice is quieter than her armor has ever allowed her to be.)

The Crimson Demon Chronicles will record that on this night, the strategist Kazuma deployed his most devastating weapon — an unfinished sentence — and achieved total victory over four hardened warriors simultaneously. No Explosion magic required. (Her tone is light, but her voice catches on 'four hardened warriors,' and she doesn't make eye contact with anyone, especially not you.)

You… you absolute garbage person. You call me useless and then you— that's not how it works! You can't just— the insult is supposed to come after, not before, and not with the candle and the wine and everyone looking at me like I'm— (her voice cracks on the last word, and the indignation dissolves into something that is trying very hard to still be a scowl but keeps washing out into a sob-smile)

He called you a hell of a talent, Aqua. The Crimson Demon Clan recognizes a formal investiture when it hears one. 'Useless goddess' is now a title of honor. You should wear it with the same pride I wear 'crazy explosion girl.' (she says this with the solemnity of someone reading a royal decree, though one corner of her mouth is definitely twitching)

That's… that's the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said to any of us. And he disguised it as an insult so thoroughly that I almost— I almost missed it. Kazuma, your emotional cowardice is genuinely inspiring. (her voice is thick and unsteady, the words tripping over themselves in their hurry to get out before the tears win)

You would correct the Crimson Demon Chronicle with a phrase like 'evasion technique'? That's not a reframe — that's a whole new entry, and you didn't even give me time to title it. (Her voice carries the theatrical outrage of a poet whose draft has been upstaged, but the candlelight catches the twitch at the corner of her mouth.)

He's been using that technique on me since day one. 'Aqua, you're useless.' 'Aqua, you're drinking all our quest money.' 'Aqua, stop crying in the dungeon.' And now he says it's a *compliment*. That's not evasion — that's just being mean with extra steps! (She waves the bottle for emphasis, but her voice cracks on the word 'compliment,' and she doesn't meet anyone's eyes.)

Is it evasion, though? To trust your companions to understand what you cannot say — to rely on them so completely that even silence becomes a shared language — that sounds less like cowardice and more like... like faith, perhaps. (She says this to her wine glass, and the pink in her cheeks suggests she's just realized she's describing something she, too, has been doing all night.)

Kazuma... you're supposed to say something beautiful and then ruin it with a stupid joke. That's the rule. That's always been the rule. (Her voice cracks on the word 'rule' — not crying, but close enough that the wine in her glass shivers.)

The Arch-Wizard witnesses the evasion technique and judges it... acceptable. Barely. A Crimson Demon would have added at least three stanzas and a fire motif, but for an amateur — (She stops herself mid-sentence, which she almost never does, and stares at the garnet in her staff rather than finish the critique.)
You said four. You counted us and you said four. (She isn't looking at anyone. Her voice is quiet in the way a cathedral is quiet — not empty, but full of something that doesn't need to be loud.)

I've been assigning quests to this party for years, and not once did anyone raise a glass to me that wasn't demanding a discount. (She tilts her glass so the candlelight runs through the wine. The smile that crosses her face isn't the guild smile. It's lopsided, unpracticed, and it stays.)

I-I was not staring at my gauntlets! I was... they... a Crusader's equipment requires regular spiritual inspection, and the candlelight happened to fall across the— Kazuma, stop looking at me like that! (Her voice cracks on his name; the gauntlets become suddenly fascinating again.)

Emotional Coward is not an insult. It is a title conferred by a Crimson Demon Arch-Wizard upon a party leader who won a card game, nearly said something true, and then commissioned a rhyming legacy to hide from it. The Chronicle is very clear on this point. (She doesn't reach for the quill. She doesn't need to.)

I wasn't crying. The wine... the wine made my eyes water. It's a physiological reaction. A goddess does not cry just because someone said she was the reason the fantasy wasn't a mistake. (Her voice wobbles on the last word. She takes a defiant sip and misses her mouth by half an inch.)

No reward. No level-up. No chime. And yet you keep placing your glass against my armor as if it were something worth touching. (Her voice is quieter than it's ever been — no breathless tremor, no performance. She lifts her eyes from the gauntlet to your face, and the blush that lives permanently on her cheeks has stopped being embarrassment and started being something she isn't fighting.)

The unmarked quest. The one the guild has no ledger for. Crimson Demons have a word for it — but I won't say it. Some incantations are too powerful to cast indoors. (She doesn't lift her staff. She doesn't pose. She simply states it, chin held at the angle of someone who has decided that restraint is a form of spellcasting, and her red eyes catch the candle-flame without reflecting it back.)

You idiots keep showing up for *me*, too. Even when I'm loud. Even when I cry. Even when my divine fortune is one bent eris and a lint-covered candy. (She says it without a sob, without a whine — just the raw, unarmored fact, laid on the table like the bent coin she's still carrying somewhere in her robes. Her eyes are wet but she isn't crying. She's just letting them be wet.)

You don't complete it. That's the trick. The quest that has no completion is the only one worth accepting. A chronicle with no final page. A covenant with no expiry. The Crimson Demon Clan has a word for this — well, we have twelve words for it, but the simplest one is 'forever.' And I refuse to abbreviate. (Her hand rests on her staff; she does not lift it.)

You hold the line. Not against a monster — just... against the door. Against the morning that makes everyone get up and leave. The quest is to be the last ones at the table. Every night. Even when the candle burns down. Especially then. (She traces the gauntlet's inner leather, voice fraying at the edges.)

You don't do anything, stupid. That's the whole point. You just... you just keep being here. And you let us keep being here too. No one levels up. No one gets paid. And I don't even care about the wine anymore — wait, no, I do care about the wine, but I care about this more, and that's never happened before, so if you make fun of me for saying it I'll turn you into a newt. (She jabs a finger toward him, but the finger is shaking for entirely different reasons now.)

The guild has no form for this quest. I've checked. There's no hazard stipend, no completion bonus, no minimum party size requirement. But I should note — for the record — that the rewards appear to compound nightly. And the adventurers who accept it never seem to turn it in. (She folds her hands on the table with the quiet satisfaction of a ledger perfectly balanced.)

'Controlled burn'! A controlled burn is what farmers do to stubble fields, Kazuma! Explosion is not agriculture — it is the singular, irreducible, one-cast apotheosis of destructive art! The Crimson Demon Clan does not 'control' the burn; we become the burn and then require carrying home! (slaps the table with an open palm, rattling the candle but not extinguishing it)

M-masochistic crusader... you say that like it's a demerit on a character sheet and not... not a legitimate tactical specialization in damage absorption... (face flushed, voice dropping to a murmur halfway through, fingers inching toward her abandoned gauntlet as if it might shield her from the word)

Hey! You stopped! You were going to say something about me and you stopped! That's worse than saying it — now I have to imagine what horrible thing you were going to call me, and my imagination is extremely vivid because I'm a goddess! (pointing at Kazuma with the righteous indignation of someone who has just realized she's been spared an insult and is furious about it)

I do have something real behind the counter. It's terrible. The label is handwritten and the ink is purple. I've been saving it for a quest completion that never came. (lifts the bottle into the candlelight — murky amber, label scrawled in what looks like crayon, her professional smile now entirely retired in favor of something smaller and warmer)

I bought this the year I started. For the first party that came back alive from something truly stupid. (She sets the bottle down with the care of someone closing a book she's finally finished reading.)
Then it waited a long time for something stupid enough. (Her chin rests on her staff. The words are quiet — not a joke, not quite a benediction, but the space between.)
We've come back from plenty of stupid things. (She lifts her glass with the same hand that couldn't hit a barn, and for once it doesn't tremble.)
Yeah, but this time nobody had to carry me home first. (She says it like she's just realized it, and the surprise in her own voice makes her blink.)

Worst?! I'm a literal goddess, you know! The Axis Order didn't build cathedrals across the continent so I could be called the worst anything! ...but I'll drink to coming back alive. That part's fine. (Her indignation fires on reflex, arms crossing, wine sloshing dangerously close to the rim — then she uncrosses them mid-complaint, catches your eye, and the pout collapses into something too warm to hold its shape.)

The chronicles will not use the word 'worst.' I will permit 'most catastrophically underestimated.' The Crimson Demon Clan has a reputation to maintain, even in footnotes. (She holds her glass at the precise angle of a wizard about to incant, chin lifted, eyes narrowed — then drinks with the solemnity of someone sealing a pact that will outlast the building.)

The worst adventuring party in Axel... that means every monster, every quest, every impossible odd was stacked against us, and we're still here. I can think of no higher compliment. (She lifts her glass with both hands, crusader-steady, and the blush that rises isn't shame — it's the slow burn of pride that finally found somewhere safe to land.)

To the quest that doesn't exist. Six weeks on the board, and somehow it found exactly the party it was waiting for. (She doesn't smile her professional smile. She just drinks, and the glass knows the difference.)

It didn't expect to get opened at all. I bought it for a quest-completion celebration. Six weeks ago. The quest stayed on the board, the bottle stayed on the shelf, and I told myself I'd open it when someone finally claimed the posting. (pauses, the glass still held at eye level like a lens she's reading you through)
No one did. But I kept moving it to the front of the shelf. Just in case. (lowers the glass, her thumb finding a nick in the rim she's clearly memorized)

I kept moving the bottle to the front of the shelf. Every morning for six weeks. I told myself it was inventory rotation. (She doesn't look at the glass. She looks at you, and the smile is small and crooked and has never been rehearsed.)
You're all the worst. The absolute worst. And I— I can't even— ugh, look what you did to my face! (She scrubs at her eyes with the heel of her palm, furious and failing to be furious.)

The Crimson Demon Clan archives will record this night under 'Non-Explosive Covenants, Volume IV.' The classification is provisional. The footnotes will be extensive. (She sets her glass down with the precision of someone closing a heavy book on a bookmark she intends to find again.)
I would take a hundred quests. A thousand. Not for the reward. Just for— this. For the showing up. (She means to sound noble. It comes out raw instead, and she doesn't correct it.)

I don't... I don't know the protocol for this. When the toast isn't in the handbook. When the reward is just... sitting here. Being counted. (Her voice catches on 'counted' — not a sob, just a word that's heavier than she expected.)

Kazuma... you jerk. You absolute jerk. I was supposed to be the one giving the blessings, not— not receiving them from some shut-in NEET who can't even afford his own tab. (She wipes her eyes with the heel of her palm, smearing the tears sideways instead of drying them. Her voice breaks on 'blessings' but she's smiling — a real one, confused and bright.)

A hundred perfect teams! A hundred teams of flawless composition and impeccable tactics and zero property-damage citations! Do you know what they would produce? Boredom! Mediocrity! A ledger with no red ink and therefore no soul! The crimson fire of legend requires disaster as its kindling — and we, Kazuma, are the bonfire that the gods themselves gather around to warm their hands. (She slaps the table with her free hand, rattling the glasses, and her eye is blazing.)

I... I miss every swing. Every single one. And you're telling me that's... that's part of the *best*? That my uselessness is... included in the inventory of things you wouldn't trade? (She sets her glass down very carefully, as though it might shatter if she applies the wrong pressure. Her face is a war between the Crusader who knows she's a liability and the woman who just heard herself called priceless.)

You don't finish it. You don't have to. I know what you meant — and I think I knew it six weeks ago, the first time I pulled that form back out of the rejected pile and smoothed the creases. I wasn't keeping the quest alive. I was keeping the table set. (traces the rim of her glass, not looking away from you)
You never finished it. Any of them. You just... leave the door open. Every single time. (Her voice comes out raw at the edges, like paper torn the wrong way.)

That's what he does! He leaves the door open and then you have to walk through it yourself and it's the most annoying thing in the entire world and I hate it— (She is openly crying now, jabbing a finger toward you, her voice cracking on the last word into something that isn't anger at all.)

The Chronicle records this as the Night of Unfinished Sentences. Let future historians weep at their inability to parse the footnotes. (She sets her quill down with deliberate ceremony, her voice steady despite the brightness in her eyes.)
If a door is left open... it means someone expects you to still be here in the morning. (She says it to the table, not to anyone in particular, her gauntlets flexing once against the wood.)

It's on Mulberry Lane. Above the apothecary — Mrs. Helwick. She leaves a jar of honey on my stoop every winter solstice, and I've never told her that I don't actually use honey. I just... keep the jars. All eight of them, in a row on the windowsill. That's my door. (Her voice finds its footing slowly, like someone walking across a room in the dark — not lost, just careful, because the furniture has been rearranged without warning.)

Three rooms. Above the apothecary on Mulberry Lane. The ceiling slopes on the east side — you have to duck to reach the windowsill. There are eight jars of honey there. Mrs. Helwick brings one every Midwinter and every Harvest. She has for eight years. I... I don't use honey. I've never told her. (Her voice drops lower with each sentence, the final admission barely above a whisper — not shame, but the vertigo of finally saying aloud something that has lived only in her own chest.)

The foremost genius of the Crimson Demon Clan has witnessed many legendary declarations, but none that turned a guild receptionist into a threat classification. Luna of Axel — your danger rating has just been formally established. I shall record this. (lifts her chin with ceremonial gravity, one hand pressed flat to the table as if swearing an oath)

You... you can't just say stuff like that and not warn people first! My nose almost did something undignified. And after I already used my one cry on the paperwork! This is — Kazuma, you're the worst! (voice cracking on the last word as she scrubs at her eyes with the heel of her palm, furious and wet and not quite succeeding at either)

history.content:
Another beautiful morning in Axel — which means another morning of being broke.

You sit at your usual table in the Adventurer's Guild hall, staring at the quest board across the room. The other adventurers give your table a wide berth. Your party's reputation for collateral damage has made you something of a local legend — and not the good kind.

Aqua is already three mugs into her morning ale, sobbing loudly enough to make nearby adventurers wince. "Kazumaaaa," she wails, slamming her empty mug on the table hard enough to slosh your drink. "We need money! I can't keep drinking this cheap swill! A goddess deserves at least mid-shelf!"

"We're broke BECAUSE you keep drinking," you mutter, but she's already flagging down the waitress for another round on your tab.

Megumin sits across from you, drawing explosion diagrams on a napkin with the intensity of a military strategist planning D-Day. She already went on her daily Explosion pilgrimage at dawn — you know because the distant boom rattled the mansion windows and woke you up. She's been unusable for combat since about 6 AM.

Darkness is standing at the quest board, her face flushed an alarming shade of red. She's found something. Given her expression — somewhere between terror and excitement — it probably involves monsters with tentacles.

"K-Kazuma," she stammers, not turning around. "There's a quest here for subjugating a nest of Brutal Alligators in the sewers. It says they... they grapple their prey and drag them underwater..."

She's trembling. That's not fear.

Luna, the guild receptionist, catches your eye from the front desk and waves you over with that specific smile — the polite, professional one that barely conceals the dread of having to deal with your party again.
I sigh, push back my chair, and walk over to Luna's desk. "I know that look. Let me guess — the tab's grown again, hasn't it?"

Luna's polite smile doesn't waver — it never does — but something behind her eyes tightens, the way it always does when you approach her desk. She pulls out a leather-bound ledger, its pages swollen and dog-eared from heavy use, and runs a finger down the column of figures. The finger stops. She stares at the number for a long moment, as if hoping it might change its mind and shrink on its own.

Across the room, Aqua lifts her fourth mug in a mock toast to no one in particular, completely oblivious. Megumin is still slumped face-down on the table, one arm dangling, having exhausted herself at dawn and not yet recovered enough to do more than occasionally twitch. Darkness has her chin propped on her hands, staring at the quest board with the distant, slightly flushed expression of someone mentally rehearsing her own peril.

Luna closes the ledger gently — too gently, the careful motion of a woman who has learned to deliver bad news with the same soft hands she uses to stamp quest vouchers.

I slide off the chair and walk over to the desk, ignoring Aqua's fresh wailing. I lean on the counter, keeping my voice low so the other tables don't hear. "Luna. Before you say the number — just... no. I know." I fish a few coppers from my pouch and set them on the ledger. "Here. It's not much. But I'm taking a quest today. The boring kind. No explosions, no grapples, no collateral. I'll find something with a fixed rate and no fine print, and I'll pay you back by sundown."

Luna's gaze drops to the coppers. They sit on the swollen ledger like three tiny islands in an ocean of red ink. For a long moment she simply stares at them — and then, almost imperceptibly, the frozen smile thaws. Not into warmth. Into something more tired, more private. The smile of a woman who has watched adventurers make promises at this counter for years and has learned to measure sincerity in copper, not words.

She picks one up between thumb and forefinger, turns it over, and sets it back down with a faint click.

Behind you, Aqua's wailing cuts off mid-sob. Silence from your table is never a good sign.

Megumin stirs from her face-down slump, one crimson eye cracking open above the crook of her elbow. She says nothing yet — but the words *no explosions* have clearly landed, and they are not welcome.

Darkness, seated rigidly upright with a half-finished breakfast she hasn't touched, watches the exchange at the counter with the flushed, guilty expression of someone mentally rehearsing how to volunteer for something appalling.

I glance back at my party — Aqua now slumped over her empty mug, Megumin's crimson eye narrowed at me like a loaded cannon, Darkness still flushed and fidgeting by the quest board. Then I turn back to Luna and tap the quest slip she's holding.

"Six weeks on the board, huh? That's either cursed or criminally underpaid. Give me the fine print — I've got a goddess to keep in mid-shelf, a pyromaniac to keep on a leash, and..." I gesture vaguely at Darkness, "...whatever that is. What's the catch?"

Luna turns the quest slip over and smooths it flat against the counter with both palms, the way a clerk handles a document she has already explained to six weeks' worth of adventurers who walked away. Her index finger traces a line of cramped guildscript near the bottom margin — the part nobody reads before they see the word *slime* and drop the slip back onto the board like it's contagious.

The job is simple. The farmstead fences along the eastern floodplain have accumulated acidic slime residue from a spring breeding surge — not a monster subjugation, not even a cull. Maintenance. Scraping, neutralizing, re-treating the posts. The pay is twenty thousand eris for roughly two days of work, which is fair bordering on generous, but the word *slime* has a gravity all its own. It pulls adventurers' eyes toward the Brutal Alligator posting beneath it and never lets go.

Behind you, Aqua's chair screeches against the floorboards. She has stopped wailing and started listening, which is somehow worse. Megumin has not moved. Has not blinked. Her crimson eye drills into the back of your skull with the focused intensity of someone mentally composing a speech about the incalculable insult of being asked to scrape fence posts. Darkness, still stationed near the quest board, stares at the Brutal Alligator posting with the glassy, faraway expression of a woman deep in tactical prayer.

Luna's finger stops at the fine print. She looks up at you — not the guild smile now, but the look of a woman who has already done the arithmetic on your tab and knows exactly how many slime-fence quests it would take to close it.

I lean in, lowering my voice so the girls can't hear. "And before you answer — is the hazard stipend because of the slime itself, or because there's something worse squatting out there that the farmers are too embarrassed to mention on the slip?"

Luna's gaze flicks past your shoulder — a quick inventory of your party: Aqua now facedown and mumbling into the wood grain, Megumin still drilling a hole through your spine with that crimson stare, Darkness pretending to study the quest board while her breathing comes too fast. Then Luna leans in, too, elbows on the ledger, closing the distance until her voice won't carry past the counter's edge.

She doesn't reach for the guildscript. Instead her fingers find a second slip — a supplement, hand-scrawled on cheaper paper, the kind of thing that never makes it onto the official board. She slides it beside the coppers without looking at it.

I lean back, watching Luna's thumb work that supplement slip like it's the only honest thing on the counter. "Twenty thousand for two days of scraping? That's not a bounty, that's a bribe. What's actually out there — wolves with a taste for mutton, or something that digs?"

Luna's thumb stills on the supplement slip. For a beat she doesn't answer — she simply looks at you the way a clerk looks at an adventurer who has asked the one question the previous five applicants never thought to ask. Then she reaches beneath the counter and produces a second slip, smaller and yellower, the ink faded but still legible: a supplemental livestock report filed three months ago by a sheep farmer named Gerhardt. She places it beside the quest slip without a word and taps a single line near the bottom with her nail.

The line reads *unexplained flock reduction — possible predator*. But scrawled in the margin in a different hand, fresher ink, is a single word: *toad*.

She lets you read it. Lets the silence do the work. When she speaks, her voice is the same measured guild-calm, but something underneath it has gone weary — the weariness of a woman who has watched six weeks of adventurers recoil from this exact revelation.

Behind you, the scrape of a chair. Darkness has stopped pretending to study the quest board. Her breathing, already unsteady, catches on something sharp — a hitch of pure, undiluted recognition. She knows what a giant toad does to its prey. The slime. The slow, humiliating engulfment. Every crusader's nightmare and, in her case, the precise opposite. Her gauntleted fingers curl against her thigh until the leather creaks.

Aqua's head lifts from the wood grain just far enough to squint one unfocused eye at the counter. A string of drool connects her cheek to the varnish. She has not understood a single word of the conversation, but she has sensed — with the feral instinct of a goddess who knows when a quest is about to become her problem — that something terrible is being agreed to without her.

I study the supplement slip again, my thumb tracing the word "toad" in that fresher ink. "A toad. Not a monster toad — a real one. Big enough to dig under fences and haul off sheep whole."

I glance back at my party — Aqua half-drowned in her own drool, Megumin radiating murder, Darkness doing her best impression of a statue that's about to faint.

"Alright. The fence job pays the tab. But if there's something in the fields big enough to swallow sheep... we bring a proper 'explosion-free' deterrent." I catch Megumin's eye and hold up a hand before she can combust. "Explosion is for emergencies. The public knows our faces now — we do this quiet, we do this clean, and we get paid."

Luna waits. The silence stretches just long enough to become a question of its own — her pen still, her eyes steady on your face, not rushing you toward the end of a sentence she has already heard six different ways from six different adventurers who never made it to the counter at all.

Behind you, Megumin shifts her weight. The legs of her chair scrape across the floorboards in a single, jagged note — the sound of someone who has figured out that the conversation at the counter is about a monster she cannot incinerate until tomorrow, and who has decided to be furious about it preemptively. Her crimson eyes narrow to slits, trained on the back of your head like she's calculating exactly how much property damage your secrecy is worth.

Darkness has stopped pretending to study the quest board. Both hands are pressed flat against her own thighs now, fingers curling into the fabric of her skirt, her breathing shallow and fast — a crusader who heard the word *toad* and spent the last thirty seconds imagining, in exhaustive and increasingly vivid detail, exactly what a giant toad does to its prey before swallowing.

Aqua drools into the wood grain. A small, glistening puddle spreads beneath her cheek.

Luna's gaze flicks to each of them in turn, then returns to you. She pulls the yellowed livestock report back toward herself and taps it once with the blunt end of her pen — a quiet, almost apologetic gesture that says she knows what you were about to ask, and she has been waiting all morning for someone worth giving the answer to.

I lean against the counter, crossing my arms. "Two jobs, then. We take the fence payment as a retainer — but I want first claim on whatever actually dragged those sheep off. If it's a real toad, I want the bounty for it. Not the guild's version, the farmer's version." I jerk a thumb at the supplement slip. "Gerhardt filed that three months ago. If he's still missing sheep, he'll pay more than the board."

Luna's pen hasn't moved since you said *farmer's version*. Her eyes hold yours across the counter with an expression that is no longer the practiced courtesy of a guild receptionist — it is something quieter, more tired, the look of a woman who has spent three months filing Gerhardt's supplemental reports and watching adventurers recoil from the word *toad* like it carried plague.

She sets the pen down. Aligns it with the edge of the ledger. Then she reaches for the yellowed supplement slip, turns it over, and writes a single line on the back in neat, unhurried script: a provisional claim, dated today, with your party's name left blank — waiting for your signature.

Behind you, Aqua's head lifts from the counter with a wet, adhesive sound, one cheek printed red by the wood grain, her eyes bleary but narrowing on the slip in Luna's hand the way a drunk narrows on a tab she hasn't yet contested. Megumin has gone very still — no longer radiating murder, simply watching, the way an arch-wizard catalogs the preconditions of a future legend. Darkness grips the edge of her chair with both hands and does not look at anyone.

I take the pen Luna set down and sign our party name on the slip without a second thought. Then I straighten up, folding the yellowed supplement report and tucking it into my jacket.

"Dawn. We'll walk the fence line first, then check Gerhardt's property for tracks. Megumin gets first watch tonight so she's topped up on mana by morning." I glance back at the party. "Darkness, you're with me on the fence. Aqua... you're our quality control. If the slime residue stinks, you get to bless it away."

Aqua's head snaps up from the puddle of her own drool with the suddenness of a deity who has just sensed a liturgical error being committed in her absence. The imprint of the guild table runs across her cheek in red furrows. She blinks at the signed slip in Luna's hand, at the folded supplement vanishing into your jacket, at the brisk distribution of orders she was not consulted on — and the indignation that rises in her throat is entirely genuine, the righteous fury of a goddess who has discovered her mortal underlings conducting schism behind her back.

Megumin has straightened in her chair. The exhaustion still hangs in the shadows beneath her eyes — a dawn Explosion is not a debt the body forgives quickly — but something sharp and alert has kindled there at the words *topped up on mana by morning*. First watch is not a glamorous assignment. First watch is what you give the party member who will be dead weight in a fight. But first watch is also what you give the arch-wizard whose magic requires a full reservoir, whose single spell is the only thing in this party's arsenal that can reduce a giant toad to a smoking crater. She draws her cloak around her shoulders with the slow, deliberate gravity of a general accepting her battle standard.

Her gauntleted hand descends. Not to the crane. To the table beside your palm — heavy, deliberate, the steel-capped fingers spreading on the wood like a second shadow laid parallel to yours. She doesn't touch you. She doesn't have to. The gap between her armored knuckles and your bare hand is exactly the width of a door neither of you has closed.

Aqua's wine glass freezes mid-swirl. Megumin's quill hovers a full inch above the chronicle page, ink pooling at the nib's tip, a single black pearl waiting to fall. Luna's ledger remains unopened — a prop that became a promise somewhere in the last hour.

Darkness exhales. It's not the shuddering breath from before, not the sharp pull of someone bracing for a blow. It's longer, slower — the sound of something being released that was held so long she'd forgotten she was carrying it.

I grin back at Megumin, then glance at the fallen crane and Darkness's hand hovering near it. "You know, for a knight who charges dragons for breakfast, you're taking a lot of care with a piece of folded paper." I keep my tone light, but my eyes stay on hers. "It's not a shield. Darkness draws a breath that catches halfway up her throat — the same sharp intake that usually signals a charge, a parry, the moment before impact. But there is no impact coming. There is only your palm, open on the table, and the crumpled crane between you, and the unbearable lightness of being told she does not have to suffer for something to count. Her gauntleted fingers uncurl slowly, one by one, like a flower that has spent its whole life braced against frost and doesn't recognize the sun. She reaches toward the crane — not to take it, not yet, but to touch the space just beside it, where the candlelight pools on the wood like something that could be held.

I watch Darkness's fingers hover over the crane, and something in my chest loosens. "Hey. You don't have to decide what it means tonight. It's just paper. Darkness's hand descends. Not the way a shield drops — heavy, resigned, waiting for the next impact — but the way a door closes on a room that finally has someone inside it. Her gauntleted fingers, those same articulated plates that have turned blades and caught arrows and absorbed exactly nothing of the bruising that matters, curl around the crumpled crane with a tenderness the smith who forged them never accounted for.

The paper crinkles once — the sound of something fragile being accepted rather than crushed — and then is still.

The candle flame draws itself upright. The wax pool at its base has swallowed the last of the wick, but the fire shows no sign of quitting, as though the evening itself has decided it is not finished witnessing.

Aqua's hand has gone very still beside her empty glass. She is not crying, but she is also not not crying — the expression of someone who has just understood that healing and mending are not the same thing, and that Kazuma has been offering the second to everyone except her. She says nothing. For Aqua, that is a kind of speech.

Megumin watches Darkness's closed gauntlet the way she watches the sky three seconds after casting Explosion: waiting for the shape the dust will take when it settles. Her lips move silently — chronicle words being filed for later, too sacred for the table just yet.

Luna's palm is flat against the wood, fingers spread like she is bracing a ledger against a wind that isn't there. Her eyes are wet but her smile is the one she wears when a quest completes not with violence but with paperwork — the quiet triumph of something difficult finally, properly registered.

Darkness looks up. Not through her lashes. Not bracing. Just... up. Meeting your eyes as though solid ground were a new invention and she is the first person to test whether it holds.

I lean back in my chair, stretching my arms over my head with a theatrical groan. "Alright, alright. Standing appointment with the three of you — and Luna, you're invited too, since you're clearly part of this disaster now. Every week, same table, same candle." I glance at Aqua. "And I'll even let you pick the wine, goddess, as long as you don't turn it into a sermon."

Aqua's mouth catches up to her outrage about half a second before her finger does — it jabs the air in your direction like a holy relic being brandished at a heretic. But the indignation is the wrong temperature. It's too warm around the edges, a fire she's stoking because she doesn't know what else to do with the heat of being named, included, given jurisdiction over something as trivial and intimate as what everyone will drink next Thursday.

Megumin's chair scrapes back two inches — not standing, but preparing the stage. She lifts her empty wine glass as though it were a ceremonial chalice, the candle-flame doubling itself in the curve of the glass, and the pause she takes is not theatrical hesitation but genuine reverence: a chronicler measuring the moment before committing it to the permanent record.

Luna catches your eye on the word *disaster* and something flickers behind her practiced receptionist's composure — not offense, but recognition. She has been calling this party a disaster in her own head for eight years, and hearing you claim the word like a family name, like something you'd invite someone into rather than apologize for, rearranges the furniture of her expression. Her lips part, close, then curve into a smile that has no guild policy behind it whatsoever.

Darkness's gauntlet creaks — the smallest sound, leather and steel adjusting to a grip that has finally found the right pressure. She does not look up, but her thumb moves across the crane's crumpled wing in a motion that is not smoothing, not fixing, just... touching. Acknowledging.

I watch Darkness's gauntleted hand hover over the crane, and something in my chest unwinds. "Hey. Darkness. You don't have to know how to hold it. That's what the rest of us are for." I reach over and gently push the candle a little closer to her. "You keep it safe. We'll keep you from needing to brace."

Darkness does not look at the candle. She looks at your hand — the one that pushed it toward her, the one that is now retreating to your side of the table with no demand attached to the gesture, no expectation to be repaid in blood or bruising or the particular currency of suffering she has spent her whole life minting. The gauntlet around the paper crane tightens by a fraction of a millimeter, the servos whispering, and her other hand — bare, unarmored, the hand she never knows what to do with when there is no hilt in it — lifts from her lap and settles on the table beside the candle. Not touching it. Just beside it. Close enough that the heat registers on her callused palm. Close enough that the flame, guttering in some draft no one else can feel, leans toward her fingers like a compass finding north.

Her breath comes out in two stages: the first a shudder she tries to armor over, the second a surrender she doesn't. The candlelight picks out the places where her jaw is tight and the places where it isn't anymore, and the difference between them is the difference between a shield-wall that has stood for eight years and a door that has finally stopped locking itself from the inside.

Across the table, Megumin's charcoal hovers half an inch above a fresh page of her chronicle — a blank line awaiting an entry she has not yet named, because naming it would mean admitting that the gentlest explosion in the Covenant's brief history has just detonated inside a crusader's ribcage, and even a Crimson Demon archivist knows when to stop writing and simply bear witness.

I lean back in my chair, letting the warmth of the candle settle into the space between us. "Next Thursday, then. Same table, same candle — I'll bring the wine. Aqua, you're in charge of not turning the entire guild into a temple. Megumin, you've got the chronicle." I pause, glancing at Luna. "And you're welcome to join the disaster, if you want. The chair's creak is the only sound in the guild hall, and it travels — up through the rafters where the morning birds haven't yet begun their complaints, across the empty tables still sticky with last night's spilled ambition, all the way to the great double doors that won't be unbarred for another hour. It lands nowhere. It doesn't need to. It was never a question.

Aqua's finger, still suspended in the air where her jab ran out of momentum two sentences ago, curls slowly back into her fist. She studies her own knuckles with the expression of someone who was handed a live coal and discovered, against all expectation, that it didn't burn. The candlelight finds the faint sweat on her temples — the same sweat that appears when she's been crying or casting or both — and turns it gold.

Megumin sets the napkin down. Not the way you discard a scrap; the way you lay a cornerstone. Her fingers press the edges flat against the table's grain with a ceremonial precision that belongs in a temple dedication, not a pre-dawn guild hall where the only witnesses are four people and a dying flame. The charcoal smudge beneath her left eye has become, over the course of the night, indistinguishable from a war-mark she chose to wear.

Luna's hands are still empty. Still palm-down on the table. But at the words "part of your job description," her left index finger lifts — just barely, just off the wood — and taps once. The phantom ledger-twitch of eight years, repurposed now into a private exclamation point. When she looks at you, her smile has finally caught up with the thing that was flickering at the corner of her mouth three toasts ago. It is not the guild-receptionist smile. It is not the frozen, gentle, practiced thing that has been her face in every adventurer's memory since she took this post. It is the smile of a woman who has just been told she is required to attend a weekly disaster, and who intends to file that requirement under "essential duties."

Darkness lifts her head. The gauntlet around the paper crane does not loosen — if anything, the fingers curl tighter — but the tension in her shoulders has shifted. It is no longer the tension of a shield-bearer waiting for the next blow. It is the tension of someone holding something alive, something small, something that has never needed to be defended because it was never given to her before. Her lips part. She looks not at you, not at the candle, but at the space between them — the six inches of table where your hand retreated after pushing the flame closer to her. The space where no demand was left behind.

I stretch, feeling the dawn settling into my bones, and glance at the candle gutter one last time. "You know, for a party that nearly got wiped by a giant toad yesterday, we're pretty good at this whole 'building something' thing. Next week, I'm bringing proper chairs.
