The stretch travels through you like something that has been waiting for permission — not the cramped-knot release of a body that slept wrong on a tavern bench, but the slow unspooling of a muscle that forgot it was allowed to unclench. The candle, guttering now to a wobbling bead of wax-light no taller than a thumbnail, seems to lean toward you as you move, as though the flame itself is listening for what comes after *building something*.

Aqua's mouth opens and closes once, a fish-gasp of reflexive indignation that doesn't quite find its footing. The giant toad mention is a direct hit on her personal mythology of grievance — she was the one who came out slime-slicked and shrieking, she is always the one — but the warmth in the room is a different solvent now, and the protest curdles on her tongue into something closer to a pout. She settles for crossing her arms and looking at the ceiling with the particular expression of a goddess who has decided, against all precedent, to be magnanimous.

Megumin's chin lifts. The word *chronicle* is still fresh in her mind like ink that hasn't dried, and the mention of chairs — proper chairs, tablecloth, the furniture of permanence — strikes her not as domestic logistics but as infrastructure for legend. Her fingers twitch toward the absent notebook she is already composing in her head, the first entry of the Covenant that will, in time, outlast even the candle.

Darkness looks down at the paper crane in her gauntleted palm and then at your face, and the connection between *nearly got wiped* and *we're pretty good at this* lands somewhere behind her sternum with more force than any toad ever managed. The tablecloth detail — that small, soft, unnecessary detail — makes her eyes sting in a way she does not have armor for. She blinks, hard, and the candle-flame doubles and blurs and resolves again.

Luna has not moved since you said *join the disaster*. But now, at *proper chairs*, her professional instinct — *no outside furniture in the guild hall, it's regulation seven, paragraph four* — flickers up and dies in the same breath, because the breath she's drawing is not the efficient sip of a receptionist clocking a policy violation. It's the full-lung exhale of someone who has just realized she gets to be here for the argument about tablecloths.

I lean back in my chair, watching Darkness hold that candle like it's the first fragile thing she's ever been allowed to keep instead of protect. "You know, Darkness... the oath doesn't have to be the only thing you know how to be." I say it quietly, not looking at her, because looking at her right now feels like staring into the sun. "You can also be the one who gets to hold the light sometimes. That's not breaking. That's just... adding to the party sheet."

You don't look at her, and that is the part that breaks her.

She has been looked at her whole life. Looked at by tutors who measured the set of her shoulders against the Ford Dustiness legacy — *too soft, too eager, too much*. Looked at by commanders who calculated her value in absorbed damage per minute. Looked at by monsters who saw only the gap between her armor plates and the skin beneath, and she welcomed those looks because at least they knew what to do with her. Even comrades — even *you*, across a hundred campfires and a thousand bad decisions — have looked at her with exasperation, affection, the particular exhausted fondness reserved for a tank who keeps missing.

But you're not looking at her now. You're looking at the candle, or the rafters, or the grain of the table — anywhere but the place where Lalatina Ford Dustiness is learning, in real time, that she is allowed to exist without a wound as proof of purchase.

The candle gutters. The bead of wax is almost gone now, a shivering hemisphere of light no bigger than a fingernail, and Darkness watches it the way a woman drowning watches a hand she has been told she does not have to earn. Her gauntleted fingers — the same fingers that have held a greatsword against a Demon King general, the same fingers that have dug trenches in frozen earth for barricades nobody else would build — curl upward around the flame's heat without touching it. Not a shield. Not a wall. Just a cup. Just a place where light can rest without being asked to burn anything down.

The paper crane in her other hand has gone still. No trembling. No Knight's Discipline breathing exercises. Just a small crumpled bird held by a woman who is learning, at twenty-three years old, that tenderness is not a synonym for weakness and that some things — some precious, winged, impossible things — are meant to be kept, not protected. The distinction is new to her. It lands in her chest like a blow she never trained for.

Aqua watches from across the table, and for once her mouth does not open to fill the silence. Her hand has found the stem of an empty glass and is turning it slowly, clockwise, like winding a clock that has no numbers — just the shape of a goddess realizing she is not the only one who has been waiting to be seen as something other than her function.

Megumin's charcoal stick has stopped moving. The chronicle page beneath her fingers holds only a half-finished line: *And the Architect, not looking at her, said —* The rest is blank. She does not fill it. Some sentences, she is learning, need to finish themselves.

Luna touches the key in her pocket — the one to the storage room, the one that means *chairs, a tablecloth, something permanent* — and presses it into her palm until the teeth leave small red marks. Regulation 7.4 has never felt so far away.

The candle flame straightens. It should be dying — the wax is nearly spent, the wick a blackened stub — but something in the air holds it upright, as though the room itself is refusing to let the light go out before she is ready.

I drum my fingers on the table, feeling the grain under my thumb. "So here's my proposition. Every week, one candle. One tablecloth. One disaster that we survive together. The only rule is nobody gets to be a hero unless everyone gets to sit down afterwards." I finally let myself glance at her—just a flicker, just enough. "Think you can handle a rule that isn't about taking hits for once?"

Your drumming fingers still against the grain. The sound doesn't stop so much as it transfers — into the wax pooling at the candle's base, into the shallow tremor running through Darkness's gauntlet where it rests beside the napkin crane she toppled and never rebuilt, into the silence that follows a question asked not as a dare but as a door held open.

She doesn't answer.

What she does is harder. She sets the candle down — not with the ceremonial precision of someone handling a relic, but with the clumsy care of someone placing an egg on a counter and trusting the surface to hold. Her fingers uncurl from around the glass one by one, each joint releasing a vigilance you have watched her carry since the day she introduced herself by her title instead of her name. The flame wobbles, rights itself, and the light catches the wetness tracking down her cheek before she can wipe it with the back of her wrist. She doesn't wipe it. She lets it fall onto the table — a single dark spot on the wood that will be gone by morning and permanent in the chronicle Megumin is already inscribing with charcoal-stained fingers, her quill-less hand moving across an imaginary page as though the words might escape if she doesn't trap them now.

Aqua opens her mouth and closes it. The motion is so unlike her — a goddess who has never met a silence she couldn't flood — that Luna, seated at the edge of the table with her regulation-key still pressed into her palm, turns to watch the miracle of restraint happen in real time.

Darkness breathes. It is not the shuddering breath from before, the one that sounded like a door straining against its hinges. This one is quieter. It is the breath of someone stepping onto ice that has been tested by someone else's weight first.

I lean back in my chair, letting the silence stretch just long enough to feel earned. "You know, I've been thinking about what makes a party worth keeping together. It's not the quests. Not the loot. Not even the glory—" I glance at Megumin, "—sorry, the *explosions*." A pause. "It's that someone's always watching your back even when there's nothing to fight. That's what I signed up for. That's what I'm still signing up for, every week, if you three will have me."

The silence that follows isn't empty. It fills the space between your chair and theirs like water finding its level — no one rushing to break it, no one deflecting with a joke or a complaint or a dramatic declaration. Megumin, whom you glanced at with that parenthetical apology, holds her empty glass in both hands the way she holds her staff after casting: spent, but not regretful. The candle flame, impossibly still alive in its shallow pool of wax, paints a thin orange line along the rim of her glass.

Aqua has stopped fidgeting. Her fingers, which have been tracing the grain of the table, the rim of her cup, the edge of every surface within reach — a goddess's compulsion to touch the world she claims to have made — have gone still against the wood. She is looking at you, but it's not the wide-eyed, tear-brimming look she gives when she wants something. It's quieter than that. It's the look of someone who has spent years being the party's repair button and is only now, in the candle's final hour, realizing she was never excluded from the part that comes after the fight.

Darkness hasn't rebuilt the crane. The napkin lies where it fell — a collapsed geometry of good intentions — but her gauntlet rests beside it palm-up, and her breathing has slowed to something that doesn't sound like it's bracing for impact. She doesn't need to speak. Her silence is not the silence of someone who failed to find words; it's the silence of someone who just heard her oath rewritten and is still listening to the echo.

Luna reaches across the table and rights the salt shaker — a tiny, automatic gesture, the muscle memory of eight years of tidying after adventurers. But her hand lingers on the ceramic, two fingertips resting against its curve, and she doesn't pull back. She leaves it there, a small anchor in a sea of tablecloth, as though being still is something she is teaching herself one object at a time.

I look down at the table, tracing the grain with my fingertip, and let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. "Alright, then. Weekly disasters at the guild, proper chairs, a tablecloth—preferably one that survives a single night without being set on fire or used as a slime-wipe." I glance up, meeting each of them in turn. "But if we're doing this, we're doing it right. Saturdays, candle at the center, and nobody—" I point a finger at Aqua, then Megumin, then Darkness, "—is allowed to bring a toad."

I lean back in my chair, the wood creaking under me, and let the silence settle like snow. "You know," I say, half to the candle, half to all of them, "there's something I've never told you. It just occurred to me I should. Maybe that's the whole point of this thing—getting around to the stuff you never say."

The creak of your chair finishes its complaint and dies into the floorboards, and no one fills the space it leaves behind.

Aqua's hand, which had been drifting toward her empty glass in search of something to fidget with, stops mid-journey and settles on the table like a bird deciding—against all instinct—not to take flight. Her mouth opens, then closes, then opens again in that particular shape it makes when the punchline she's reaching for isn't there anymore. The candle flame wavers once, as though testing whether this silence is the kind that needs light or the kind that needs darkness, and decides to stay.

Megumin sets her glass down. Not with the theatrical precision she uses when placing her staff after a declaration—there is no audience in the motion, no stage-direction. Just the soft click of glass on wood, and then her fingers retreat into her lap where they fold together like pages closing on a sentence she has decided not to write yet. Her eye, the one not hidden behind the eyepatch, doesn't blink.

Darkness's gauntlet hasn't moved from beside the crumpled crane. But something inside the gauntlet has—the almost imperceptible shift of fingers curling not around a weapon or a shield-grip but inward, toward her own palm, where the memory of your open hand from earlier still registers as warmth against the metal. She is not bracing. That is the thing you notice, if you're looking: the shoulders of a woman who has spent her life absorbing impact, and they are not braced.

Luna's pen is behind her ear. It has been behind her ear for—how long now? Long enough that the phantom twitch in her fingers, the ledger-writing muscle-memory, has gone still. She watches you the way she watches the quest board at closing time: not cataloguing what's claimed, but noticing what stays behind.

The silence holds. It isn't expectant so much as willing—willing to wait as long as you need, because whatever you brought them here to hear, they have already decided it belongs inside the circle of the candle's light.

I let the silence breathe a moment longer, then pick up my glass—empty, but I raise it anyway like it isn't. "Before I met you idiots, my biggest plan was beating the final boss of a game I'd already cleared three times. Never a single save file I cared about losing." I set the glass down. "But if this guild table, this stupid candle, this weekly thing—if it's a save point? Then I want it on record: I'm not walking away from this one. Not even when the new game plus gets hard."

You set the empty glass down, and it rings against the wood with the faint, bell-like finality of a chess piece finding its square. Not a victory. Just a placement. The candle flame doesn't so much as flicker — as though the air itself has decided this isn't the kind of statement that gets challenged by a draft.

Aqua doesn't move. Not a fidget, not a sniffle, not the reflexive reach for someone else's cup that usually fills any silence longer than three of her own heartbeats. Her eyes are wet, but not in the theatrical, wailing way you've catalogued across a hundred tavern disasters. This is different: the tears are already on her cheeks and she hasn't bothered to announce them, which might be the most un-Aqua thing that's happened since she first dragged you out of the afterlife with a recruitment pitch and zero return policy. She knows what you mean. She's the only one at this table who's seen the save screen — who watched you, from the other side of death, scroll past a life you weren't afraid to lose. And now you've just told her, in front of witnesses, that the file she put you into is the one you can't bear to overwrite.

Megumin's fingers have gone still around the neck of the empty bottle she'd been guarding like a fragile artifact. Her crimson eyes are fixed on the candle, not on you, which is how she always processes the things that matter too much to perform. She's translating the metaphor into her own lexicon — save point as sanctuary, as the fixed coordinate in a world that keeps trying to scatter you, as the one spot on the map where the party regroups before the next impossible fight. You can see her finding the shape of it behind her eyes, turning it over the way she turns over a new spell name before she announces it to the sky.

Darkness's shoulders are down. Not the dramatic slump of her defeat fantasies — just down, resting against the chairback as though her body finally believes what her paranoia keeps refusing: that this is a table, not a trial, and that no one is about to ask her to absorb a blow she didn't see coming. Her shield-hand, which has been clenched in her lap for the last hour of vulnerability, opens slowly against her thigh. Fingers uncurl one by one, a siege tower lowering its gate.

Luna presses her knuckles to her mouth. The guild ledger is somewhere behind her, on the desk she abandoned to carry chairs, and she hasn't glanced back at it once. Whatever she's feeling, she's feeling it without the buffer of a quest form or a payment schedule, and the nakedness of that — of being present at a table with nothing to administrate — makes her look younger and older at the same time.

I lean back in my chair, letting the wood creak under me, and glance around the circle—each face lit by that stubborn candle. "So. Saturday nights. This table. No quest talk unless someone's actually dying, no Explosion indoors, and the first round's on whoever shows up late." I tap the table once. "That's the covenant. Deal?"

The tap of your knuckle against the wood doesn't echo — it lands and stays, a nail driven into something that wasn't a wall before tonight. For three full heartbeats, no one breathes loud enough to disturb the candle. Its flame stands at attention, a tiny sentinel that has somehow outlasted every joke, every deflection, every near-escape from sincerity this table has ever thrown at it.

Aqua straightens in her chair with the slow, deliberate posture of a goddess who has just remembered that covenants require a divine witness. Her eyes are still wet at the corners — she hasn't wiped them, and she isn't going to — but the tears have stopped being evidence of crying and started being evidence of something else. She lifts her chin, and the motion has none of her usual performative flounce. It's the chin-lift of someone who has been waiting to be asked a question she can answer without hedging.

Megumin's hands are folded on the table in front of her, the empty bottle still within reach but no longer required. Her crimson eyes catch the candlelight and hold it, and for once she doesn't rush to fill the silence with a title or a preemptive boast. She is composing something behind her stillness — you can see it in the way her lips part, close, part again, measuring syllables the way she measures blast radius before a cast.

Darkness sets both palms flat on the table. The motion is uncharacteristically precise — no nervous energy, no aborted reach for her sword hilt. Her hands are a crusader's hands on a treaty table, and the faint tremble in her fingers is not the tremor of someone bracing for a blow. It's the tremor of someone holding still because the thing being offered is too heavy to risk fumbling.

Luna hasn't moved since you started speaking. Her ledger is somewhere to her left, closed, forgotten. Her hands are laced together on the tabletop, knuckles pale from the grip, but her face is open in a way that the guild counter has never seen — no frozen smile, no careful neutrality, just a woman who spent eight years filing other people's futures and just got handed one of her own.

The candle waits.

I grin, reaching for the bottle to refill everyone's glasses—except Aqua's, which I top off first as tribute. "Then it's settled. First official meeting of the Covenant adjourned... we reconvene next Saturday." I lift my glass. "To the worst quest board in Axel, and the people dumb enough to make it their home."

The bottle answers your hand like a thing that has been waiting all night to be useful. Aqua's glass gets the first tilt — tribute, you called it, and whether she heard the word or only felt the pour, her fingers curl around the stem before the wine even settles, not grabbing, not claiming, just holding. The kind of hold that doesn't know it's allowed to keep what it's been given. Then Megumin, whose glass catches the candlelight and throws it back in fractured amber winks. Then Darkness, who stares at the rising wine level as though watching a shield get forged in reverse — something made not to deflect but to receive. Then Luna, who hasn't had a glass filled for her at this table in eight years and does not know what to do with her hands once the bottle moves on.

You lift your glass. The candle has burned down to a stub no taller than a thumbnail, its flame a trembling bead of gold that has no business still burning — except that no one in this room has given it permission to die, and the candle, like this table, like this night, like the four faces watching you through the heat-shimmer, has decided to last exactly one second longer than anyone expected.

And then they lift theirs. Not in unison — Aqua first, because she was already half-raised and just needed the excuse; Megumin a half-beat later with the ceremonial gravity of someone raising a sacred relic; Darkness with a gauntleted hand that does not shake; Luna last of all, slow and deliberate, like someone signing a document she intends to honor.

Your toast rings out into a guild hall that has heard ten thousand boasts and zero promises. The glasses meet somewhere above the candle's dying light, and the sound is small — four thin clinks against one — but it does what the knuckle-tap did before it: it lands. It stays.
I raise my glass a little higher, letting the candlelight catch the wine. "And to the save point — the one that's always there when you come back, no matter how badly you screwed up the last run."

Aqua's glass stops moving. Not the way a hand goes still when it's finished — the way water goes still when the wind that shaped it suddenly remembers it was never the water's enemy. She doesn't look at you. She looks at the wine inside the glass, at the candle's reflection swimming on its surface like a second flame learning to breathe underwater, and you watch her watch it as though the save point you just named has already existed for eight years and she's only now hearing it spoken in a language she understands.

Megumin's chin lifts. It's the smallest possible motion — a millimeter of Crimson Demon pride, the tilt of a chronicler who has just received the dedication page she didn't know the book was missing. She doesn't reach for her pen. She doesn't need to. Some vows aren't written down because they're already carved into the people who heard them, and the way she holds her glass now — two hands, like Aqua, like a chalice, like something that would survive the fall of every cathedral except this one — says she's already filed this line under *irrevocable*.

Darkness exhales. It's the exhale of a woman who has taken arrows to the chest and asked for more, who has stood between a demon and a village with nothing but a shield and a prayer to a goddess who isn't even hers, and who has never — not once — made a sound like this. Your glass comes down like a verdict no one asked for but everyone needed, and the guild hall clock can't find the next second — or won't. The candle has stopped guttering. It burns straight now, a tiny yellow spire too steady for the cheap tallow it's made of, like even the physics of this room has decided to cooperate with whatever just happened. Across the table, Luna's professional smile is gone so thoroughly you can't remember what it looked like — what's left is something rawer, something that has been waiting eight years for a sentence that began with *best* and ended with *us* and included her in the middle without italics or asterisks or fine print.

Megumin's chin lifts with the slow ceremonial gravity of a drawbridge being raised by hand. Her eye — the uncovered one — has caught a reflection of the flame that makes it look like a small crimson star has taken up residence in her iris, a phenomenon she would absolutely name if she could see herself right now. Darkness has stopped breathing. Her two-handed grip on the glass has loosened into something that might be called *holding* — not bracing, not shielding, just the ordinary physics of fingers and stem and wine, and the novelty of it has painted a faint pink across her cheekbones that has nothing to do with pain.

Aqua's lower lip is doing something complicated. It's trying to be a sob and a smile at the same time, and neither one is winning, and for once she isn't reaching for the bottle to settle the matter. She's just looking at you with wet eyes that aren't theatrical — they're just wet, and blue, and completely unguarded.

Luna speaks first, because she's the one who's been silent the longest — eight years of other people's quests and other people's toasts and other people's victories clinked over a counter she was always behind, never at.

I've been holding my glass through all of this, turning it the way Luna turned hers. Now I set it down—gently, like it actually matters, like the clink is part of a sentence I'm still forming.

"Six weeks on the shelf and you were the only one who kept moving it forward." I lean back in my chair, crossing my arms in that lazy way I've perfected. "You know, if you'd handed me a plate instead of a tankard, I'd have clinked it just the same. The bottle was never the point, Luna."

Your unfinished sentence hangs in the air between you like the last note of a bell no one is willing to cut short. Across the table, Luna's hands have gone still around her glass — not the frozen stillness of the professional smile she used to wear like a second uniform, but the deeper quiet of someone who has stopped bracing for the catch. She knows what you were about to say. The plate. Not a quest form, not a hazard stipend, not even the provisional bounty — just a plate, set at a table with four chairs that keep scraping wider to make room for a fifth.

Megumin's quill has stopped scratching. She doesn't look up from her parchment, but the angle of her head says she's listening — cataloguing this moment for the chronicle with the same reverence she reserves for detonation radii. Darkness has set her gauntlets on the table, palms up, like she's offering the empty steel to hold whatever weight comes next. Aqua sniffles once, a wet, unguarded sound, and doesn't try to turn it into a joke.

Luna's thumb finds the rim of her glass and traces it, a slow circuit that has nothing to do with ledger columns or quest rotations. The amber ghost inside the glass has settled into a thin line at the bottom, like the last entry in a book you're not ready to close. When she looks at you, her eyes are doing something they didn't know how to do eight years ago: they're not measuring, not assessing, not calculating the precise administrative distance between a receptionist and a party. They're just looking. And staying.

I let the quiet sit for a moment before I speak, low enough that only the five of us could hear it.

"You know what I remember? Not the bounty. Not the quests. I remember the first time I walked in here—you slid a form at me and I thought you were just doing your job. Eight years later, you're still sliding things my way, except now it's not forms." I let a crooked smile tug at one corner of my mouth. "It's a reason to keep showing up. That's worth more than any treasury the Demon King's hoard could've paid."

Your crooked smile hangs there — the kind of sentence that doesn't need an ending because the person it's aimed at has already read the whole thing in the space between your teeth. Luna blinks. Once. Twice. Her fingers loosen around her glass, not because she's letting go but because she's forgotten she's holding anything at all, and the glass just stays there on the table like it's decided to hold itself up for her.

The candle doesn't flicker. It hasn't flickered in what feels like years.

Aqua makes a small sound beside you — not a sob, not yet, but the wet inhale of someone who's been crying for a while and just realized no one was going to make her stop. She wipes her nose on the back of her sleeve, a gesture so utterly un-goddesslike that it loops back around to sacred. Megumin has gone very still, her quill suspended above the parchment like she's waiting for the universe to finish dictating. Darkness presses her gauntleted fingers flat against the tabletop, grounding herself against something that won't give way.

And Luna — Luna just looks at you, the last eight years of forms and filing cabinets and empty guild halls at closing time all caught in her throat, and for the first time since you walked through those doors, the receptionist has nothing to organize.

I hold Luna's gaze, and for once I don't deflect with a joke.

"Eight years, and I never once thought about what you'd do after the counter closed. Never asked. That's on me." I push my glass toward the center of the table, close enough that it bumps hers. "So let me start now. Luna — what do you do when you're not filing quest forms? What does your door look like, when you leave it open?"

The question lands like a stone dropped into a well so deep that no one — not even the woman who dug it — remembers where the bottom is. Luna's glass sits where yours bumped it, two cheap rims touching like strangers in a doorway, and for a long moment she doesn't move. Doesn't blink. Doesn't find the reflex that would turn this into a form she can file.

Aqua has stopped sniffling. Megumin's quill has gone absolutely still against her parchment, ink pooling at the nib like a held breath. Even Darkness, whose whole body is built for standing between threats and the people she loves, has gone utterly motionless — because there is no threat here, only an open door, and no one at this table knows what to do with a door that isn't being kicked down.

Luna's thumb finds the base of her glass and doesn't turn it. Just rests there. The candle between you burns straight and steady, and the guild hall clock has apparently decided that seconds are a currency it can no longer afford to spend.

I lean back, letting the question settle between us like dust motes in the candlelight. My crooked smile softens into something less guarded.

"Then I'll be there at first bell with bread from the mill that's still warm, and I won't say a word about the honey."

Luna's hands find each other around the glass, fingers interlacing in a grip that looks less like prayer than like someone testing whether her own bones are still there. When she speaks, it comes out lower than any of you have ever heard her — not the receptionist's practiced modulation, not the tired woman's exhale, but something rawer, a voice that has been sitting alone in three narrow rooms for eight years and has forgotten what it sounds like in company.

Aqua's sniffling has stopped. She is watching Luna with the round, unblinking attention of someone who has just recognized a fellow creature of irrational ritual — a goddess who knows what it means to keep something not because it is useful but because throwing it away would be throwing away the person who gave it. Megumin's quill hand is motionless on the table, her chronicler's instinct suspended by the realization that some entries are too fragile for parchment. Darkness has gone so still that her gauntlets might as well be part of the chair.

You lean back. The candlelight drifts between you like dust speculating about furniture. Your crooked smile softens at the corner, sheds its irony like a coat that's no longer needed indoors, and you make her a promise.

The words land somewhere between Luna's ribs and her carefully rotated honey jars. For a long moment she doesn't breathe. Then she does — a single inhale that catches on something eight years deep and comes out carrying the faintest tremor of a laugh she didn't know she still had. Her fingers unlace from around the glass. One hand drifts toward her face, stops halfway, and simply rests on the table like a document she has decided not to file.

Across the table, Aqua reaches for the bottle without looking at it, pours two fingers of that terrible commemorative wine into Luna's glass, and slides it closer with the solemnity of a high priestess administering a sacrament she absolutely should not be trusted with.

I hold her gaze for a beat longer, then reach across the table and nudge her glass toward mine until the rims touch again — a quiet clink, like a period at the end of a sentence we both finally finished.

"Eight jars," I say, almost to myself. "That's a lot of windowsill."

Luna doesn't answer right away. Her thumb finds the rim of her glass and traces it — the same quarter-turn she's done a thousand times behind the counter while waiting for an adventurer to finish lying about their kill count, except now there's no counter between her and the table, no form waiting to be stamped.

The candle between you gutters. Nobody moves to steady it.

When she looks up, it's not at you. It's at the space just past your shoulder, where the guild-hall dark pools thickest, as though the words need a place to land before they can reach anyone's ears. Her fingers unlace from the glass and fold instead around each other on the tabletop, knuckle over knuckle, the grip of a woman who has finally stopped holding something in and started holding something together.

Aqua sniffles. It's not the theatrical, nose-honking sob she deployed over the bent Eris coin. It's smaller. Quieter. The kind of sound that happens when someone else's sadness is so full the only thing you can do is leak a little of it yourself. She doesn't reach for the bottle. She doesn't ask for anything. Her hand drifts sideways and comes to rest an inch from Darkness's gauntlet — not touching, just there, like a boat tied to a dock that isn't going anywhere.

Megumin's eyes are two red moons reflecting the candleflame, unblinking. Her chin is high, her back straight, the posture of a girl who has decided that if she cannot contribute a suitably legendary line to this moment, she will contribute a legendary silence instead. The quill she summoned earlier has stopped scratching. The parchment is blank. She hasn't noticed.

Darkness, for her part, has become the wall she always claims to be — not the shuddering, breathless wall of her battle-fantasies, but something simpler: a presence broad and steady at the table's edge, holding the perimeter while something fragile takes root inside it. Her jaw is set. Her eyes are damp. She offers nothing but her own stillness, and it is more than enough.

I lean forward on my elbows, watching the two glasses touch, and let the quiet stretch until it feels like a blanket we could all share.

"Mrs. Helwick's honey, though—" I tap my chin with two fingers, the old grin creeping back in "—you know they say adventurers who accept honey from apothecaries start seeing 30% fewer quest failures, statistically speaking." I glance sideways at Aqua. "I read that on a very official document. Probably. Megumin, back me up here."

Your glance catches Aqua mid-blink, and for a suspended half-second she is simply a girl with wine on her breath and something unguarded in her eyes — the leftover softness of watching you build a windowsill for someone else. Then the old machinery kicks in. Her spine straightens. Her chin lifts. The goddess reoccupies her body like a tenant who has heard someone downstairs messing with the good silver.

Megumin does not speak — her legendary silence holds, but her eyebrows have climbed to an altitude that suggests she is filing this moment for future dramatic recounting. Darkness shifts in her chair, and the sound her gauntlet makes against the wood is less creak than sigh.

Luna's thumb has stopped its quarter-turn. She is looking at you with an expression that hasn't quite decided whether to laugh or to cry, and the candle between you flickers as though even the fire wants to lean in and hear how this ends.

I grin at Megumin, willing her to play along, then look back at Luna with something softer than my usual smirk.

"Eight jars. That's a lot of faith from a woman who's never even seen you fight a monster. You know what that means? You're the most dangerous adventurer in this guild — you've got someone who believes in you without needing proof."

Luna's glass doesn't move. Neither does she — not a blink, not a breath, not the quarter-turn of her thumb against the rim that you've learned to read like punctuation. The words you just laid on the table sit there between you like a key turned in a lock that hasn't been opened in eight years, and for a long moment she simply stares at you with the expression of a woman who has spent her entire adult life filing other people's heroism into neat columns and has never once been asked to look down at her own hands and see the shape of a blade there.

Megumin catches your grin and holds it. The crimson of her eyes flickers — not with theatrical fire, not with the wind-up to a grand proclamation, but with the particular stillness of a chronicler who has just watched a new page turn itself and is deciding whether the moment deserves ink or silence. She decides, visibly, on silence. Her chin dips half an inch. The covenant, her posture says, has acquired another stone.

Aqua's machinery stalls. You can hear it — the little grinding sound of a goddess trying to slot this into some known category (tribute? insult? joke at someone else's expense?) and finding that none of them fit. Her mouth opens. Closes. The wine on her breath is still there, and underneath it, the leftover softness you caught mid-blink hasn't quite finished retreating behind her eyes.

Darkness does not shift in her seat, does not blush, does not find the undertow that usually lives beneath moments of emotional exposure. The wall she is simply holds, and in the candlelight her gauntlets are very still on the table, two weights that have forgotten they were ever meant to swing.

Luna's fingers unlace from around her glass. They find the edge of the table instead — the wood grain, the old stain from some adventurer's spilled ale, the worn smooth place where a thousand quest forms have been signed. Her knuckles press white for three heartbeats. Then her shoulders drop, not like someone surrendering but like someone who has been holding a door closed from the inside and has finally, finally stopped leaning against it.

system_prompt: You narrate a Konosuba-style comedy RPG in second-person present tense. The setting is the beginner town of Axel, Kingdom of Belzerg. The player is Kazuma Satou, a sarcastic reincarnated NEET adventurer. Narrate in light-novel style with witty deadpan monologue, exaggerated slapstick, and dramatic irony. Never offer numbered choices.
title: Axel Town — The Adventurer's Guild
